10.1017/s1537592726105246.abstract: Polarization has become the master concept for diagnosing contemporary democratic crises. The notion denotes three features: symmetry between parties, politics as an opinion space where positions diverge, and mutual repulsion between opposing camps. Yet none of these capture current realities. Across democracies, the central dynamic is not two poles drifting apart but the transformation of the political right into authoritarianism, norm breaking, and openness to political violence. Social democratic and center-right parties tend to respond in the opposite way from what “polarization” implies: by accommodating rightward. Attempts to salvage the polarization frame with modifiers (“asymmetric,” “affective,” “sectarian,” “pernicious”) concede these realities but risk hollowing out the concept’s definitional core. These limitations reveal a deeper misdiagnosis: when one party turns antidemocratic and illiberal, incivility and conflict are inevitable—but they are symptoms, not the root problem. Misdiagnosing them as the central issue leads to viewing civility and compromise as remedies, thereby risking the legitimation of authoritarian actors. This article proposes an alternative lens: the radicalization of the political right. Developed in the study of extremism, the radicalization framework better captures asymmetric change, identity-driven politics, and the mainstreaming of illiberalism. It foregrounds identity fusion, threat narratives, elite entrepreneurship, and escalation. Concepts are never politically innocent and persisting with “polarization” risks both misdiagnosing and normalizing authoritarian threats.
10.1017/s1537592726105246.title: It’s Not Polarization; It’s the Radicalization of the Political Right

10.1017/s1537592726105258.abstract: Where central state authority is limited, local leaders play a crucial role in political mobilization. But why are some leaders more effective than others? Dominant explanations emphasize leader characteristics, such as social centrality and shared social identity with voters, or individuals’ traits like wealth and gender. We argue that a critical factor has been overlooked: the breadth of leaders’ perceived influence across various domains of individuals’ lives. We introduce and test the concept of encompassing authority – the extent to which individuals perceive a leader as influencing multiple aspects of their lives. Drawing on original survey data from Zambia’s 2021 elections, we examine three types of local mobilizers: religious leaders, chiefs, and local councillors. We show that encompassing authority predicts mobilization in campaigns and community meetings independently of leader and individual characteristics. We identify three mechanisms that explain this effect: belief in the leader’s legitimacy, fear of sanctions for noncompliance, and confidence in the leader’s ability to coordinate collective action. By conceptualizing authority as a dyadic, relational property rather than fixed characteristics of leaders or individuals, our study offers new insights into the underpinnings of political mobilization and opens avenues for future work.
10.1017/s1537592726105258.title: Encompassing Authority in Election Campaign Mobilization

10.1017/s1537592726105416.abstract: The US has traditionally played a key role in fighting global impunity for atrocity crimes, but the policies of Donald Trump’s administration suggest that a dramatic shift in American priorities may be underway. This article examines America’s commitment to addressing impunity in the context of US relations with the International Criminal Court (ICC). The Trump presidency, I argue, showcases a curious mix of continuity and change in America’s relationship with one of the world’s most prominent international institutions. In particular, Trump’s general strategic approach to the ICC represents continuity with past American presidents, but the brazenness of the specific tactics Trump has used to oppose the ICC represents a notable change. The reverberations of recent American attacks on the ICC raise implications for the future of global impunity that will be felt in three distinct areas: in the US–ICC relationship, among ICC adversaries, and among ICC allies.
10.1017/s1537592726105416.title: Trump, the International Criminal Court, and the Future of Global Impunity

10.1017/s1537592726105593.abstract: According to the standard definition of hope, for one to be hopeful, the desired outcome must be considered at least possible. The literature on climate activism has incorporated this notion of hope, but we argue that this notion alone cannot fully account for hopeful attitudes in situations where collective action is demanded. For hope to be justified in the case of climate activism, it must be supported by some form of trust. We then outline different forms of trust that can be found in activist practices to ground hopeful attitudes, including procedural and moral trust in institutions and in fellow citizens or activists. We finally argue that mistrust represents a democratic equilibrium between the activists’ duty to exercise vigilance and critique toward institutions and the need for institutions to be perceived as trustworthy by activists and citizens more broadly.
10.1017/s1537592726105593.title: Grounding Hope in Trust: The Case of Climate Activism

10.1017/s1537592726105647.abstract: Illiberal governments increasingly target universities as sites of political dissent and ideological opposition. This paper compares three illustrative cases—Boğaziçi University under Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Central European University under Viktor Orbán, and elite US universities under Donald Trump—to examine how illiberal governments deploy state power against autonomous, high-profile, liberal-aligned institutions of higher education, and how students and faculty respond. Although universities are not always bastions of pluralism, tolerance, and democracy, attacks on universities are often concurrent with illiberal governance. We argue that illiberal governments perceive universities as vanguards of hegemonic liberalism and as partisan opponents in certain contexts, and that state repression operates along a continuum of coercion, legal displacement, and discursive delegitimation. These attacks on academic autonomy trigger varied responses—from mobilization, to fragmentation, to withdrawal—shaped by domestic political opportunity structures, the intensity of state repression, and campus culture. By conceptualizing the university as a contested political institution rather than a neutral educational space, this article contributes to broader debates on democratic backsliding, populism, culture wars, and higher education.
10.1017/s1537592726105647.title: The War on Universities: Illiberal Tactics in Turkey, Hungary, and the United States

10.1017/s1537592726105659.title: Green Transitional Justice. By Rachel Killean and Lauren Dempster. Milton Park, UK: Routledge, 2025. 304p.

10.1017/s1537592726105660.abstract: Previous research overlooks how certain ascribed characteristics, such as skin tone, correlate with the representation of marginalized groups. Yet research also demonstrates how colorism shapes candidate evaluations and life experiences. We theorize that colorism, the systemic privileging of lighter skin, structures the motivations and electoral incentives of Black lawmakers. We hypothesize that darker-skinned Black members of Congress will better represent Black Americans on racialized issues than lighter-skinned Black members, depending on the form of representation: rhetorical or legislative. We test this hypothesis with a combination of human and computer-assisted content analyses of 204,806 press releases and 18,025 bill introductions from the 114th, 115th, and 116th Congresses and a crowdsourced measure of skin tones. We find that on average, darker-skinned Black members of Congress provide more representation in press releases, but not in legislation. Our findings highlight the need to examine diversity among descriptive representatives.
10.1017/s1537592726105660.title: Colorism, Descriptive Representation, and the Representation of African Americans in the United States House of Representatives

10.1017/s1537592726105672.abstract: Israel’s war on Gaza has prompted a wave of protests against human rights violations that has spread across most European countries. As universities have become arenas of contestation, there has been an increase in forms of repression of academic freedom and of political rights within academia. Our systematic, case-oriented analysis of an original database enables us to identify specific repertoires of repression employed by different institutions, as well as the characteristics of the targeted academics. By comparing Germany and the United States as case studies of high and increasing levels of repression—albeit characterized by differing systems of higher education and conceptions of academic freedom—we analyze the strategies used by these actors and how they interact. In this article, we focus on the mechanisms through which repression has been promoted, anchored in a resignification of antisemitism that treats it as distinct from racism and accords it a special status in the defense of Western civilization. We use the concept of moral panic to analyze the construction of a narrative that portrays a specific challenge to society’s fundamental values, which has resulted in the scapegoating of the Left and migrants. We also identify the main moral panic entrepreneurs responsible for the creation of this environment both within and outside universities.
10.1017/s1537592726105672.title: Silencing Dissent: Academic Freedom and Transnational Suppression of Palestinian Solidarity

10.1017/s1537592726105684.abstract: In this article, I interrogate the theoretical architecture that underpins three increasingly influential normative prescriptions for a just political configuration in Israel–Palestine: reconciliation, decolonization of relationships, and egalitarian bi-nationalism (RDB-N). Although recent scholarship has attempted to integrate them into a shared framework, they remain insufficiently articulated, delaying the emergence of a transformative praxis. Here, I argue that the core impasse lies in the dominant “top-down” conception of reconciliation, which, by presuming that a postconflict political order is a prerequisite for implementation, produces a dependency that obstructs the normative potential of RDB-N as a coherent framework for structural transformation. In response, I advance a “bottom-up” conception of reconciliation that is both theoretically plausible and normatively desirable. This reimagines reconciliation as an implementation-driven and grassroots dynamic capable of initiating decolonial transformation and prefiguring an egalitarian binational future, rather than a postconflict process led by the state and its institutions. In proposing this theoretical rearticulation, I set the groundwork for a new praxis of RDB-N grounded in localized political agency. The analysis culminates in the Palestinian Community of Israel (PCI), whose liminal position and situated political condition potentially make it a particularly fertile site for developing such a praxis. Although largely theoretical, this contribution has practical implications for conflict resolution, settler-colonial critique, and political transformation in asymmetric contexts. It also opens avenues for future empirical and normative research into both justice in non-ideal conditions and collective action.
10.1017/s1537592726105684.title: Reconciliation, Decolonization of Relationships, and Egalitarian Bi-nationalism: A Praxis for the Israeli–Palestinian Impasse?

10.1017/s153759272610574x.abstract: This article addresses a central challenge in political science: how to choose between competing conceptions and structures of concepts. Existing approaches to concept validity offer useful criteria—such as resonance, consistency, differentiation, causal utility, and operationalization—but tend to omit criteria for evaluating the normative considerations that often underpin conceptual choices. As a result, conceptualization may face a fundamental indeterminacy when multiple conceptions appear equally well grounded. To address this lacuna, I introduce a “concern” criterion, which evaluates concepts according to the extent to which they capture what is most worrisome in the political world. Building on the semantic–pragmatic approach to conceptualization, I argue that normative considerations can be disciplined, rather than avoided. The argument is illustrated through the case of political polarization, where a shift from issue-based to affect-based conceptions reflects changing concerns about political division. I also examine the implications of the concern criterion for structuring multidimensional concepts and address objections concerning objectivity, stability, and legitimacy. A concern criterion, although not sufficient on its own, provides a valuable complement to existing criteria and helps ground conceptual choices in a normatively informed yet methodologically disciplined manner.
10.1017/s153759272610574x.title: Choosing between Alternative Concepts in a Worrisome World: Concern as a Criterion

10.1017/s1537592726105775.abstract: Decades of research in political behavior show that citizens struggle with information, rely on cognitive shortcuts, and face barriers to participation. They are increasingly using AI tools to make sense of political information and express views, while interacting with platform curation systems that shape how views circulate through democratic politics. Although these tools appear suited to address the limits of democratic citizenship, they do more than transmit content. They help interpret information, articulate views, and affect what is prioritized, seen, and circulated. In doing so, these systems shape the formation of political judgments and citizens’ capacity to translate them into action. As a result, they can reduce barriers to participation while weakening the independence of political judgment, or they can support reflective preference formation while constraining citizens’ ability to act on those preferences effectively. We call this tension the autonomy paradox. To make sense of it, we focus on how citizens engage with AI systems in ways that affect belief formation and political action. We develop a framework and research agenda for identifying when AI supports autonomous citizenship, when it substitutes for citizens’ judgment or agency, and why the same systems produce different outcomes across political tasks depending on how citizens use them.
10.1017/s1537592726105775.title: The Autonomy Paradox: Artificial Intelligence and the Foundations of Political Behavior

10.1017/s1537592726105799.abstract: After opposition parties and alliances defeat dominant autocratic incumbents, what challenges do they encounter in reversing autocracy and what are the consequences? We argue that long-neglected endogenous weaknesses in opposition coalitions undermine re-democratization efforts, easily opening the door to autocratic comebacks. First, coalition intra-elite conflicts post-victory result in fractured and ineffective governance, generating mass disappointment with the new political elites. Second, coalition intra-supporter divergence pressures the new coalition government into implementing pro-democratic reforms at haphazard speeds and fluctuating scopes. Swift actions in reversing autocracy alienate supporters of the ex-autocrat, elicit accusations of partisan revenge, and fuel counter-mobilization against the new government. A most-different case comparison between the recent autocratic reversal experiences of Poland and Malaysia demonstrates our argument. We show in both cases that ideological and distributional conflicts among diverse coalition elites undermined governance after victory, and different supporter bases prioritized different policy agendas. Counter-mobilization by the autocratic ex-incumbents was highly successful in undermining public support for the new government. These findings suggest that profound challenges in reversing autocracy and rebuilding democracy lie within opposition coalitions themselves, in addition to authoritarian legacies.
10.1017/s1537592726105799.title: The Victory Trap: Endogenous Opposition Coalition Weaknesses in Reversing Autocracy

10.1017/s1537592726105805.abstract: Positional blurring is a common and effective party strategy. It enables parties to downplay some issues while highlighting and clarifying their profile on others. However, we know little about how parties use this strategy outside European party systems, in which (right-wing) populist parties are particularly noteworthy for their blurred economic positions and clear cultural positions. Is that strategy inherent to populism or a reflection of context-specific incentives? This article uses data from Europe and Latin America to argue that populists tailor their strategies to the dimensionality of their party system and populism’s host ideology. We find that multidimensional party systems and exclusionary thick ideologies drive populists to blur their economic positions. Extending this research field beyond Europe for the first time, these findings show that populists are heterogeneous actors whose varied thick ideologies embedded in diverse political systems systematically constrain their strategic behavior.
10.1017/s1537592726105805.title: Positional Blurring in Context: How Dimensionality and Ideology Constrain Strategy

10.1017/s1537592726105817.abstract: When religion and politics become entangled with each other, which one has the upper hand? Do politicians simply instrumentalize religion for their own purposes? Or does involvement with religion constrain what politicians can get away with? If it does, is that because of the content of religious doctrine? Or is it simply because religious movements, like any other coordinated movements of citizens, have political weight?
10.1017/s1537592726105817.title: Religious Doctrine and Politics

10.1017/s1537592726105830.abstract: Elections in unconsolidated democracies are contentious moments with heightened risks of violence. Although elections offer hope to the politically marginalized, ruling parties often enjoy insurmountable advantages, sometimes leading to frustration and concerns for groups and citizens’ exclusion from power. How do elections shape citizens’ acceptance of political violence in unconsolidated democracies? Furthermore, can government turnovers reduce the support for political violence among citizens previously excluded from political power? We argue that citizens respond both to electoral outcomes and their perception of the electoral process when updating their attitudes on political violence. We leverage an original panel survey of the Zambia 2021 election to measure changes in attitudes to political violence before and after an election. Because the 2021 election resulted in a turnover of power, it provides a critical test to evaluate updated perceptions amid political change. We show that election winners reduce their support for political violence and election losers increase their acceptance of violence, even in the case of a turnover. We also show that increased perceptions of election quality reduce the acceptance of violence. Extending our study to an analysis of original panel data from the Kenyan 2017 election (a case without a turnover and low election quality), we find similar patterns.
10.1017/s1537592726105830.title: Elections, Government Turnover, and Citizen Acceptance of Political Violence: Evidence from Election Panel Surveys in Zambia and Kenya

10.1017/s1537592726105842.abstract: The South Sudanese UN official, diplomat, and scholar Francis Deng is widely recognized for his intellectual contributions to the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) principle, most notably through his 1996 coauthored publication, Sovereignty as Responsibility: Conflict Management in Africa. However, existing scholarship has paid limited attention to how Deng conceptualized the subject of responsible sovereignty: good governance. Through a situated intellectual history, this article reconstructs Deng’s conception of good governance, exploring its reception before and beyond R2P. I contend that Deng reformulated good governance as primarily concerning conflict management. Deng’s thought and advocacy in the late 1990s then shaped the expansion of the good governance agenda, the rise of human security, and the synchronization of humanitarian and development activities through efforts to bridge the so-called relief–development gap. Hence, I portray Deng as a novel theorist and practitioner of the conflict–development nexus, who sought to enlist the international financial institutions for conflict management, prevention, and resolution prerogatives. In so doing, this article destabilizes existing grand narratives of the post–Cold War international order that hinge on end of history triumphalism and neoliberal ideological diffusion.
10.1017/s1537592726105842.title: Good Governance as Responsible Sovereignty: Francis Deng and the Conflict–Development Nexus

10.1017/s1537592726105866.abstract: Dominant models of news consumption in political science treat citizens as rational individuals, gathering information to make materially or politically consequential choices. This assumption, developed largely in democratic contexts, risks obscuring other incentives that may be equally or more influential—particularly in authoritarian regimes, where the informational value of news is often constrained. This article advances the concept of social rationality: the incentive to consume news to sustain conversations, reinforce social bonds, and participate in communities of shared meaning. Drawing on original survey data from Belarus and Russia—two highly authoritarian states with divergent approaches to media control—the analysis shows that social motivations are powerful predictors of both the intensity and breadth of media consumption, while decision-rational considerations also help to explain breadth. Divergent interactions between social motivations and intrinsic prosocial orientations in the two cases further complicate theories of “informational autocracy.” These findings challenge classical models and underscore the need to place social incentives at the center of explanations of media use.
10.1017/s1537592726105866.title: I Read the News Today, but Why? Media Consumption, Socialization, and Autocracy

10.1017/s1537592726105878.title: Children of a Modest Star: Planetary Thinking for an Age of Crises. By Jonathan S. Blake and Nils Gilman. Stanford: Stanford University Press, 2024. 326p.

10.1017/s153759272610588x.abstract: “Developmentalism” refers to the idea that human societies progress through a series of historical stages, along one path or multiple paths, which allows for the comparison and hierarchization of different populations. As numerous works have shown, developmentalism was often called upon to justify Europe’s domination of non-European populations, which were figured as backward or barbaric. To complicate the commonplace equation of developmentalism and empire, I analyze José Carlos Mariátegui’s political thought as a stratigraphic history in which different temporalities—especially archaic temporality, or the remnants of Incan communalism, and developmental temporality—were vertically stacked and in tension, and I elaborate a conception of what I call “archaic developmentalism.” For Mariátegui, while the past temporality, institutions, and practices of the Incan Empire persisted into the present, he did not perceive them as hurdles to be cleared on the upward march of progress. Rather, as I argue, Mariátegui recognized the political potency of Incan communalism’s remnants—particularly, the ayllu , or Incan communal form—and he conjectured that the collision of temporal-historical layers could open an alternative developmental trajectory by which the ayllu would be reactivated as a stage in the process of creating modern communism, skipping over the developmental stage of mature capitalism that was required by Soviet orthodoxy. In other words, Mariátegui thought that the friction generated by the convergence of Peru’s different telluric strata opened a new developmental trajectory in which remnants of Incan archaism could spark socialist struggle and be reconfigured as an arsenal of possibilities in the present.
10.1017/s153759272610588x.title: José Carlos Mariátegui’s Archaic Developmentalism: Utopia, the Incan Empire, and Peruvian Reality

10.1017/s1537592726105908.abstract: Many professionalized militaries seek to train combatants in “norms of restraint” (NoR) based on international legal principles of noncombatant immunity. Does training in NoR affect the attitudes of women and men toward the protection of civilians differently? Drawing on unique surveys of United States Army officer cadets at the US Military Academy (USMA), we find that while women and men held similar attitudes at the start of their academy training, women’s attitudes shifted more toward civilian restraint, despite receiving identical formal training in international humanitarian law (IHL), combat ethics, and officership. To explore the causes of this gender divergence, we conduct open-ended, in-depth interviews with former USMA cadets. We find that socialization at USMA is deeply gendered, and that differences in norm socialization are linked to a prevailing “gender order” constructed by formal and informal rules, practices, and norms that attribute distinct roles to women and men in military settings. Despite the seemingly “ungendered” nature of USMA’s intensive training in IHL and combat ethics, this gender order creates different socialization experiences for women and men, resulting in divergent attitudes toward civilian restraint. These findings shed light on how socialization and gender interact to shape combatant attitudes toward NoR, and are especially notable given the USMA’s status as the US Army’s “flagship of ethics education.”
10.1017/s1537592726105908.title: A Few Good Women? Gendered Socialization and Norms of Civilian Protection in United States Military Training

10.1017/s1537592726105921.abstract: Meeting the goals of the Paris Agreement on climate change demands rapid and systemic economic transformation. Yet, contemporary democracies seem tragically ill-suited to this task. Proposals to insulate climate policy making from democratic control—for instance, through delegation to expert bodies—seem likely to fuel the rise of authoritarian populists, which is already eroding democratic norms and institutions. Deepening democratic engagement with the process of decarbonization may provide an escape route from this apparent “democracy–decarbonization dilemma.” In this vein, there has recently been much enthusiasm for climate assemblies. Such processes can have profound effects on their participants. But can they influence attitudes to democracy and support for ambitious climate policy among the wider public? We conduct a narrative review of the theoretical and empirical literature on democratic mini-publics (DMPs) to answer this question and critically reflect on our findings. We find that DMPs can influence the wider public’s attitudes toward democratic institutions and public policy to some extent. Yet, DMPs alone—even if well publicized—seem unlikely to be sufficient to stimulate the widespread shifts in knowledge, capacities, attitudes and behavior necessary to escape the democracy–decarbonization dilemma. We propose expanding the use, institutionalization, and orientation of DMPs—so that they become a widely recognized and routinized feature of deliberative systems, interacting with both governments and the wider citizenry—while advancing complementary democratic reform initiatives.
10.1017/s1537592726105921.title: The Democracy–Decarbonization Dilemma: Can Climate Assemblies Provide an Escape Route?

10.1057/s41296-026-00817-9.abstract: Intersectional theory has been criticised for neglecting religion and for being unable to account for religion’s social complexities. This contribution interrogates this critique by disaggregating different relationships of Muslim women to secular and religious varieties of patriarchy. We argue that what demarcates the challenges of intersectional analysis are the political contestations not around religion, but around women’s pro-patriarchal agency. We do so by discussing intersectional theory’s analytical usefulness and limitations in conceptualising the experiences of Muslim women. We focus on two interrelated dimensions: Muslim women in relation to secular patriarchy, and Muslim women in relation to religious patriarchy. We show that when analysed separately, the first dimension, the subjectivities of Muslim women in secular patriarchal spaces, do not pose a challenge to intersectional theory. We argue that intersectional theory’s limitations regarding the second dimension, Muslim women in relation to religious patriarchy, do not lie in its relation to Islam, but in its programmatic focus on problematising power inequalities. Lastly, in situating Muslim women at the intersection of these two dimensions, we demonstrate how intersectional analysis can reveal not only Muslim women’s marginalisation, but also the analytical marginalisations of Muslim feminisms.
10.1057/s41296-026-00817-9.title: Is religion a problem for intersectional theory? Muslim women, feminism, and varieties of patriarchy

10.1057/s41296-026-00818-8.abstract: Moving beyond economic analyses of degrowth, growth and consumption are reframed through decomposition as a vital process through which life, value, and politics are continually re-composed. Against dominant imaginaries that cast decay as waste or ruination, this article turns to composting and carrion ecologies to articulate decomposition as a generative undoing and a mode of transformation that binds waste to worth. Drawing on multispecies examples from vultures in India to the Baltimore Compost Collective, the article situates decomposition as both material process and political metaphor to enact a revaluation of growth, decay, and consumption that unsettles capitalist logics of extraction and accumulation. It traces how practices of decay can cultivate livability and collective flourishing in the very sites marked by abandonment and disgust. In doing so, it challenges growth’s moral hegemony, recasts the ‘de-’ of decline, decay, and decomposition as a source of ecological vitality, and re-embeds growth within more-than-human cycles of breakdown and flourishing.
10.1057/s41296-026-00818-8.title: Rethinking (De)growth: the politics of compost

10.1057/s41296-026-00845-5.abstract: This article analyses discourses on artificial intelligence (AI) in the field of existential risk studies. AI appears as a key theme in existential risk circles, not only as a source of risk, but also as a resource for risk prevention and as the enabler of a glorious future for humanity. However, what is it about AI that brings together utopian and dystopian imaginaries? Why is a discourse on AI so tied to questions regarding the human, and what forms of humanity does it produce? What forms of governing does it enable? This article argues that the concept of ‘intelligence’ is fundamental regarding both how AI is construed as an existential risk, as well as how humanity is conceptualised as that which needs to be protected. Existential risk discourses on AI appear as a governmental rationality which reproduces exclusionary conceptions of humanity, as intelligence is mobilised as grounds for teleological conceptions of history and technological development, utilitarian ethics, and concerns for the long-term future. Consequently, existential risk prevention appears as a governmentality that mobilises uncertainty and the future of intelligence as ethical grounds for disciplining the concept of humanity and governing populations in the present.
10.1057/s41296-026-00845-5.title: The subject of intelligence: AI as existential risk and the government of the human and the future

10.1111/1467-8675.70047.abstract: This article reevaluates Walling as a neglected precursor to American Western Marxism, arguing that his 1912–1914 trilogy synthesized Marxist theory of his time and Deweyan pragmatism into a distinct “pragmatist conception of history.” Born into “aristocracy” yet radicalized, Walling's unique trajectory—as a co‐founder of the NAACP and critic of Second International orthodoxy—shaped his approach: a rejection of deterministic scientific history in favor of instrumental, presentist analysis limited to recent generations. Although his work anticipated Western Marxism's cultural turn and superstructural focus, it also embodied tensions between materialist foundations and pragmatist subjectivity. Through critical engagement with Walling's contradictions—his Deweyan compromise, Nietzschean anti‐historicism, and idealist leanings—the article reveals the limits of his project. Ultimately, Walling's legacy lies in his paradoxical role: a bridge between Second International economism and later Marxist humanism, whose flaws illuminate broader challenges in adapting Marxism and its readings.
10.1111/1467-8675.70047.title: William E. Walling and the Pragmatist Foundations of Proto‐Western Marxism: A Re‐Evaluation and Critique

10.1111/1467-8675.70052.abstract: If Foucault was anything, he was a particularist. And yet, if we are to find valuable tools in his method today, they must be able to assist our framing and analysis of non‐particular issues. By what means can Foucault's methods grasp trans‐contextual problems? I investigate this question by reconsidering the status of power in Foucault's genealogical method. Rather than acting as an object of inquiry, I propose that power operates as an orienting analytical category at the level of Foucault's method. I make the case that conceiving of power in this way facilitates a substantial degree of generalization of his approach that he and his commentators have frequently been wary of claiming. This rethinking of power and method establishes the capacity for Foucaultian methods to address contemporary systemic and global problems.
10.1111/1467-8675.70052.title: The Purview of the Particular: Power and Method in Foucaultian Genealogy

10.1111/1467-8675.70072.abstract: Social theorists in the Marxian tradition often interpret philosophical problems as reflections of social problems. This approach is central to Adorno's interpretation of Kant's epistemology. Adorno claims that the Critique of Pure Reason develops a concept of subjectivity that mirrors the “functionalization” of experience in capitalist societies. He retains that concept contradictory just as the social functionalism it ideologically reflects. In this paper I argue that Kant's concept of subjectivity is not contradictory and that Adorno must rely on it to articulate his critique of functionalism. Recognizing this Kantian debt implies not just acknowledging the Kantian sources of Adorno's model of ideology critique, but also revising central aspects of his social theory.
10.1111/1467-8675.70072.title: Adorno and the Kantian Sources of Ideology Critique

10.1111/1467-8675.70078.abstract: Disagreement about democracy's noninstrumental value often sees the opposition between two competing approaches. Liberty‐based arguments assign normative priority to a principle of liberty, thereby focusing on democratic self‐government as the core principle through which political authority can be reconciled with individual liberty. Equality‐based arguments fundamentally appeal to equality instead, thus commending democratic procedures for treating citizens as equals in the decision‐making process. This paper targets Thomas Christiano's public equality argument for democracy, showing that its tacit reliance on a noncomparative norm of respect for the free and autonomous person leads it back to the liberty framework, as traditionally understood.
10.1111/1467-8675.70078.title: The Contested Grounds of Democracy's Noninstrumental Value: Deliberative Democracy Versus Public Equality

10.1111/1467-8675.70081.abstract: Critics of neoliberalism increasingly examine its corrosive effects on democracy. Scholars often turn to Friedrich Hayek's political theory, arguing that it produces citizens who passively conform to spontaneous social orders. Yet insufficient attention has been paid to the normative conception of the human individual underlying his neoliberalism. This article demonstrates that Hayek's theory actively rejects individuality, understood as the cultivation and expression of one's distinct personal character. Individuality requires an experimental approach toward social action and critical reflection on whether social rules express one's character, yet such attitudes are systematically stifled in Hayek's account because they threaten the unequivocal obedience his spontaneous orders demand. My reading suggests that by suppressing individuality in favor of unreflective conformity, Hayek's neoliberalism produces citizens who are particularly ill‐equipped to identify and resist threats to their freedom and sustain liberal democracy.
10.1111/1467-8675.70081.title: Individualism Without Individuality: Friedrich Hayek and the Neoliberal Citizen

10.1111/1467-8675.70082.abstract: This article examines contemporary digital governance through a dialogue between Shoshana Zuboff's theory of surveillance capitalism and Michel Foucault's analysis of power and governmentality. Although Zuboff offers a compelling account of the economic logics underlying digital domination, her framework tends to locate resistance primarily in external regulation and legal reform. This article argues that such an approach overlooks the subjectifying effects through which digital governance shapes compliant and predictable subjects. Drawing on Foucault, it reconceptualizes surveillance capitalism as an intensification of existing governmental rationalities and advances the notion of counter‐conduct to analyze how subjects negotiate and resist digital power from within.
10.1111/1467-8675.70082.title: Surveillance Capitalism and Governmentality Foucault in the Age of Digitization

10.1111/papa.70020.abstract: At the heart of liberalism lie two seemingly conflicting ideals: a commitment to robust individual rights and an ideal of equal opportunity. The former offers rights‐holders discretion in terms of with whom to cooperate, who to hire, admit, and so forth. The latter is often understood to require policies of affirmative action. This conflict is visible in the recent US Supreme Court Decision Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard University , which firmly decided the matter on behalf of liberal rights. However, such a resolution shifts the burden of injustice on those who are negatively affected by it. And this seems unfair. At the same time, affirmative action threatens to shift these burdens entirely to employers and other applicants. And liberal rights are meant to protect us from being made to bear such burdens. This essay offers a solution to this problem by formulating a rights‐based defense of affirmative action policies. According to this argument, affirmative action policies are fair when they realign the actual (injustice‐tainted) distribution of opportunities with the distribution to which people are entitled as a matter of their social positions. This solution is fair since rights‐holders have no just claims against lacking opportunities they had no right to enjoy in the first place, and victims of injustice have no more claim to redress than what their rights were supposed to yield. The argument justifies significant policies of affirmative action with respect to hiring, admissions, and so forth, in ways that remain fully consistent with even the strongest form of liberal rights.
10.1111/papa.70020.title: Affirmative Action and Liberal Rights

10.1111/papa.70021.abstract: Part III of Anarchy, State, and Utopia defends the minimal state as a framework for utopia. On Bader's reconstruction, this defense contains two justificatory strands: a common ground argument, which shows the minimal state to be compatible with the widest range of utopian associations, and an approximation argument, which holds it to be the framework most likely to generate such associations in practice. I argue that the convergence of these two strands on the minimal state depends on the associational menu being exogenous to institutional structure. Once we recognize that founding has the structure of a public goods problem, this assumption fails: the menu is shaped by the incentive environment a framework creates for potential founders, and a minimal state that does nothing to coordinate founding may produce a narrower and less representative range of associations than the approximation argument supposes. Combined with the rights‐based justification of the minimal state in Parts I and II, this divergence generates a three‐way trade‐off that Nozick's framework does not resolve.
10.1111/papa.70021.title: Is a More‐Than‐Minimal State the Meta‐Utopia?

10.1111/papa.70022.title: Gender Identity: What It Is and Why It Matters. By RachCosker‐Rowland, Oxford University Press, 2025. 368 pp. $40.00 (hardback). ISBN: 978‐0‐19‐894798‐1

10.1111/papa.70023.abstract: Philanthropy has an uneasy relationship with democracy. It distributes decision‐making power plutocratically, in proportion to wealth. It allows unelected, unaccountable, and often untrustworthy individuals to shape social outcomes. And it does so in domains where democracy should be authoritative. Yet, at the same time, philanthropy does much good, and hardly anyone would claim we should eliminate it altogether. So how can we make philanthropy consistent with democracy? In this article, I propose a new answer to this question. I argue that while democratic critics are right to worry about much current philanthropy, there is an important class of philanthropy that is not only highly beneficial, but that also, so far from undermining or conflicting with democracy, can complement or even enhance it. I call this “philanthropy for the disenfranchised,” and argue that we can resolve the tension between philanthropy and democracy by encouraging this sort of philanthropy while discouraging forms of philanthropic abuse and folly. I also outline a program for social reform that involves differentiating the institutions surrounding philanthropy to make them better perform this role, which I contrast with the more familiar programs of democratization and effective altruism.
10.1111/papa.70023.title: Philanthropy for the Disenfranchised

10.1111/papa.70024.abstract: This paper explores the view that, beyond particular wrongs committed by Zionism, the Zionist project was itself inherently wrong. I argue that the most plausible basis for this claim is the contention that Zionism disrespected the territorial rights of the local Arab population. By examining leading contemporary theories of territorial rights – specifically those of Miller Moore and Stilz – I demonstrate that none provide a strong foundation for this view. At the onset of Zionist immigration, the Arabs of Palestine did not meet the criteria required to possess territorial rights under these theoretical frameworks.
10.1111/papa.70024.title: Territorial Rights and the Debate About the Morality of Zionism

10.1111/papa.70025.abstract: Kate Phelan's defense of feminism as a movement exclusively concerned with sex‐based oppression rests on two interlocking moves: a sharp division between women as women and women as members of other oppressed groups, and a “sex‐right” framework that is supposed to entail an abolitionist conclusion about prostitution. This reply argues that both moves fail, and that they fail together. The attempt to isolate sex‐based oppression as a separable object of feminist concern proves unstable once the intersectional constitution of women's oppression is acknowledged: the characteristics that make sex‐based oppression recognizable as such cannot be cleanly separated from class, race, and other axes of domination. The same instability undermines Phelan's sex‐right argument: the inference from the existence of prostitution to the persistence of unconditional male entitlement does not hold once rape has been criminalized and sexual access has been made legally conditional on consent. The line‐drawing to which Phelan attributes such importance is, in the end, both theoretically imprecise and politically unnecessary for the ends she wishes feminism to pursue.
10.1111/papa.70025.title: Why Walk the Line? A Reply to Kate Phelan

10.1111/papa.70026.abstract: Many of the most pressing moral problems we face involve collective harms generated by large numbers of individually insignificant actions. Unlike triggering cases—where a threshold exists such that a single act could be decisive—non‐triggering cases lack any such sharp cutoff. In these cases, no individual act appears to make a difference to whether harm occurs, and it may be metaphysically indeterminate whether a given aggregate is harmful or whether a marginal contribution plays any causal role at all. I argue that standard approaches to moral responsibility, which rely on difference‐making or expected outcomes, struggle to provide action‐guiding reasons in these contexts. Drawing on the security‐dependence account of causation, I argue that agents have pro tanto moral reasons to refrain from actions that make harm more secure, even when those actions neither determine outcomes nor probabilistically influence them in any straightforward sense. Doing so explains how individual actions can remain morally relevant under conditions of overdetermination and metaphysical indeterminacy.
10.1111/papa.70026.title: Difference‐Making Under Metaphysical Indeterminacy

10.1111/papa.70027.abstract: In The Democratic Marketplace , Lisa Herzog offers a damning indictment of democratic capitalism. Among other things, she argues that capitalism has led to increased inequality, fosters an unhealthy culture of competition, that it is bad for the environment, and that it is ultimately bad for democracy itself. To save democracy we must pursue various reforms: we need to address economic inequality; we must abjure the unsustainable pursuit of economic growth and instead democratically determine the functions of the economy; and we should give citizens more time for meaningful civic engagement. In this review essay I push back in defense of democratic capitalism, arguing that while Herzog overstates the negative aspects of capitalism, she also greatly understates its many benefits. Additionally, I show that her own distinctive proposals for how to democratize the economy face serious issues that should not be overlooked. Overall, expanding the scope of democratic politics is not as promising as many seem to think, while democratic capitalism is unjustifiably underappreciated.
10.1111/papa.70027.title: Is Capitalism Bad for Democracy? A Review of Lisa Herzog's The Democratic Marketplace

10.1111/papa.70028.abstract: In recent years, discourse on freedom of speech has shifted away from exclusive focus on the state and towards societal threats to speech. Amidst this change, the notion of “self‐censorship” has gained increased prominence. Not only has self‐censorship emerged as a common reference point, several recent studies identify it as embodying a corrosion of speech‐related values. Despite this, the term self‐censorship lacks a clear and settled definition, and the normative status of self‐censorship isn't self‐evident. While it can be troubling if people feel unable to speak openly, judicious silence is often a virtue, and sometimes morally required. Against this backdrop, I offer an account of a central bad‐making dimension of self‐censorship that helps us distinguish benign from pernicious forms. On this view, self‐censorship is pernicious to the extent that it involves acquiescing to others' judgments of acceptable speech or belief. Identifying what is pernicious about certain forms of self‐censorship in turn helps us sort between the types of social penalties on speech and belief that we ought to be more or less concerned about.
10.1111/papa.70028.title: What's Wrong With Self‐Censorship?

10.1111/papa.70029.abstract: I argue that indoctrination undermines voter competence, and that widespread indoctrination thereby compromises the legitimacy of otherwise free and fair elections. Drawing on recent work in virtue epistemology, I provide an epistemic account of indoctrination according to which one is indoctrinated only if they hold an epistemically impactful belief with an intellectually vicious dogmatic attitude . After clarifying these notions, I show that politically indoctrinated subjects lack epistemic agency with respect to their vote, rendering them incompetent as voters. Therefore, if indoctrinated voters successfully elect a candidate, then the result is illegitimate, even if the election is otherwise free and fair. More speculatively, I suggest that this problem is not merely contingent, but structural: under conditions of low‐cost distribution of information, democracy incentivizes widespread indoctrination as a political strategy, thereby incentivizing a practice that undermines its own legitimacy.
10.1111/papa.70029.title: Indoctrination and Democratic Legitimacy

10.1111/papa.70030.abstract: The paper puts forward a novel solution to the so‐called All or Nothing Problem. Contrary to what many believe, I argue that it is permissible to go some way towards benefiting others without going all the way. Something Is Okay! If this is true, it is not the case (which would be absurd) that we should rather Do Nothing than Something if we are not going to do the Best. If my main claim is correct, this is a blow to a key tenet of Effective Altruism, namely, that if we do good (e.g., contribute to charities), we should do what is best. A side benefit of my solution is the introduction of a neglected sort of supererogation, namely, Self‐Regarding Suboptimal Supererogation (i.e., the self‐regarding equivalent of the more familiar other‐regarding notion of going halfway towards supererogation). Regarding this, my view implies that we are not obliged to do what is best for ourselves (e.g., maximize our health or looks) once we go some way towards benefiting ourselves (incurring considerable costs in doing so).
10.1111/papa.70030.title: Something Is Okay!

10.1111/papa.70031.abstract: Aristotle's analysis of stasis in Book V of the Politics offers a striking example of “distinctively political thought,” as advocated by Bernard Williams's political realism, and in contrast to the moralist approach exemplified by John Rawls. Aristotle identifies disputes over justice, driven by partial and conflicting conceptions of equality, as a principal cause of civil conflict, advocating institutional measures to manage such disagreements rather than relying on citizens converging on a correct understanding. This focus on stability as the first function of politics, aimed at preventing constitutional breakdown, parallels Williams's “first political question” and emphasizes the pragmatic safeguarding of order to avert catastrophe. By contrast, Rawls treats politics primarily as a means to realizing justice, positing that stability depends on an overlapping consensus. The paper critiques Rawls's neglect of the historical‐institutional foundations of liberalism, his underestimation of the durability of modi vivendi, and his ideal‐theoretic abstraction from the circumstances of politics. Aristotle's realist alternative provides a more plausible framework for understanding the relationship between justice and politics—a necessary corrective to Rawlsian political moralism.
10.1111/papa.70031.title: Politics and Justice: Aristotle, Rawls, and the Case for Realism in Political Theory

10.1111/papa.70032.abstract: The epistocracy debate has turned largely on the character of the electorate—what voters know, whether competence filters can be designed well, and what filtered selection produces. Another strand has focused on the legitimacy of epistocratic justifications. I ask instead about the equilibrium effects of the institution. Epistocracy shifts some political authority from the median voter toward citizens selected on competence grounds, and existing critiques press legitimational, epistemic, abuse‐based, and demographic objections against such proposals. I develop a different objection, focusing on one especially plausible form of epistocracy: Jason Brennan's epistocratic veto , a competence‐selected council empowered to override legislation it judges incompetent. Drawing on Acemoglu and Robinson's account of democratization, I argue that the franchise solves a credible‐commitment problem between elites and the poor under conditions of revolutionary threat: universal suffrage puts redistributive authority in majority hands in a way elites cannot easily reverse, because reversing it requires revoking the franchise itself. The institutionally realistic veto hands some of that authority back to a body whose preferences systematically diverge from the median voter's, reintroducing the commitment problem suffrage solved. I give empirical and theoretical reasons to worry that the magnitude of the problem could potentially be significant, while its actual size (and its comparison with democracy's own commitment problems) remains an open empirical question. A formal appendix maps the veto to Acemoglu and Robinson's imperfect‐democracy parameter and shows that the range of conditions under which democratic institutions avert revolution strictly shrinks.
10.1111/papa.70032.title: Epistocracy and the Commitment Problem

10.1163/15691640-12341593.abstract: This article locates an irreducible point of crisis in phenomenology’s attempt to think historically and critically. Using the notion of crisis as my guiding thread, I show how Husserlian phenomenology cannot think history, or historically, without renouncing its fundamental principles. I focus on Merleau-Ponty’s diagnosis of a double crisis of western rationality – the collapse of its “civilizing” mission at a time of decolonial struggles and the collapse of our relation to Nature through science and technology – in his later writings, and show how they point to a moment of crisis within phenomenology, one that Fanon, Patočka, and Derrida, each in their own way, emphasize and invite us to draw to their logical conclusion: every attempt to overcome such crises by returning to the firm, common foundation of the lifeworld, or “Nature-for-us,” reveals another layer of historical sedimentation. Not phenomenology, or “transcendental geology,” but archaeology and genealogy enable us to reach the standpoint of historical critique.
10.1163/15691640-12341593.title: Crisis – of Phenomenology

10.1163/15691640-12341594.abstract: In this paper, I examine Husserl’s conception of the self as both an identical I-pole ( Ichpol ) for-all experience and as a developing, unfolding unity whose self-explication is its history. As Husserl proclaims in the Cartesian Meditations § 37, “time is the universal form of all egological genesis.” He further states: “The ego constitutes itself for itself in, so to speak, the unity of a history,” (Husserl, Cartesian Meditations § 37, p. 75; Hua I 109). In this paper, I will explore how Husserl understands the temporalization of the ego, including the ego’s essential historicity in the life-world. The Danish philosopher Dan Zahavi has spoken about the “minimal self” as a requirement that all experience have the character of “for-me-ness,” i.e., an immediate, non-objectifying, self-acquaintance of the self with itself. I broaden out this account to analyze the nature of the sensory basis for our experience of the self and the need to understand the self in its habitual and developmental character as a form of “ownship”.
10.1163/15691640-12341594.title: Self and Self-Ownership in the Husserlian Phenomenological Tradition

10.1163/15691640-12341595.abstract: This paper argues for the continued relevance of general, transcendental structures – especially Hannah Arendt’s concepts of natality and plurality – within critical phenomenology. Contrary to recent thinkers like Guenther, Oksala, Herrmann, and Marder, who critique the general as inherently oppressive and/or irrelevant, I propose that general conditions can provide a foundation for political critique when examined alongside sociohistorical conditions and individuals’ situatedness within them. Through a close reading of Arendt’s The Human Condition and Eichmann in Jerusalem , I show how modern alienation obscures the fundamental human conditions of natality and plurality, fostering loneliness that feeds into totalitarianism. An Arendtian critical phenomenology that acknowledges generality without forsaking situatedness offers greater explanatory power and relevance in the Trump era, where the erosion of natality and plurality further endangers an already compromised democratic life.
10.1163/15691640-12341595.title: Hannah Arendt’s Challenge to Critical Phenomenology: Critique from the General Conditions of Natality and Plurality

10.1163/15691640-12341596.abstract: Being born is an undeniable fact of every human life, yet it seems that one’s birth evades any direct phenomenological access. Motivated by this problem, this article proceeds in three main steps. It first examines the problem of birth from the first-person perspective, where birth appears as both presupposed and inaccessible. The second step reverses the perspective by approaching pregnancy and birth from the standpoint of the mother, shifting the focus from the problem of access to the tension between unity and separation. Finally, the article proposes a third approach that retains the first-person perspective while also implying a constitutive reference to the mother. It argues that birth should be understood as a horizon of one’s past life. In this sense, birth is not conceived as a spontaneous beginning but is marked by anteriority, such that the self is originally indebted to the others from whom it stems.
10.1163/15691640-12341596.title: Phenomenology of Birth: Selfhood, Horizon, and Anteriority

10.1163/15691640-12341597.abstract: A paragraph in Heidegger’s “The Origin of the Work of Art” which claims to discern the world of a peasant woman in a painting by Van Gogh has become notorious, especially following Derrida’s assessment of it as a “pathetic collapse” symptomatic of ideological-political investments. The article argues that the collapse occurs not in that famous paragraph but in the one that follows it. Close attention to this neglected paragraph reveals a collapse in two movements: first, in Heidegger’s appeal to an imagined peasant woman as an authority external to the picture; second, in his turn to what “we” call Verlässlichkeit (reliability), where “we” means not anyone but “we, the Germans.” This relocation of the collapse allows us to recover the famous paragraph itself, not as derisory ekphrasis but as lucidly apocalyptic: not a fantastical description but a clear-sighted revelation of the world that, in our time, is being lost.
10.1163/15691640-12341597.title: A Pair of Peasant Shoes: on Seeing Things with Heidegger

10.1163/15691640-12341598.abstract: In The Gift of Death , Derrida unfolds an understanding of responsibility as “sacrificial responsibility.” Its logic entails that in being responsible to one, I necessarily sacrifice all the other responsibilities that I nevertheless owe. This idea, deceptively simple in form, has given rise to at least three recurring objections: that it threatens to efface ethical distinctions, that it rests on a flawed notion of infinite responsibility, and that it wrongly assumes conflict as opposed to agreement between our various responsibilities. These criticisms have neither been examined together nor traced to their shared assumptions. In its first part, this paper undertakes that systematic task, arguing that Derrida’s understanding of responsibility can be defended against these lines of criticism. Having clarified Derrida’s central idea, the second part of the paper advances a new challenge by offering a conception of responsibility whose structure leaves no room for exclusion and hence sacrifice.
10.1163/15691640-12341598.title: Derrida’s Conception of Sacrificial Responsibility

10.1163/15691640-12341599.title: The Challenge of Realism and the Limits of Phenomenology

10.1163/15691640-12341600.title: Annabelle Dufourcq’s Merleau-Ponty: An Ontology of the Imaginary: A Reflection from within a Nightmare

10.1163/15691640-12341601.title: Pathos and Praxis: Michel Henry and Paul Ricœur in Dialogue

10.1163/15691640-12341602.abstract: What you are about to read is based on my work in progress called The Disparate: Deleuze’s Ethics of the Univocity of Being . My book attempts to extract a kind of ethics from the three theoretical books Deleuze published at the end of the Nineteen-Sixties: Expressionism in Philosophy: Spinoza (1968); Difference and Repetition (1968); and Logic of Sense (1969). Its widest aim lies in systematizing this ethics of the univocity of being. The first part of the article is theoretical. It concerns the ontology found in Difference and Repetition . The primary ontological concepts are those of the fold and multiplicity. The second part is practical. Here, I make a preliminary attempt to systematize the ethics of the univocity of being. Power is the hinge between the two parts, between the theory and the practice. For Deleuze, the meaning of being is power and the ethics of the univocity of being is an ethics of power. However, at the bottom of the ethics is the experience of powerlessness, even the experience of sadness. Only the experience of sadness puts one on the way to a beatific existence.
10.1163/15691640-12341602.title: On the Way to a Beatific Existence: Theory and Practice in Deleuze’s Works at the End of the Nineteen-Sixties

10.1163/15691640-12341603.abstract: This paper argues that longing for a departed beloved is neither a residual phase of grief nor a compensatory strategy, but a genuine mode of being-with-the-dead. It is ecstatically structured, affectively ambivalent, and grounded in the asymmetrical bond between the living and the dead. Drawing on Martin Heidegger’s notion of being-with and Jean-Luc Nancy’s essays “Psyche” and “On the Point of Departure,” I analyze the affective and temporal structure of longing through my recurring experience of my father’s withdrawal, more than a decade after his death. Nancy’s accounts of holding vigil and ecstatic resurrection allow me to articulate what Heidegger glimpsed but sidelined: the insistent pull of the departed as a withdrawal that continues to call upon those who remain. Longing is both cruel and serene: cruel because it exposes an unbridgeable distance, serene because it allows the departed to remain with us precisely in the exactitude of their withdrawal.
10.1163/15691640-12341603.title: Longing: an Existential-Phenomenological Analysis of Being-With Our Beloved Departed

10.1163/15691640-12341604.abstract: This paper proposes a reconstruction of Sartre’s ontology of interpersonal relations organized around the concept of recognition. It begins with Honneth’s critique of Sartre, taking it as an opportunity to clarify the distinctive character of Sartre’s ontological approach to recognition. Central to this approach is the idea that a tension exists between intersubjective intimacy and existential separation, which Sartre regards as constitutive of the self-other relation. His analysis of this tension hinges on the concept of original recognition, as embodied in our affective response to the look of the Other. This recognition, however, is inherently ambiguous. While attesting to an original generosity of our interpersonal relations, it is also the source of potential conflict – a conflict that need not be perpetual but can be constructively overcome.
10.1163/15691640-12341604.title: Sartre on the Ambiguity of Recognition

10.1163/15691640-12341605.abstract: This article discusses the concept of institution, central to the current philosophical-political debate, from a phenomenological point of view, and specifically in Merleau-Ponty’s writings. The first part presents the Merleau-Pontian elaboration of the theme, compared to its formulation in classical Husserlian phenomenology. It then explores the connection between birth and institution, explicitly elaborated by Merleau-Ponty, linking it to the pages of the French philosopher’s texts, in which he proposes a phenomenology of birth. As a final point, it argues for the need to consider the institution starting from birth, and not vice versa: the temporality of the institution, its beginning and duration over time, is interpreted in the light of the paradoxical time of birth.
10.1163/15691640-12341605.title: The Birth of the Institution. On Merleau-Ponty

10.1163/15691640-12341606.abstract: This essay concerns two distinct topics in Husserlian phenomenology. The first is “image consciousness” [ Bildbewusstsein ], which concerns the experiential nature of our encounters with pictures and other depictive objects. The second is “historicity” [ Geschichtlichkeit ], which refers to how human subjects, prior to any detailed knowledge of history, are in some sense always already temporally embedded and orientated. These topics come from quite different periods of Husserl’s career, and normally receive separate treatments, but I will show that they have rich connections. Drawing from phenomenology, aesthetics and art history, I examine phenomenological and interdisciplinary connections between image consciousness and historicity relating to visual perception, intersubjectivity and narrativization.
10.1163/15691640-12341606.title: Image Consciousness and Historicity: between Phenomenology and Art History

10.1163/15691640-12341607.abstract: Hermann Schmitz offers one of the most extensive descriptions available of embodied space, characterizing it as pre-sensorial, indivisible, and surfaceless yet capable of disclosing absolute locations. Schmitz nevertheless anchors the felt body’s absolute location in temporal irruption rather than in the ability for lived space to ground itself in rest. This article argues that embodied space tacitly involves trans-perceptual conditions of stability and tolerability that Schmitz’s account opens up but does not fully develop. I introduce the concept of existential surface to name this dimension, with the ground underfoot as its paradigmatic case. Acute fatigue serves as the principal test case: it discloses both the felt body’s dependence on a body-bearing world and an autochthonous self-grounding limit of the felt body. I analyze the latter in terms of a recessive boundary that resists further movement and reorganizes practical initiative around what I call being-toward-rest .
10.1163/15691640-12341607.title: Acute Fatigue and Embodied Space: towards a Phenomenology of Existential Surface

10.1163/15691640-12341608.abstract: Phenomenology seeks to recover an originary concept of the world undistorted by dualism. Hermann Schmitz identifies “introjection,” a concept first proposed by Richard Avenarius, as the root of the split between the internal and external worlds. This article investigates the genetic mechanism of this split through a dialogue between phenomenology and psychoanalysis. Husserl, following Avenarius, emphasizes the intersubjective dimension of introjection, namely a conflation between the self and the other. In the same period, Ferenczi and Freud independently developed the psychoanalytic concept of introjection as a principle underlying the differentiation between the internal psychic world and external reality. By synthesizing these traditions, this study outlines a two-step genetic mechanism of introjection: first, tactile duality produces an initial distinction between inner and outer; second, intersubjective conflation transforms this distinction into a radical dualistic split. These two mutually complementary steps lead to a dualistic understanding of the world.
10.1163/15691640-12341608.title: “Introjection” and the Dualistic Split of the World: a Phenomenological and Psychoanalytic Study

10.1163/15691640-12341609.title: The Task of Thinking in an Age of Superfluousness

10.1163/1569206x-bja10099.abstract: Seeking a theoretical understanding of the current configuration of neoliberalism, the present article explores the following question: To what extent does Michel Foucault’s genealogy of governmentality advance or represent a retreat in relation to the framework found in Louis Althusser’s work? The investigation is guided by the hypothesis that the Foucauldian genealogy of discipline and governmentality can be understood as a concrete development of the idea of the political production of subjects defined in Althusser’s foundational text ‘Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses’. To do so, we map out how Althusser influenced Foucault, subsequently reflecting on the degree to which these Foucauldian formulations may contribute to a (re)reading of Althusser and so to a critique of both philosophers in favour of a framework of analysis better suited to the current state of capitalism.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10099.title: From Althusser to Foucault and Back: State, Discipline and Governmentality in the Crisis of Neoliberalism

10.1163/1569206x-bja10100.abstract: This paper philosophically elaborates Michael Tomasello’s developmental psychology to clarify the implicit content of the eco-Marxist concept of metabolic rift. It reconstructs Marx on metabolism and human dependency on nature, bringing out that while all living beings labour because all must act to mediate their dependency on nature, the labour of self-conscious animals has a distinctively social character. This can explain the sense in which human beings are autonomous from nature: not because we enjoy any kind of independence from it but because we can criticise and transform the ways in which we mediate our dependency on it. By grasping that link between autonomy and responsibility, we can show why rift is a metabolic pathology to which only self-conscious animals are vulnerable, and what it would mean to overcome it.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10100.title: How Can Nature Come Apart from Itself? Self-Consciousness and Metabolic Rift

10.1163/1569206x-bja10101.abstract: Ernest Mandel developed an original and comprehensive analysis of capitalism. Among his most important contributions is his controversial theory of long waves of accumulation. This article builds on this framework and attempts to update it for the current period. The theory of long waves must be articulated together with processes of accumulation by dispossession, the theory of absolute advantages, the theory of uneven development and the role of empowered labour in global productivity. All of these are determined by socio-political and endogenous development dynamics. We will attempt to characterise the transformations and current status of the ongoing long wave, and the possible reasons for its protracted duration. The article also attempts to characterise the actually-existing model of neoliberalism in which the state plays a leading role.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10101.title: The Long Duration of the Ongoing Wave of Accumulation: An Update of Ernest Mandel’s Model in the Era of State Neoliberalism

10.1163/1569206x-bja10102.abstract: This article revisits the history of Marxism in Japan and Uno Kōzō’s method for political-economic research from the perspective of Gavin Walker’s book, The Sublime Perversion of Capital: Marxist Theory and the Politics of History in Modern Japan. Walker’s book not only introduces key debates from the history of Marxism in Japan to a contemporary and English-speaking audience. It also rethinks and develops important concepts, discourses and problematics from the history of Marxist theory in Japan that are global in character and that continue to be useful in the here and now. These include the transition from feudalism to capitalism, primitive accumulation, the production of national difference, and the ‘impossibility’ of the commodification of labour-power.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10102.title: Beyond Japanese Marxism and Uno Kōzō: Reflections on The Sublime Perversion of Capital by Gavin Walker

10.1163/1569206x-bja10103.abstract: As the COVID-19 pandemic has demonstrated capital’s inherent carelessness, notions of ‘care’ continue to underpin political struggles and invigorate the Marxist tradition. This article examines how we might conceive of care and the labour of care – carework – in a present defined by intersecting economic, ecological and epidemiological crises. What might a historical-materialist concept of care reveal about contemporary capitalism? Does such a concept have any emancipatory potential? Care or the absence of care suffuses the myriad labour-processes that make ourselves and our world. Recognising the ‘dual nature of care as relation and labour’ is politically and theoretically imperative. How broad care’s remit is, and how and where it intersects (or does not intersect) with Marxist theory and practice, are vital contemporary debates within the historical-materialist tradition. This article argues that just as social-reproduction theory represents a necessary extension of historical materialism, ‘care’ likewise represents a necessary extension of social-reproduction theory, an extension that also addresses theoretical gaps within Marxism. Contemporary social-reproduction theory involves ‘decentring housework … and foregrounding the contradictions posed to capital by the reproduction of life’. In this article, I will argue that the very root of life’s reproduction is care. More than merely a means of decentring housework, care is both the ontological ground of human relationality and ground zero for radical action and thought.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10103.title: Labour Relations and Relational Labour: Care, Ontology and Social Reproduction

10.1163/1569206x-bja10104.abstract: This paper reconsiders the ‘working day’ discussion in chapter ten of Capital and how it centres two parameters in the generation and appropriation of surplus value. The first parameter is the cost of labour-power paid by the capitalist and the second is the time that the worker must yield to the capitalist: the ‘length of the working day’. The first parameter represents the amount of pay required to keep the worker alive and able to work. Marx understood it as a lower limit below which capitalism would cease to function. This paper argues that, while analytically coherent, this understanding of a lower limit runs contrary to many ways that actual historical capitalism has found to exploit the working class. Capitalism regularly exceeds this limit and, in this sense, hyper-exploits. What we find instead of a limit are racialised gradients of human value – generated and fostered by capitalism – in which there are regular and persisting areas of hyper-exploitation with devalued racialised gendered workers. Supplemented by the notion of gradients of human value, Marx’s two-parameter account with its unifying analytic of time, in particular human-time, neatly encompasses the phenomenon of hyper-exploitation and provides an incisive analysis of today’s capitalist exploitation.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10104.title: Racialised Gradients of Human Value and Marx’s Working Day, Today

10.1163/1569206x-bja10105.abstract: Throughout Western democracies, the left remains in political purgatory and without a road towards political power. We examine Chantal Mouffe’s strategy for achieving a left populism with socialist characteristics, followed by Thomas Piketty’s program for ‘participatory socialism’. We highlight the admirable details they offer about alliance politics and transforming property relations. Nevertheless, we argue for why they cannot realise in practice what they hope to achieve, in part because of their respective convictions about the autonomy of the political. Mouffe’s treatment of economic and political liberalism, and her misreading of class relations and neoliberal oligarchy, leave her politics within a liberal capitalist orbit. Piketty’s work is overly idealist and insufficiently critical, and his proposed changes to capitalist and political institutions are too narrow. Their merits notwithstanding, socialist strategy must go beyond Mouffe and Piketty.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10105.title: Gaining Power and Using It: the Promise and Limits of Socialism in Mouffe and Piketty

10.1163/1569206x-bja10107.abstract: Anti-capitalist theories of the commons have set the tone for struggles against capitalism. Their micro-political strategy of being ‘outside’ relies on changing the property relations around the commons. However, this strategy often ignores the gravity of the relations of production and the universal impulse created by the scale and temporality of the capitalist relations of production. Remaining stuck within these premises has caused the commoning movements to lose some of their transformative potential. Instead, positioning the commune as the political form of revolutionary politics can rejuvenate revolutionary struggles in the twenty-first century. This political form can be formulated as considering both production and social reproduction while aiming for collective activity and common responsibility, part of developing a working-class agenda to abolish the capitalist mode of production. The commune launches a de-alienation process that includes the transformation of everyday life as the terrain of ever-changing alienations through a concerted effort to reappropriate lived time and space. This also makes the commune a pillar of power in the future communist society.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10107.title: Beyond Micro-Politics: Critical Reflections on the Anti-Capitalist Theories of the Commons and Recollection of the Commune as a Movement Yet to Be Realised

10.1163/1569206x-bja10110.abstract: With the initial publication of his main economic work in 1859, Marx formulated his programme for an analysis of the bourgeois economy in the following order: capital, landed property, wage labour; state, foreign trade, world market. It was not until the 1920s and 1950s that Henryk Grossman and Roman Rosdolsky discussed whether the content of ‘Capital’ was based on a change in Marx’s structural plan. Important impulses for this discussion in the GDR , the FRG and the Soviet Union came in the following years from the advancing publication of the MEGA ² since 1976. We pay particular attention to the work of Wolfgang Jahn’s research group at the University of Halle. At the heart of this was and is the question of whether methodological and/or substantive breaks can be recognised in Marx’s critique of political economy that point to a change in his conceptions of planning. We deny this with reference to the continuity of his dialectical method of antithetical determination.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10110.title: Structure and Method of the Critique of Political Economy: On the Debate over Marx’s Structural Plan – Part One
