10.1163/1569206x-bja10111.abstract: This paper offers an intellectual history of the reception of Robert Brenner and Ellen Meiksins Wood’s work in relation to the concepts of Eurocentrism, imperialism and capitalist development. We trace Political Marxism’s reputation for disregarding the importance of colonialism to the history of capitalism back to the debates of the 1970s on capitalist development, underdevelopment and imperialism. We unpack the political subtext of these debates and examine how Brenner’s intervention against Dependency Theory and World Systems Analysis shaped subsequent interpretations of class-structural accounts of the origins of capitalist development. The paper then evaluates the resurgence of similar criticisms in the reception of Wood’s intervention in the mode-of-production debate, regarding the centrality of colonialism and extra-economic coercion to capitalist society. We develop an interpretation of Brenner and Wood’s theories that highlights the positive contributions of Political Marxism while assuaging the concerns of its critics.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10111.title: In the Tracks of Political Marxism: Eurocentrism, Imperialism, and Capitalist Development

10.1163/1569206x-bja10112.abstract: In this text I reconstruct the thinking behind Althusser’s work to define philosophy, which culminated in his 1976 presentation at the Granada conference. I start by exploring how philosophy exploits and reorganises other forms of knowledge and social practices by means of an analysis of Althusser’s works in the later part of the 1960s. Subsequently, I examine and outline the debates on how the mode of production affects the superstructure. I then turn to the positions of Althusser’s interlocutor at the Granada conference, Juan Carlos Rodríguez, who defended the idea that philosophy was affected by the mode of production. Finally, I examine the implications of the changes and innovations in Althusserian thought set out at the conference for the conception of philosophy.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10112.title: The Althusserian Transformation of Philosophy

10.1163/1569206x-bja10113.abstract: Which kinds of leadership are appropriate for emancipatory politics? Moving beyond a dichotomy of vanguardism and horizontalism, I advance rearguardism. Supplementing vanguardism, rearguardism involves defensive leadership and legitimation of existing movements, protecting these from attacks by dominant forces and actively propagating their struggles without co-opting or directing these from the front. I first outline vanguardism, focusing on the work of Vladimir Lenin and Rosa Luxemburg. I then reconstruct the most prominent account of rearguardism, by Boaventura de Sousa Santos, before arguing that his account is too dematerialised and confined to an epistemic realm. I therefore reformulate a different vision of rearguardism by turning to Antonio Gramsci.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10113.title: Rearguard Politics: Rethinking Political Leadership From the Back

10.1163/1569206x-bja10115.abstract: This text proposes an understanding of hegemony not as a concept, theory or historical narrative, but as a distinctive method of political work. It thematises this strategic perspective in terms of four central dimensions of Gramsci’s political thought in the Prison Notebooks : the goal of constructing a new order, the nature of self-emancipatory politics as the production of historical progress, the method of leadership conceived as fragility and experimentation, and the organisational form of the party as a pedagogical laboratory. Taken in their productive dialectical interaction, these four perspectives enable us to restore political strategy to the centre of the notion of hegemony, and offer a sophisticated perspective well placed to dialogue with some of the central concerns of contemporary radical social and political movements.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10115.title: New Orders: Hegemony as a Method of Political Work

10.1163/1569206x-bja10116.abstract: Is the strategic question back on the agenda? Construed as awareness of the relative autonomy of political intervention, its return presents a challenge. Amid persistent but fragile neo-liberal hegemony, vigorous but scattered social struggles, and alternatives that are theoretically developed but disconnected from real conditions, strategy involves reinventing the ways and means of an effective break with the capitalist organisation of the world. Reconsidering the classical question of property in conjunction with the production and reproduction of labour-power, I shall endeavour to show that the perspective of reappropriation can unify existing mobilisations without infringing their autonomy or forsaking their aggressive political structuration. To this end, I shall suggest a critical analysis of the theses of Negri and Hardt on the common, in as much as they invite us to re-read Marx from the political and strategic angle of social reappropriation as both means and end of collective and individual emancipation.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10116.title: Towards a Communist Strategy of Reappropriation

10.1163/1569206x-bja10117.abstract: This essay intervenes in contemporary debates around neoliberalism and its relationship to both authoritarianism and social democracy. It does so by reconstructing the debate on Thatcherism that took place between Stuart Hall and Bob Jessop in the 1980s. Both authors provide materialist analyses of Thatcherism that point to important continuities, at the level of both political economy and authoritarian political technique, between her hegemonic project and late-stage social democracy. I argue that this provides an antidote to the social democratic nostalgia that is the potential product of the ways that neoliberalism is frequently theorised in the contemporary literature. While both thinkers highlight these continuities, they are more obviousin Jessop’s institutional approach to hegemony than in Hall’s analysis of Thatcher’s ideology.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10117.title: The Origins of Neoliberal Authoritarianism: Hall and Jessop on the Crisis of Social Democracy and the Rise of Thatcher

10.1163/1569206x-bja10118.abstract: Prefigurative politics, the belief in and commitment to an identity or accord between present political action and a desired future (or between means and ends), has become a significant preoccupation of social movement theory and practice. Understood as demanding the deliberate implementation of future social relations in the present, it often appears as an explicit criticism of Marxism, even of strategic politics in general. For this reason it has often been rejected by Marxists as idealist, utopian or voluntarist. Against this framing, this article makes the case that there are resources within the tradition of revolutionary Marxism for thinking about prefigurative politics. These in turn can help us reflect on strategic debates within and across the radical left. The article traces the outlines of a Marxist approach to prefigurative politics, rooted in concepts of revolutionary practice and self-emancipation as collective learning processes. Finally, it considers how these ideas can inform broader strategic debates.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10118.title: On ‘The Real Movement Which Abolishes the Present State of Things’: Marxism and Prefigurative Politics

10.1163/1569206x-bja10119.abstract: While abolition and revolution might appear complementary, it is not always easy to see how they can relate with each other as part of a coherent conception of emancipatory struggle, nor how such complementarity might inform political strategy. In response to this problem, the objective of this paper is to contribute to a critical reappraisal of the revolutionary heritage of abolitionist thought by drawing attention to what Joy James called ‘the revolutionary era’ of abolitionist politics of the late 1960s and early 1970s USA, focusing on the organisational politics of George Jackson who I consider to be one of the period’s most original thinkers. The claim I would like the reader to consider is that the type of vanguardism once presented by revolutionary abolitionists like George Jackson can help us to re-evaluate the political and ideological basis upon which a greater socialisation of struggles can be built today in view of the constitution of potential counter-hegemonic blocks capable of contesting the demands that capital makes on the planet and our lives. To put it in broader terms, the paper hopes to contribute to a widening of the conversation on how the question of abolition can help us rethink revolutionary politics in the twenty-first century.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10119.title: ‘Seize the Time’ – Abolition & Revolution at the Crossroads

10.1163/1569206x-bja10120.abstract: This article argues that UK labour law scholarship has failed to engage sufficiently with Marxian insights about the nature and basis of employer power and exploitation, and about the limits of law as a means through which to overcome them. As a result, it lacks a strategic orientation, commitment to structural change and theoretical foundations that would enable it to overcome the causes of the problems against which labour law is traditionally directed. The article begins by elaborating a Marxian inspired account of employer-power and the associated problem of exploitation, teasing out its strategic implications. It then explores a range of Marxian contributions to the question of the role of law in the struggle for structural change. It then uses insights from this discussion to explain the potentially important role that labour law scholarship might play in advancing such struggles, before exploring whether UK labour law scholarship has ever embraced such a role for itself in practice. Concluding that UK labour law scholarship has never embraced such a role, the article suggests how UK labour law scholarship might more effectively perform such a strategic role today.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10120.title: Labour Law, Strategy, and the Structural Critique of Capitalism

10.1163/1569206x-bja10121.abstract: The current hegemonic crisis of neoliberal capitalism has relaunched debates on socialist strategy. These discussions have largely crystallised around a polarisation between a ‘democratic road’ to socialism and the insurrectionary approach associated with Lenin and Trotsky. This article seeks to problematise that polarisation and to advance an alternative perspective. It does so by rethinking the concept of dual power not as the embryonic form of a new state nor as entirely external to existing institutions, but as a centralised organ of power from below, capable of autonomous initiative, through which mass radicalisation can most fully express itself in moments of intensified class struggle.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10121.title: Antinomies of Socialist Strategy?

10.1163/1569206x-bja10122.abstract: In a period marked by the inability of all variants of the Left to overcome the burden of defeat and fragmentation, of constant vacillations between reformism and sectarianism, this special issue of Historical Materialism attempts to reopen questions of strategy.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10122.title: Special Issue on Strategy

10.1163/1569206x-bja10123.abstract: Stasis amidst crisis defines the present conjuncture, while the left seems trapped in a fractured sequence between short-lived and fundamentally constrained uprisings and electoral bids. This essay attempts to define the terrain of contemporary struggles in reference to their impasses, especially as these relate to transformations in capitalist nation-states. Tracing the limits of opposed strategic poles – a strong ‘protective’ state and ‘prolonged’ forms of dual power – it situates their common turn to social reproduction struggles and criticises their common presupposition: that states have abandoned core aspects of social reproduction, opening new paths for resistance. Instead we have ‘organised abandonment’: the developing, if still contradictory, integration of state capacities and international capital, extending into new modalities of social reproduction. State capacities have come to be structured in ways that impose impasses on traditional aims of working-class autonomy. In this light, the key strategic question is how we can conceive of an ascending sequence of struggles.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10123.title: Strategy at an Impasse: Prolonged Dual Power, State Capacities and Social Reproduction Struggles

10.1163/1569206x-bja10124.abstract: This article discusses the concept of strategy and how contemporary military thinking can contribute to strategy from below. First it discusses the military lineages of the term ‘strategy’. Second, the evolution of its meaning and its entry into the labour movement. Third, the relationship with ‘tactics’. Fourth, it analyses the concept of ‘operational art’ and explores how it can be used outside the military field. Fifth, it reviews some key debates on contemporary military strategy to enrich the understanding of strategy. Sixth, it explores new military analogies based on the concepts of asymmetric, unrestricted and hybrid warfare. Finally, it considers the term ‘grand strategy’ to assess its value for strategy from below.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10124.title: On Strategy: Thinking with the Military

10.1163/1569206x-bja10126.abstract: This article starts from the continuing pertinence of Daniel Bensaïd’s notion of the ‘strategic hypothesis’. To the hypotheses suggested by Bensaïd, it adds another hypothesis, that of ‘left government’, retracing the complex and uneven relation between Marxism and questions of governance. It revisits the ways strategic questions have been posed since the early 2000s, stressing that the strategic debate in the Marxist Left never really took off. As a result, the question of left government was posed in the mid-20omg10s in a terrain marked by a deficient strategic debate, leading to a series of failures and defeats. The article then attempts to point to some crucial strategic lines of demarcation for the reopening of the strategic debate.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10126.title: Revolutionary Strategy Revisited: Strategic Hypotheses and Open Questions

10.1163/1569206x-bja10130.abstract: This paper argues that both fascist and queer politics are animated by the erotics of transgression: the pleasure that derives from the act of violating normative boundaries concerning gender, sexuality, and the body. Yet while fascism eroticises the restoration of hierarchies of human value, queerness eroticises the destruction of those hierarchical classifications. Against economistic and orthodox psychoanalytic accounts, this paper argues that the erotic charge of transgression emerges from capitalism’s devaluation of embodied needs and desires. By hierarchising needs according to their representability within the terms of value production, capitalism produces a historically specific distinction between profitable and unprofitable needs. Because the body resists full subsumption, many of our bodily needs, desires and capacities are abandoned by capital and can often only be met, if at all, through relations of dependency in the reproductive sphere. It is around this site of abandonment that erotic fantasies of transgression cluster.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10130.title: Desire Beyond Value: On Reproduction, Queerness, and (Anti-) Fascism

10.1163/1569206x-bja10132.abstract: Under neoliberalism, capitalist accumulation has become increasingly dependent on finance, including the financialisation of social reproduction. The centrality of finance to the reproduction of capital has been linked to both the global spread of informal and precarious forms of labour and the reconfiguration of state institutions according to the interests of finance capital. While the recomposition of capital, the working class, and the state has occurred unevenly, these processes have everywhere made the global working class more reliant on debt to ensure their own social reproduction, and these debt relations have become increasingly tied to the reproduction of finance capital. This paper demonstrates how, over the last several decades, intensified financialisation – defined as interest bearing capital ( IBC ) playing a key role in capitalist accumulation – has made both the reproduction of capital and the reproduction of the worker more dependent on finance, without displacing the pivotal role in accumulation played by value-producing wage labour.
10.1163/1569206x-bja10132.title: Integrating Finance and Social Reproduction: Capital, Labour-Power, and Working-Class Formation

10.1177/00323217261422032.abstract: Despite strong support for democratic ideals, citizens are often not democratically active, a situation Dahl described as the ‘Democratic Paradox’. This paradox remains relevant, as many express a desire for more citizen involvement in decision-making processes, yet actual participation falls short of ideals. Understanding the gap between citizens’ democratic ideals and their actual participation is essential to addressing declining civic engagement. This paper examines the discrepancy between citizens’ decision-making preferences and their actual and intended participation in democratic innovations by analysing survey data from over 27,000 European respondents. The findings reveal that, while citizens generally support the notion of greater civic influence, those who favour direct democracy are not the most participatory. Instead, clusters with technocratic or politician-averse views demonstrate higher engagement levels. These findings highlight a paradox where people who normatively endorse greater influence by ordinary citizens simultaneously show limited willingness to exercise such influence, posing significant democratic challenges.
10.1177/00323217261422032.title: A Paradox Revisited: Understanding Participation Gaps

10.1177/00323217261423322.abstract: Does variation in local economic environments help explain why some areas exhibit systematically higher support for radical-right parties? To address this question, I focus on two drivers related to the type of industry where individuals work and socially interact. First, in contrast to knowledge-based industries, labour-intensive industries are characterised by a clustering of individuals with high job vulnerability and low education. Second, when they coincide spatially, these two socioeconomic characteristics give rise to nativist preferences and exclusionary attitudes, which drive support for radical-right parties. I test these claims with two empirical strategies. In geographical municipal-level data from Spain, I confirm that support for radical-right parties is determined by exposure to labour-intensive activities such as certain sectors of agriculture and tourism. In addition, survey data from 17 European democracies confirm that working in labour-intensive industries boosts the roles of job vulnerability and education in developing and expressing exclusionary political behaviours.
10.1177/00323217261423322.title: Labour-Intensive Geographies and Support for Radical-Right Parties

10.1177/00323217261428857.abstract: Authoritarian legislatures are often portrayed as “rubber stamps” that merely formalize predetermined decisions. Yet growing evidence suggests that they can influence policy through deliberation and bill modification. This study investigates legislative modification in China’s National People’s Congress. Drawing on an original dataset of 133 bill–law pairs enacted between 2008 and 2023, we employ an improved minimum edit-distance algorithm to quantify textual change and identify conditions that generate more extensive modification. Results reveal that Congress has become proactive in shaping legislative outcomes. Party attention and public concern significantly amplify modification, whereas bureaucratic fragmentation constrains it. A qualitative case study of the Food Safety Law illustrates how bureaucratic competition creates drafting ambiguity, while public concern weakens departmental interests and facilitates consensus. These findings demonstrate that bill modification functions as a mechanism of controlled coordination that reconciles party priorities, societal pressures, and bureaucratic fragmentation within a centralized authoritarian policymaking system.
10.1177/00323217261428857.title: Decoding Legislative Dynamics: Empirics on Bill Modifications in China

10.1177/00323217261429650.abstract: How do citizens in autocracies respond to government-provided information? While scholars have explored various forms of information manipulation used by autocrats, we still know little about how the dissemination of government statistics affects public perceptions and behavior in everyday life. In a survey experiment conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic in Kazakhstan, we investigate whether government-provided data and message influence citizens’ risk perceptions and behavioral intentions. After asking respondents to estimate the number of infections and deaths during the pandemic, we corrected their estimates using official statistics or exposed them to a message that optimistically interprets the statistics, with the information source randomly attributed either to the Kazakh government or the World Health Organization. Our findings suggest that government-provided information did not significantly alter respondents’ perceptions of the virus. These results indicate that citizens in autocracies may not always be decisively influenced by government information manipulation.
10.1177/00323217261429650.title: Government Information and Popular Reactions in Autocracies: An Information-Correction Experiment on COVID-19 in Kazakhstan

10.1177/00323217261429722.abstract: Analyses of the politics of defense spending have often assumed a guns–butter tradeoff that maps onto the standard left–right political spectrum, with dovish leftists favoring less military spending and hawkish rightists supporting more. But in Europe, plotting parties’ positions on military spending against their left–right position reveals almost nothing. To address this puzzle, I advance three arguments—first, that nationalism should be understood as a separate axis influencing defense spending preferences; second, that party positioning is conditioned by GDP; and third, that the USSR’s role as an external ideological pole played a key role in structuring left party positions on military spending. I use Manifesto Project data to test these hypotheses and find support for the third. In doing so, I shed light on the sources of party positioning in an under-analyzed issue space, and I offer evidence for the international order’s role in constituting the domestic one.
10.1177/00323217261429722.title: The Party Politics of Defense Spending in Western Europe

10.1177/00323217261430412.abstract: How do collective memories of war shape inter-group social attitudes in post-conflict societies? Can the legacy of wartime violence hinder reconciliation for years or even decades after the conflict ends? While prior research shows that war memories influence a range of political processes and outcomes, their effects on how members of formerly opposing groups perceive one another remain underexplored. To address this gap, I conducted a survey experiment in post-war Bosnia, investigating whether the activation of these memories affects hostility toward out-groups. The results show that making war memories salient intensifies hostility, especially among individuals who personally experienced violence during the war. These findings suggest that deeply ingrained war memories pose a significant barrier to reconciliation, but their impact may gradually diminish through the generational replacement of the wartime population.
10.1177/00323217261430412.title: Collective Memories, Personal Experiences, and Inter-Group Attitudes

10.1177/00323217261431497.abstract: This study examines how partisan identities shape citizens’ perceptions of democratic and undemocratic behavior by politicians. Drawing on theories of partisan-motivated reasoning, we argue that partisan identities serve as powerful directional goals that unconsciously bias how citizens evaluate political behaviors against democratic principles. Crucially, we theorize that affective polarization amplifies these partisan rationalization biases by strengthening in-party attachment and out-party animosity. Through a survey experiment in South Korea, we find that citizens systematically rationalize their democratic perceptions based on partisan affiliation, perceiving both regular and undemocratic behaviors by co-partisan politicians as more democratic than similar behaviors by out-partisan politicians. Remarkably, citizens even view undemocratic behaviors by co-partisan politicians as more democratic than regular behaviors by out-partisan politicians. Furthermore, we demonstrate that affective polarization significantly amplifies these partisan rationalization biases. Citizens with higher levels of affective polarization are more susceptible to partisan rationalization of democratic perceptions and show stronger perceptual biases compared to those with lower affective polarization. These findings help explain how partisan rationalization and affective polarization can distort citizens’ perceptions of democracy, potentially undermining their ability to serve as a check against democratic backsliding.
10.1177/00323217261431497.title: Partisan Rationalization and Evaluations of (Un)Democratic Behaviors: The Amplifying Role of Affective Polarization

10.1177/00323217261431905.abstract: How confident should we be in the answers we get when using existing measures of corruption? Scholars routinely rely on country-level corruption indices to study democratic accountability, representation, development, and institutional reform. Yet a great deal of research argues that country-level corruption indicators are incomparable to each other and over time. We present evidence that these indicators all track a shared component identifiable as a change within country in overall corruption, but despite this, they remain problematically inconsistent with each other. As a result, we argue that empirical findings about corruption based on these designs will be particularly sensitive to the choice of measure. To address this problem, we introduce a new synthetic measure of within-country change in corruption that is robust to bias and measurement error that may be present in those existing measures. Our new measure allows researchers to explain changes in corruption that are common to all measures, rather than privileging any single index. We employ our new measure to revisit a published analysis of the effect of women’s representation on corruption, finding a more consistent relationship and more balanced dynamics using our measure than with others’.
10.1177/00323217261431905.title: Measuring Changes in Corruption Over Time

10.1177/00323217261432360.abstract: How do opposition parties become viable alternatives under dominant-party rule? Existing studies often attribute opposition change to electoral shocks or short-term campaign strategies, offering limited insight into how governing capacity is constructed under asymmetric political conditions. This article introduces the concept of transformative accumulation to analyze the recent trajectory of Turkey’s Republican People’s Party under the long-standing dominance of the Justice and Development Party. Drawing on 13 elite-level interviews with incumbent and former party officials, campaign consultants, and local leaders, the study identifies three interwoven narratives—ideological, institutional, and leadership—that structure this transformation. It shows how the Republican People’s Party recalibrated its ideological appeal, adopted a more inclusive leadership model, and strengthened its administrative and communicative capacities despite persistent institutional constraints. While acknowledging the continued structural advantages enjoyed by the Justice and Development Party, the article demonstrates how opposition parties can reposition themselves as viable alternatives within competitive authoritarian regimes. Conceptually, it shifts the analysis of opposition politics away from episodic electoral moments toward a process-based framework for studying opposition agency under dominant-party rule.
10.1177/00323217261432360.title: Transformative Accumulation Under Dominant-Party Rule: Turkey’s CHP and the Making of a Viable Opposition

10.1177/00323217261433303.abstract: The fracture between citizens and elites on European integration remains understudied, most notably when it comes to specific issues. One of these issues, particularly salient in the aftermath of Brexit, is holding further European Union exit referendums across the Union. While regularly floated by (Eurosceptic) parties for electoral purposes, it remains unclear to what extent parties and citizens agree to actually hold European Union exit referendums. We examine the relationship between party and citizen stances on this issue in 10 European Union member states, leveraging original cross-country survey data and expert survey data on parties’ positions, both collected in 2019. The results show that parties tend to be more against holding a European Union exit referendum than their voters, less so the more extreme parties. Moreover, higher media saliency correlates with greater party–voter congruence, and the issue is more polarised among the electorate than at the party level.
10.1177/00323217261433303.title: Nexit, Frexit or Grexit? A Comparison of Party and Citizen Positions Towards European Union Exit Referendums

10.1177/00323217261435272.abstract: We assess the impact of former President Joe Biden’s unprecedented decision to exit the 2024 Presidential race 2 months before election day by analyzing a naturally-occurring experiment surrounding the incumbent President’s decision to exit the 2024 race, a period in which we fielded the second wave (N Wave 2 = 831) of a nationally-representative panel study (N Wave 1 = 1400), with random invitation assignment (from the original response pool) throughout Wave 2. Pre-registered difference-in-difference (DID) analyses reveal no evidence of significant turnout or down-ballot effects across either the US adult population or partisan subgroups. However, post hoc tests reveal substantial gains in excitement about the 2024 campaign across both the general population and (especially) among self-identified Democrats after President Biden’s decision to drop out. Elevated excitement coincided with (a) increased belief in core democratic principles and (b) increased donation to Democrats up and down the ballot.
10.1177/00323217261435272.title: A Naturally-Occurring Experiment on the Electoral Impact of President Biden’s Decision to Exit the 2024 Presidential Race

10.1177/00323217261442716.abstract: This article examines the relationship between crisis concerns and conspiracy-related and populist attitudes, viewed as facets of anti-establishment sentiment. Research shows that crises can trigger fear, uncertainty, and loss of control, making individuals more receptive to conspiracism and populism, as both provide simple explanations for complex problems. Yet most studies have treated ‘crisis’ as a uniform concept, whether linked to the Covid-19 pandemic, the economy, or migration, overlooking how different crises may resonate differently with citizens. We refine this understanding by analysing concerns across five domains: Covid-19, the climate crisis, the immigration emergency, the Russia–Ukraine war, and the energy crisis, assessing their distinctive effects on three facets of anti-establishment attitudes. Drawing on survey data from seven European countries, our findings reveal variation in perceptions of different crises and their associations with conspiracism and populism. Since not all crises are equally associated with the spread of anti-establishment attitudes, this nuanced analysis highlights the need for more tailored approaches to understanding crises and their political consequences.
10.1177/00323217261442716.title: Not all crises are alike: Crisis concerns and anti-establishment attitudes in comparative perspective

10.1177/00323217261444560.abstract: What structures voting behaviour under conditions of electoral and political constraints? The impact of authoritarian legacies from dictatorship on voting behaviour is well documented, but we know comparatively less about voting in constrained democracies. This study focuses on the 1963 and 1964 Greek legislative elections, analysing a novel archive of opinion polls. It contributes to the understanding of voting decisions and preference formation under democratic constraints, highlighting the role of the centrist vote in bringing about political and economic change in Greece. We show that political concerns linked to authoritarian practices and political repression were not the most prominent at these elections, but concerns over economic conditions, social welfare and education were. We demonstrate the role of age group, socio-economic stratification, newspaper readership and economic concerns for voting for the centre and left-wing parties. This indicates an emerging political realignment which can produce meaningful political change even in cases of constrained democracy.
10.1177/00323217261444560.title: Voting in a constrained democracy: Evidence from the 1963 and 1964 legislative elections in Greece

10.1177/00323217261444654.abstract: Political parties expect youth wings to recruit and socialize young people into the norms and values of the party, nurturing aligned future grassroots members, officials, and candidates. However, embeddedness in youth wings – understood in terms of membership length and activity levels – may not necessarily deliver this. In our study, we examine whether youth wings nurture the members parties want using YOUMEM survey data from over 5000 members of 12 youth wings in six countries. Specifically, we assess whether embeddedness is associated with greater ideological alignment and desire for long-term party engagement. We find that active members are more ideologically aligned and inclined to remain in the party, while passive members display the opposite trend. However, length of membership is associated with reduced aspirations among all for intra-party and public office. Our findings suggest that the added value of youth wings as future-oriented socialization vehicles for parties is less than generally assumed.
10.1177/00323217261444654.title: The added value of youth wings: Do they nurture the members their parties want?

10.1177/00323217261448018.abstract: Authoritarianism, populism, and radicalism are considered important risks to citizens’ support for democratic institutions. Most studies have so far analyzed varying combinations of these, making it difficult to understand the potentially damaging effects of either of these separately. Analyzing a survey of 14,000 British, French, German, and Italian citizens, I show that studying authoritarianism, populism, and radicalism together reveals important differences in citizens’ support for and understandings of democracy. Authoritarians do not support democracy. Populists support democracy as much as non-populists, while they are highly critical of its real-world implementation. Their open-ended responses refer less often to liberal democracy than those of other respondents. Radicalism in itself correlates little with citizens’ democratic attitudes. Importantly, findings differ for left- and right-wing radicals. These findings urge us not to overlook the harmful effects of authoritarianism. We should not underestimate the extent to which some citizens, in particular authoritarians, consciously reject liberal democracy.
10.1177/00323217261448018.title: Support for (liberal) democracy among authoritarian, populist, and radical Western Europeans

10.1177/00323217261448797.abstract: Understanding when and why social cleavages shape electoral behaviour is a central concern in the study of democratic politics. While many accounts emphasise the long-term social changes, others point to the role of party strategy. We contribute to this debate by analysing the political evolution of one of the central cleavages of the twentieth century—class—in one of the world’s longest-standing democracies—Britain. Analysing a unique new dataset combining constituency-level results across 37 general elections from 1885 to 2024 with data from eight censuses, applying geospatial redistricting methods, we describe the rise, stability and eventual decline of class-based voting, showing that a strong class cleavage emerged in the early twentieth century, remained stable for decades, but then unravelled rapidly after the 1990s. These patterns are difficult to reconcile with theories that emphasise gradual social change and are more consistent with accounts that stress political agency and representation.
10.1177/00323217261448797.title: The rise and fall of class voting in Britain, 1885–2024

10.1177/00323217261449611.abstract: In many parliamentary democracies, incumbents can call early elections. This is thought to provide incumbent governments with an advantage due to the ability to time elections to favorable economic conditions. This article explores an additional incumbency advantage of early elections. Due to information asymmetry about election timing, government parties can better plan fundraising and campaign spending in early elections years compared to nongovernment parties giving government parties a relative financial advantage. This argument is tested on campaign-spending data from British parliamentary candidates 1950–2019. The results supports the argument. Government party candidates gain a relative financial advantage in early elections years compared to scheduled election years. The effect is found only for non-incumbent candidates and may have been eliminated by the Fixed-term Parliaments Act of 2011, which removed government election-calling power. The results suggest that government election-calling power provides incumbent parties with a relative financial advantage.
10.1177/00323217261449611.title: The government financial advantage of early elections: Evidence from UK MP candidate spending

10.1177/00323217261450437.abstract: Language is central to political representation, yet the role of dialects remains understudied. This study examines how dialects are associated with citizens’ feelings of and preferences for political representation. We argue that dialect use can be a part of social identity: politicians who share their constituents’ dialect may signal local attachment and social proximity. However, dialects also carry social stigma, potentially leading to underrepresentation in a political sphere dominated by standard language. Using original survey data from Germany, we test whether dialect-speaking citizens (1) feel less represented and (2) prefer politicians who speak a dialect. We find support for both: dialect speakers feel less represented and have stronger preferences for dialect-speaking representatives. These results suggest that dialects can serve as a subtle but meaningful form of descriptive representation. Our findings underscore the role of linguistic identity in political inclusion and call for greater attention to language in research on political behaviour.
10.1177/00323217261450437.title: Feeling overlooked and underrepresented? Citizens’ preferences for dialect-speaking representatives

10.1177/00323217261450950.abstract: As democracies grow more diverse through immigration, a key question arises: when should immigrants participate in political decision-making? We examine citizens’ beliefs about when immigrants should vote in national elections (before citizenship, with citizenship, or never) and whether these views depend on immigrants’ integration markers. We assess how exclusionary worldviews and psychological predispositions—authoritarianism, social dominance orientation (SDO), and ethnocentrism—shape views of democratic membership and how malleable those views are. Using 2021 survey data from Denmark, Germany, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States, we find that integration criteria matter most to those who view citizenship as the primary gateway to political inclusion. High levels of SDO and ethnocentrism are associated with exclusionary preferences, though integration efforts reduce resistance among individuals high in SDO. Authoritarian-leaning individuals are simultaneously more willing to include immigrants pre-naturalization and more likely to support permanent exclusion. These findings highlight the conditional nature of political inclusion in diverse democracies.
10.1177/00323217261450950.title: (Un)conditional? The role of integration and psychological predispositions in citizens’ attitudes toward immigrant enfranchisement

10.1177/00323217261450951.abstract: Science and expertise are frequently invoked to legitimize policy decisions. However, while prior research suggests broad support for expert-led governance, it often overlooks how citizens differentiate between types of experts and how political beliefs shape these perceptions. This study examines how institutional affiliations of experts—universities, government, and think tanks—influence citizens’ perceptions of legitimacy in political decision-making. Drawing on two pre-registered factorial survey experiments embedded in a survey from Finland (N = 2546), we investigate (1) differences in how actors affect decision-making legitimacy, and (2) how these effects differ depending on the type of issue, outcome favourability and issue salience. Our results show that proposals involving university researchers frequently gain legitimacy, but the exact effects hinge on the type of issue, outcome favourability, and salience. These findings contribute to a more nuanced understanding of how citizens perceive the role of expertise in democratic governance.
10.1177/00323217261450951.title: Experts, Experts Everywhere! Survey Experimental Evidence on How Involving Expertise Affects Decision-Making Legitimacy

10.1177/00323217261450953.abstract: Trust in civil servants is essential for effective governance, enabling policy implementation, public service delivery, and compliance. However, the lack of comparable cross-national data on trust in bureaucracy has limited our ability to systematically examine these relationships. To address this gap, we develop the Trust in Civil Servants (TCS) dataset with an advanced latent-variable modeling technique, using 123 national and cross-national surveys from 98 countries and territories (1986–2022). Our measures reveal variations in trust both within and between countries and territories. We find that economic performance and public security enhance trust in the short term, whereas government quality and effectiveness have more enduring, long-term impacts on trust in civil service. The TCS dataset opens new avenues for examining connections between trust, governance quality, and complex policy challenges across different contexts.
10.1177/00323217261450953.title: Trust in civil servants: A cross-national dataset for public policy research, 1986–2022

10.1177/00323217261457621.abstract: The ‘directional’ definition of negative campaigning (i.e. when candidates leverage critiques against their political opponents) has been criticized for lacking reliability and validity. Does this critical assessment resist scrutiny? We propose, via nine different original studies, a full-scale reassessment of this critical assessment. Building on novel evidence from sources as disparate as expert ratings of elections across the world, automated and manual coding of social media posts, candidate self-ratings, cross-sectional surveys, experimental evidence, and more, we provide a much less pessimistic outlook. The evidence discussed in the nine studies showcases high levels of (self-)observer agreement (i.e. different people evaluate the same phenomenon similarly), situational consistency (evaluations are stable across time and space), convergent validity (different independent measures of the same phenomenon are strongly correlated), construct validity (measures can be used to provide empirical support for theoretically cogent hypotheses), and discriminant validity (proximate phenomena are perceived differently). The directional measure of campaign negativity is not perfect, but it is very much alive and kicking. The data and materials for all nine studies are open for replication and re-analysis.
10.1177/00323217261457621.title: Unreliable and Invalid? Not So Fast: A Multistudy Empirical Assessment of the ‘Directional’ Measure of Negative Campaigning

10.1177/00323217261460583.abstract: Political stereotypes—beliefs about the attributes of politically defined groups—can deepen polarization by obscuring commonalities among citizens. Yet little is known about their nature outside the United States. Using open-ended survey responses from Brazil, the United Kingdom, Germany, and Poland (N = 5381), we analyze how citizens describe political adversaries in their own words—focusing on issues, social groups, and traits. Combining deductive and inductive coding, we uncover both cross-national patterns and context-specific dynamics. Our content analysis shows that issue- and trait-based stereotypes dominate, but boundaries between categories are blurred. Respondents often conflate politicians and voters, use group labels to suggest traits or views (and vice versa), and deploy trait language to express moral condemnation. These tendencies vary by country, reflecting salient debates and historical cleavages. Our findings suggest treating political stereotypes as webs of associations that go beyond discrete categories, with implications for the comparative study of stereotypes and polarization.
10.1177/00323217261460583.title: Blurred boundaries: Exploring political stereotyping in Brazil, the United Kingdom, Germany, and Poland

10.1177/00323217261460721.abstract: Compulsory voting (CV) reliably raises turnout, but its effects on invalid ballots and the inequalities these produce are less well understood. Chile’s return to CV in 2022 provides a rare within-country test of how the shift from voluntary to compulsory participation reshapes invalid voting and what this produces in the context of shifting inequalities. We analyse the last local elections held under voluntary voting (VV, 2021) and the first under CV (2024) across all 345 municipalities, exploiting concurrent contests held under distinct electoral rules. Our central finding is that CV shifts inequality from participation to vote validity, with rates of invalid voting varying across majoritarian and proportional elections. Specifically: (1) invalid voting increased substantially under CV, though valid votes for parties and candidates also rose; (2) the entry of new voters is associated with a shift from abstention under VV to invalid ballots under CV; (3) ballot size is more strongly associated with invalid voting under CV in proportional than in relative-majority systems; (4) poverty is unrelated to invalid voting under VV but becomes significant under CV, especially in the capital; and (5) rurality is negatively associated with invalid voting under CV but not under VV. These results contribute to debates on whether CV corrects or displaces class bias in participation, on the structural determinants of invalid voting, and on how electoral system type conditions invalid ballot rates under compulsory participation.
10.1177/00323217261460721.title: The return to compulsory voting: Invalid voting and its representational challenges in Chile’s subnational elections

10.1177/00323217261462390.abstract: On 3 December 2024, South Korea experienced an unprecedented political crisis when the president declared martial law. While the declaration was rapidly reversed and condemned by key democratic institutions, public opinion did not converge on rejection. Instead, support for—and tolerance of—the measure persisted among a nontrivial share of citizens. Why, in a democracy with functioning institutions, are some citizens willing to accept extraordinary executive measures? Using original nationwide survey data, this research shows that public support for martial law is strongly associated with affective polarization. Individuals who express strong partisan and leader-based affective alignment with the incumbent are significantly more likely to accept martial law, while those polarized in the opposite direction overwhelmingly reject it. The findings suggest that affective polarization can align evaluations of executive overreach with partisan loyalties, weakening normative constraints even in consolidated democracies where institutional safeguards continue to function effectively.
10.1177/00323217261462390.title: Who supports martial law in a democracy? Lessons from South Korea

10.1177/00323217261463105.abstract: Regime legitimacy and survival rely on citizens’ consent to election results, even when these results are unfavorable. Theories posit that individuals with pro-democratic attitudes are more accepting of electoral losses. We test this assumption by analyzing the empirical relationship between support for democratic principles, such as universal suffrage, and electoral consent to randomly generated, hypothetical but plausible electoral outcomes. Using data from a representative sample of Germans, we find a negative correlation between the two variables. Furthermore, those with the strongest democratic convictions are those most influenced in their consent by partisan preferences. Part of the explanation stems from reactions to the far-right, anti-democratic party Alternative for Germany, as many respondents strongly dislike this party and are unwilling to consent to outcomes in which it performs well. However, even among other respondents, democratic support does not correlate positively with losers’ consent.
10.1177/00323217261463105.title: Does support for democracy increase losers’ consent?

10.1177/00323217261463299.abstract: As Western democracies become increasingly diverse, political influence often depends on effective alliances and solidarity that cut across group boundaries. While the intergroup solidarity literature points to shared grievances as a central driver, it remains unclear exactly what kind of grievance information promotes political solidarity between which groups. To test this, we conducted a survey experiment in the United Kingdom among respondents from three distinct groups: migrants from Eastern Europe, migrants from the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), and natives. The treatments vary based on which immigrant group is described as experiencing discrimination, making potentially shared group grievances salient. We find that discrimination information increases support for prospective MENA immigrants among migrants from Eastern Europe, but not vice versa, and we find no effects among UK natives. Moreover, discrimination information is more effective among migrants without British citizenship. Importantly, discrimination information may not uniformly foster political solidarity or interest alignment across all population groups.
10.1177/00323217261463299.title: Testing political solidarity: The effect of discrimination information on groups’ immigration attitudes

10.1177/00323217261464836.abstract: According to Tang and Huhe, individuals “are nested in a multiplicity of governments,” including national and local governments, “and . . . constantly find themselves in variant relationships with government at different levels”. Yet, previous research has mostly concentrated on individuals’ assessments of national governments, or supranational organizations such as the European Union, overlooking assessments of local governments and their effects. To address this, we fielded a four-wave survey in England in 2020–2021 capturing local and national government trust, as well as contemporaneous indicators of performance across these levels of government. Disaggregating between- and within-individual explanations for variation, we find distinct influences on trust in national and local government, and that trust in local government exerts an influence on pro-social behaviour whereas national government trust does not. Importantly, for future research on political trust, our findings show that the level of government matters for both the drivers and consequences of political trust.
10.1177/00323217261464836.title: The trust in government gap: National trust, local trust, and compliance

10.1177/00323217261464880.abstract: Democratic accountability requires citizens’ political trust to reflect institutional performance, making it crucial to understand what fosters such responsiveness. While existing studies suggest that education shapes evaluative attitudes, direct evidence remains limited because many analyses struggle to separate educational effects from those of parental background. This paper offers a comprehensive test of these explanations by examining adolescents within the same target grade and by assessing school-level civic education characteristics often credited with cultivating critical citizenship norms. It then compares school-level patterns with parental background to evaluate the proxy-versus-cause debate. Using data from three waves of the International Civic and Citizenship Education Study, the analysis shows that structurally low and declining institutional performance depresses political trust among adolescents. However, consistent with the education-as-proxy argument, the positive association between performance and trust is significantly stronger among adolescents with higher parental socio-economic status, while school-level civic education shows no meaningful moderating effect.
10.1177/00323217261464880.title: Evaluations of institutional performance among adolescents: Comparing the socializing roles of schools and families

10.1177/00323217261466241.abstract: Trade among major powers is never purely economic; it is also a site of political conflict over blame, threat, and national interest. Why, then, do legislators facing similar trade shocks respond in such different ways? Focusing on US Senate rhetoric on trade with China between 2009 and 2023, this paper examines how partisanship conditions the translation of economic disruption into elite political speech. Drawing on sentiment analysis of Senate floor speeches and state-level measures of Chinese import exposure across two periods, it develops a partisan-conditioning argument: trade disruption acquires political meaning as parties interpret it. Democratic senators grew markedly more critical as local import exposure increased, especially under the earlier China Shock window. Republicans showed a much flatter response to early-period exposure and even a slightly positive association with later-period penetration. The China Shock left a durable mark on Senate discourse, but one structured by party, not geography alone.
10.1177/00323217261466241.title: Whose China Shock? Partisanship, import exposure, and trade rhetoric in the US Senate

10.1177/00323217261467233.abstract: Government identifiability – the degree to which the party composition of the eventual government can be predicted given the election results – is a desirable characteristic of a political system. But the measurement of identifiability has remained impressionistic, limiting our ability to speak precisely about trade-offs between identifiability and other characteristics of the political system. I show that a recent measure of bargaining complexity by Cronert and Nyman acts as a ratio-level measure of government identifiability measured in bits – or equivalently, the number of yes/no questions needed to identify the composition of the government. I then show how identifiability is linearly related to the number of seat-winning parties in three different contexts: parliamentary governments, presidential cabinets, and municipal governments. Across all three contexts, an additional seat-winning party increases entropy of government formation by between 0.7 and 0.8 bits. Since identifiability is linearly related to the number of parties, any increase in the number of parties through electoral reform will worsen identifiability by the same amount. Conversely, there are no “sweet spots” where we can achieve high levels of identifiability at low cost in terms of the number of parties.
10.1177/00323217261467233.title: Government identifiability and the number of parties: No sweet spots, just a steady linear increase

10.1177/00323217261468169.abstract: Why do governments prevent crime in some places while neglecting others? Crime prevention policies are often viewed as too slow, diffuse, and politically intangible to generate electoral rewards. When implemented, existing research suggests they primarily serve to reward co-partisans or mobilize ideologically aligned voters. This article challenges that view by arguing that incumbents allocate crime prevention resources to electorally competitive municipalities because these investments yield electoral returns. Using detailed project-level data from Colombia, I show that national incumbents disproportionately direct crime prevention funds to municipalities where recent presidential elections were closely contested, rather than to areas with higher crime rates or strong partisan loyalties. I then show that these allocations increase the vote share of the right-wing incumbent coalition in subsequent elections. Drawing on quantitative analyses and interviews with policymakers and bureaucrats, I argue that these effects operate primarily through the visibility and attribution of crime prevention projects, particularly those aligned with right-wing issue ownership of public security.
10.1177/00323217261468169.title: The politics of crime prevention: Evidence from Colombia

10.1177/00323217261469290.abstract: The work of being an elected representative today is increasingly demanding as they seek to perform representation amid political distrust, polarised electorates, and rising populism. In response, elected representatives and their teams invest heavily in developing and showcasing their capacities to represent. This variously involves constructing representative personas, designing participatory events, curating diverse digital content, and communicating evidence on how and where they are representing. Extending Saward’s representative claim-making framework, this article develops the concept of representative-capacity-making to better understand this overlooked (‘backstage’) aspect of modern representation. The article explores – in concept only – the work involved in developing and demonstrating four key representative capacities. The normative implications of representative-capacity-making in an era of democratic strain are considered. While representative-capacity-making can be read as a response to the challenges of democratic representation today, the extent to which it can be a solution is mixed, in specified ways.
10.1177/00323217261469290.title: Representative-capacity-making: The strategic backstage work of political representation

10.1177/00323217261469493.abstract: Over the last few decades, interconnected debates about Scottish independence and Brexit have shaped politics in the United Kingdom and raised questions of constituent power that remain controversial both politically and theoretically. Against this backdrop, this article proposes a nuanced democratic conception of constituent power that serves as an alternative to orthodox sovereigntist accounts. This conception is theoretically more compelling and, moreover, enables fruitful engagement with contemporary constitutional controversies. By establishing a dialogue between theoretical discussion and the Scottish and UK case, the article, first, explores constituent power as one dimension of popular sovereignty and its interplay with constituted powers over time. Second, it examines how constituent collectives can and, in recent history, have become subject to contestation and change. Third, it sketches monist and pluralist conceptions of constituent power and peoples that co-exist, yet conflict within the United Kingdom, thereby mapping distinct trajectories for possible constitutional futures in a union setting.
10.1177/00323217261469493.title: Constituent power and constituent collectives in a Union context: Deciding the futures of Scotland and the United Kingdom

10.1177/00323217261470570.abstract: Drawing on an inductive analysis of 21 interviews with women candidates at the 2024 elections in Belgium, our article questions how the perpetuation of sexism in politics is facilitated by its invisibilization, even among its victims. First, we show that despite an awareness of the prevalence of sexism in politics, women candidates often struggle to clearly identify its expressions. We show how the type of target (candidates’ profile), the type of sexism (benevolent vs hostile), and the context of its expression (online vs offline) affect the type of mechanisms women candidates turn to, but that it ultimately all leads to the same outcome: the invisibilization of sexism and its disconnect from candidates’ experience. We argue that the mechanisms uncovered can serve as an analytical grid in other contexts. Our findings call for a reconsideration of how sexism in politics is defined, understood, measured, and addressed by actors and institutions.
10.1177/00323217261470570.title: Too burdensome to be acknowledged? How sexism is rendered invisible to women candidates through seven mechanisms

10.1177/00323217261470674.abstract: Should all European Union (EU) citizens enjoy the same welfare benefits as nationals when they migrate within Europe? Which categories of EU migrants (workers, job-seekers and non-economically active ones) should be entitled to full equal treatment? I discuss reciprocity as a moral basis of EU law, extending White’s account of fair reciprocity to the supranational context of the EU. I suggest that the concept of workers in EU law should be reformed to account for a plurality of valuable contributions. I also discuss the implications of reciprocity in non-ideal conditions, arguing that EU migrants have a reduced contributive obligation when they face injustice in the host member state. The seriousness of such injustice may even imply lifting the contributive obligation entirely. The contributive obligation of non-economically active individuals is a duty to seek work, and I suggest it entitles them to limited equal treatment.
10.1177/00323217261470674.title: Fair reciprocity and EU law

10.1177/00323217261471324.abstract: Rational choice theories offer one of the major explanations for citizens’ voting behavior. The most prominent models within the rational choice framework – spatial and valence voting – share the same roots but differ in central aspects, emphasizing ideological congruence and competence evaluations, respectively. In this note, we provide a direct test of the models’ relative strength. Does a party’s issue congruence with a voter (spatial) or its effectiveness in handling important issues (valence) have a larger effect on vote choice? Our results from lab-like conditions using a novel conjoint experiment show strong evidence for both models, but valence evaluations consistently trump spatial considerations. These results have important implications for research on electoral behavior, party politics, and democratic representation.
10.1177/00323217261471324.title: Two competing giants: An experimental test of spatial and valence models of voting

10.1177/00323217261471745.abstract: Normative research on greenwashing has largely focused on the environmental and economic consequences of false or misleading green claims. This article introduces a new perspective that sheds light on its democratic costs. First, I argue that by interfering with the transmission of a public political culture through deceptive claims, greenwashing constitutes a particularly problematic form of corporate capture of democratic rhetoric. I further contend that greenwashing should also be examined against ordinary patterns of language use, given their capacity to shape the range of communicative possibilities available. At the normative level, I then defend a duty to counter-frame: a duty of ordinary citizens to play their part in avoiding reinforcing the communicative conditions that facilitate corporate capture of public rhetoric. This duty aims to initiate processes of reciprocal reason-giving about responsible language use within everyday conversations.
10.1177/00323217261471745.title: The undemocratic face of greenwashing and the duty to counter-frame

10.1177/00323217261472280.abstract: Differences in political participation between social classes are well documented, yet less is known about the mechanisms that may reduce these gaps. This article adopts a life-course perspective to investigate whether youth volunteering can mitigate class-based inequalities in electoral participation. Using longitudinal data from Germany, we analyse how class of origin affects voting for the newly enfranchised, how volunteering influences turnout, and how both factors interact. Our findings show that, while individuals from working-class backgrounds are less likely to vote and youth volunteering increases electoral participation for all, volunteering during youth nearly closes the participation gap linked to social origin and uplifts specifically blue-collar working-class children’s electoral participation. These results suggest that voluntary engagement in youth can serve as a “school of democracy,” reducing class-based inequalities in political participation starting at an early age, which remain persistent otherwise.
10.1177/00323217261472280.title: Class of origin and voting: The activating role of volunteering during youth

10.1177/00323217261476864.abstract: Democracies around the world have increasingly faced concerted efforts to dismantle democratic institutions. How should public speakers respond to such attempts at democratic backsliding? A widespread rhetorical strategy is to affirm democracy —that is, to publicly invoke the value of democracy and vigorously insist on the need to defend it. I argue that this practice gives rise to an underappreciated democratic dilemma. On one hand, distinctive features of the backsliding process seemingly require us to affirm democracy. Yet, on the other hand, this practice also poses serious dangers for democracy. For one, it risks accelerating democratic erosion. Moreover, efforts to limit this risk seemingly violate democratic requirements of truthfulness. So, both affirming democracy and failing to do so involve significant democratic pitfalls. The best way to navigate this dilemma, I contend, is not to forgo affirming democracy. Instead, it is to do so in a way that emphasises elites’ concrete attacks on democracy, while insisting that most people are strongly committed to democracy. While this approach may indeed involve some deception—insofar as it may knowingly overstate support for democracy—this is often all-things-considered justified.
10.1177/00323217261476864.title: Affirming democracy: Should we exaggerate support for democracy to save it?

10.1177/00323217261477312.abstract: This article argues that the case of an idiosyncratic digital movement in Paris—#saccageparis—has much to contribute to recent debates around social media’s democratic potential. #saccageparis leaders paint themselves as contemporary tribunes of the plebs, a permanent counter-power representing the “small people” of Paris against the municipality. Based on ethnographic fieldwork, I examine in this article such claim. On the one hand, Twitter’s affordances enabled ordinary citizens to gain some of the attributes of a popular tribunate standing up to power while, on the other hand, the movement only gained this foothold because it was not itself popular. #saccageparis’s composition therefore contradicts its tactics, and the movement is best described as “bourgeois populism.” This case shows us how social media’s populist affordances can be exploited by elites and, as a result, offers precious insights for those interested in rescuing social media’s radical-democratic possibilities from elite capture.
10.1177/00323217261477312.title: Popular tribunate or bourgeois populism? #saccageparis and social media’s radical-democratic paradox

10.1177/00323217261479182.abstract: Worker cooperatives are often lauded as the ideal institutional form of workplace democracy. While the traditional firm subjects workers to hierarchical authority, cooperatives establish workers as owners and managers of their own venture. However, since 1911 Robert Michels popularised the phrase of an “iron law of oligarchy” to argue how nominally democratic institutions, like worker cooperatives, often fall back into hierarchical patterns. I claim that this criticism against workplace democracy is based on a misreading of Michels’ philosophy and a misrepresentation of today’s empirical research on cooperative management. Both present worker cooperatives as hybrid institutions torn between oligarchic and democratic pulls. By counterbalancing tendencies towards a concentration of power at the top with countervailing institutions that help rank-and-file workers contest managerial decision-making, worker cooperatives can safeguard themselves against degeneration and the iron law of oligarchy. This proposal of instituting workplace democracy through constant anti-hierarchical conflict, I call “plebeian cooperativism.”
10.1177/00323217261479182.title: Plebeian cooperativism: Reconciling workplace democracy with the iron law of oligarchy

10.1177/00323217261481637.abstract: Understanding how voters use the left-right scale is essential, as it is not only related to vote choice but also underpins how political scientists study ideology. This article finds that the way voters use the left-right scale is variable. Using British Election Study Internet Panel data from 2014 to 2024, I find that while economic and cultural values are both related to left-right self-placement, this varies both between individuals and over time. Those on the left of the self-placement scale can best be differentiated from one another by the strength of their economic values. For those on the right, cultural values are more useful in separating between different self-placement levels. Over time, left-right self-placement has become increasingly related to cultural values alongside economic values, driven by movements by people on both sides of the left-right scale. These findings indicate that even within one country, the meanings of ‘left’ and ‘right’ vary.
10.1177/00323217261481637.title: The changing meaning of left-right self-placement in the United Kingdom

10.1177/00323217261483794.abstract: Electoral success of radical right parties is often argued to normalize previously stigmatized anti-immigration attitudes. Yet, it remains unclear whether such normalization reflects genuine within-individual persuasion or shifts in the local climate of political expression. We address this question by linking highly disaggregated district-level vote shares to individual-level panel survey data from Sweden (2018–2022), a period marked by sustained growth and partial normalization of the Sweden Democrats. Cross-sectional analyses reveal pronounced contextual patterns: Restrictive immigration attitudes are more prevalent in districts with higher local radical right support, particularly among voters who do not support the party, while core supporters remain comparatively stable. However, first-difference panel analyses provide little evidence that changes in local radical right support are associated with attitudinal change. The findings suggest that what appears as normalization in ecological analyses is more consistent with contextual alignment than with rapid persuasion, clarifying the micro-foundations of radical right normalization.
10.1177/00323217261483794.title: Right up my alley: Local radical right success, contextual alignment, and immigration attitudes in Sweden

10.1177/00323217261484352.abstract: Do political parties shape where International Climate Funds are allocated? We examine this question in the context of India, where International Climate Funds create opportunities for the central government to leverage externally funded resources to advance domestic political interests. Drawing on a novel geo-coded dataset of project locations from the Kyoto Protocol’s Clean Development Mechanism, we show that projects are more likely to be allocated to constituencies represented by co-partisans of the Prime Minister’s party, and that this effect is strongest in competitive constituencies within states governed by opposition parties, where the central government has the sharpest incentives to build new support. This is surprising because existing literature on the Clean Development Mechanism suggests that decisions on project allocations are depoliticized. By demonstrating otherwise, this article contributes to the literature on International Climate Funds by demonstrating the importance of domestic politics in shaping its distribution.
10.1177/00323217261484352.title: The spatial politics of International Climate Finance: A case of India

10.1177/00323217261485652.abstract: Does exposure to conflict displacement amplify support for far-right parties? This study investigates the political consequences of conflict-induced displacement in northern Israel by exploiting a natural experiment arising from government-ordered evacuations during military conflicts. Using a pre-registered survey and a regression discontinuity design based on an exogenous 5 km threshold, I assess changes in retrospective and prospective voting behavior as well as self-reported political ideology. The analysis reveals no evidence that displacement increases far-right support or induces partisan realignment. Rather, evacuees demonstrate a modest rightward shift in ideological self-placement without corresponding changes in voting behavior. This divergence suggests that displacement influences symbolic political positioning without prompting corresponding changes in voting behavior. These patterns unfold against a broader backdrop of political frustration and electoral disengagement that affects both displaced and non-displaced populations. The findings reveal troubling implications for democratic accountability during external conflict: leaders may be shielded from electoral consequences of security failures even as civic engagement deteriorates, challenging models of wartime accountability.
10.1177/00323217261485652.title: Shifting sands? The impact of conflict displacement on voting

10.1177/00323217261490244.title: Corrigendum to “Trust in civil servants: A cross-national dataset for public policy research, 1986–2022”

10.1177/00905917251372301.title: Book Review: Arendt’s Solidarity: Anti-Semitism and Racism in the Atlantic World , by David D. Kim Arendt’s Solidarity: Anti-Semitism and Racism in the Atlantic World, by KimDavid D., Stanford University Press, 2024, 362 pages.

10.1177/00905917261430917.title: Review Essay: Where the State Cares to Care Dying Abroad: The Political Afterlives of Migration in Europe, by BalkanOsman, Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2023, 254 pp.Edges of Care: Living and Dying in No Man’s Land, by LeshemNoam, Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2025, 304 pp.

10.1177/00905917261433967.abstract: This article examines Ludwig von Mises’s utilitarianism in the context of his liberal social theory. It contends that he sought to reorient classical liberalism away from natural law theory and refound it in utilitarianism. This significant shift distinguishes and differentiates Misesian liberalism from the classical liberal tradition with which Mises consciously identified it, as well as later Rothbardian libertarianism, which, while identifying with the Misesian tradition, reverted to a natural law philosophy that produced irreconcilable differences with Misesian liberalism over the legitimacy of the state.
10.1177/00905917261433967.title: The Utilitarian Classical Liberalism of Ludwig von Mises and Its Libertarian Misreception

10.1177/00905917261433978.abstract: This article argues that Carl Schmitt’s approach to the visual expression of political power evolves from an early reliance on symbolic form to a later adoption of allegory, influenced by Walter Benjamin. Initially attracted to the Catholic Church as a symbolic synthesis of bureaucracy and charisma, Schmitt grew disillusioned with its modes of visual representation. He then turned to political myth, envisioning the national leader as the symbolic incarnation of a unified people. This model, however, also proved untenable. In search of an alternative, Schmitt drew on Benjamin’s theory of allegory to retrieve the Baroque tradition of state personification: Sovereigns, like actors on a stage, outwardly represent the state without claiming to exhaust its meaning. I contend that this allegorical framework allowed Schmitt not only to sidestep the totalizing tendencies of political myth but also to open a conceptual path for reimagining Europe’s postwar fractured space.
10.1177/00905917261433978.title: The Visibility of the State: Symbolic and Allegorical Representations in the Work of Carl Schmitt

10.1177/00905917261433990.abstract: The fact that Toward Perpetual Peace is presented as a satirical peace treaty is a detail that has been largely overlooked in the literature. This article argues that when one reads Toward Perpetual Peace with its formal presentation in mind, what emerges is a work of philosophical literature that acts politically through its rhetorical form. The article shows how Kant—through what is here called his rhetoric of hope—offers a political education to two kinds of readers: the many, who are susceptible to a “despotic” moralism, and the elite, who embrace the principles of a selfish despotism. The main elements of this education are Kant’s teaching on republicanism, as the only regime both prudent and morally legitimate, and his account of “Nature’s Guarantee” of human progress, which seeks to reorient how readers experience the apparent disagreement between morality and politics. The article then examines a third audience: philosophers who “dream that sweet dream” of perpetual peace. Kant teaches philosophers how to intervene in political life through philosophical uses of rhetorical modes of speech—such as irony, satire, and regulative narratives—designed to reorient the moral judgment of these different audiences.
10.1177/00905917261433990.title: Kant’s Rhetoric of Hope and the Philosopher’s Speech in Toward Perpetual Peace

10.1177/00905917261436337.abstract: In a democracy, ordinary citizens enjoy formal unaccountability, a condition that characterized classical Athens and that persists in a modified form in modern representative democracies. Popular unaccountability is both constitutive of democratic rule and inherently risky: Will citizens vote responsibly, and what might encourage them to do so?
