This article returns to classical Athens to analyze a paradigmatic scene of democratic politics whose dynamics remain relevant today: Elite orators addressing large, empowered, and formally unaccountable audiences. As the Athenian case indicates, democratic plurality, answerability, and intersubjective identity together create the conditions for what I call “reflexive accountability.” “Reflexive accountability” refers to citizens endeavoring to hold themselves accountable to those on behalf of whom, or in whose interest, they are expected to make political decisions. Political orators addressing empowered audiences initiate reflexive accountability when they ask citizens to imagine what they will say when other citizens, neighbors, or family members ask them how they voted and why. Reflexive accountability, as a distinctly democratic form of accountability and as a democratic ideal, is a litmus test for a healthy democratic regime, one in which citizens are encouraged to hold in mind those who will be affected by their actions and to take seriously another’s claim to a persuasive account of the soundness and justice of their vote.
10.1177/00905917261436337.title: “What Will You Tell Them When They Ask You?” Reflexive Accountability in a Democratic Regime

10.1177/00905917261441873.title: Book Review: Concrete Utopianism: The Politics of Temporality and Solidarity , by Gary Wilder Concrete Utopianism: The Politics of Temporality and Solidarity, by WilderGary, New York: Fordham University Press, 2022, 352pp.

10.1177/00905917261441874.title: Book Review: Prison Abolition for Realists , by Anna Terwiel Prison Abolition for Realists, by TerwielAnna, Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 2026, 248pp.

10.1177/00905917261444071.abstract: This article contests the tendency to see Islam as overwhelmingly collective and theorizes the individual from Islamic history and tradition of thought. It does so by recovering and recasting the ideas of Abul Hashim (1905–1974), a prominent South Asian anticolonial Muslim thinker and political actor. It examines how Hashim reconstructs Qur’anic ideas to oppose modern individualism primarily due to its loss of moral unity and advances a theory of the individual that argues for a unified ethical framework, which binds the individual, God, and others in an embedded relationship of love and care in the community. The article explores a unique trajectory for self-constitution developed within Islamic history and tradition—a trajectory that goes beyond the rise of the autonomous, reflexive, and self-serving individual without compromising the importance of one’s intention and conscience in shaping the self. This theory of the individual from the Islamic tradition refutes the Eurocentric framework of theorizing the concept by presenting a distinct framework that transcends the dichotomy between the individual and the community, a battle that is pervasive in contemporary Euro-American political thought.
10.1177/00905917261444071.title: Theorizing the Individual in Anticolonial Muslim Thought

10.1177/00905917261444336.abstract: This article makes the case for Locke as an early and important theorist of constituent power. His politics rests on the distinction between a constituent people or “Society” capable of generating its own laws and the constituted order or “Government.” The people are taken to possess not just ultimate sovereignty but also the agency to enforce that sovereignty if the need arises. The implications of this framework are traced through the lifecycle of the Lockean constitution—its birth (state of nature), maturity (civil condition), decline (prerogative), fall (dissolution), and renewal (promises and agreements).
10.1177/00905917261444336.title: Constituent Force: Creation and Destruction in Locke’s Political Thought

10.1177/00905917261446528.abstract: Can contemporary Confucian political theory contribute to both a culturally relevant and politically practicable public philosophy for East Asian societies, while simultaneously providing a model of comparative political theory that aspires to deprovincialize the West? This state-of-the-field essay examines how contemporary Confucian political theory has evolved in the past two decades in Anglophone academia, what challenges are posed to its further development, and how they could be addressed to anticipate a new epoch of modern political Confucianism in which Confucian political theory becomes more engaged and grounded as a public philosophy that can also inspire Western political theory for mutual learning and growth. After critically examining various contemporary Confucian political theories—Confucian communitarianism, Confucian democracy, Confucian meritocracy, Confucian perfectionism, progressive Confucianism, and public-reason Confucianism—and their liberal challenges, this essay diagnoses the current crisis of Confucian political theory and shows a way to overcome it.
10.1177/00905917261446528.title: State-of-the-Field Essay: Contemporary Confucian Political Theory: Its Origin, Evolution, and Challenges

10.1177/00905917261447494.title: Book Review: Power in the Anthropocene , by Lars Tønder Power in the Anthropocene, by TønderLars. Edinburgh University Press. 272pp.

10.1177/00905917261448201.abstract: During the first decades of the twentieth century, the word “democracy” was rarely used to describe existing political systems. Rather, it was usually employed polemically to criticize European parliamentary regimes for their incapacity to actualize the principle of popular power. Critiques of parliamentarism in the name of democracy were numerous and came from all sides of the political spectrum. This paper analyses them through the lens offered by debates about the use of the referendum. The “direct appeal to the people” was widely discussed at the turn between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries: It was the lowest common denominator of otherwise highly divergent political projects, all of which appealed to democracy to overcome the failures of parliamentarism. Yet their diagnoses of what was wrong with parliamentary regimes differed widely, as did their interpretations of the democratic nature of the referendum. In what follows, I will analyze three different critiques of parliamentarism, and their corresponding theories of democracy, as outlined through debates about the referendum in Europe from 1890 to 1935.
10.1177/00905917261448201.title: “Barricades Across the Road to Democracy”: The Referendum and the Crisis of Parliamentarism in Europe, 1890–1930

10.1177/00905917261450923.abstract: The “vanguard perspective” in Marxist revolutionary theory has long been a focal point of debate within leftist political thought, and it also represents an alternative path of social transformation beyond capitalist democracy and authoritarian rule. However, even in certain strands of contemporary leftist political thought, especially within post-Marxist thought, this perspective has essentially been misread as “vanguardism,” in which the binary opposition between the vanguard and the masses implies authoritarianism and is therefore to be thoroughly rejected. Among these critiques, Rancière, with his egalitarian thought, argues that vanguardism diminishes the subjectivity and agency of proletarians, thus creating an unequal power structure within. Despite Rancière’s profound critique of vanguardism, the fundamental issue lies in the fact that Marxist revolutionary theory upholds the “vanguard perspective,” not “vanguardism.” When returning to the thoughts of classical Marxist revolutionary theorists, one can see that the wisdom of Marxist vanguard stems from the proletariat and reflects its interests, with the connection between the two being grounded in democracy. Therefore, by reinterpreting the vanguard perspective, a form of substantive democracy and equality can be envisioned.
10.1177/00905917261450923.title: Reinterpreting the Vanguard Perspective Within Marxism: From the Critique of Vanguardism Back to Marxism Itself

10.1177/00905917261452990.abstract: How to address the grief that attends the inevitable loss in war of those we love? How to turn victims of war into heroes? How to resolve the agonizing choices that war imposes on us? Euripides’s Iphigenia at Aulis , the tale of Agamemnon’s sacrifice of his daughter, and Pericles’s Funeral Oration as imagined by Thucydides were both written during the Peloponnesian War, and each points to the creation of stories told to assuage the grief that follows the loss of loved ones and to obscure the challenging moral choices that wars demand. Euripides’s characters are trapped by the moral ambiguities that plague our political decision-making and, through a startling conclusion to the play that recalls the language of Pericles’s Funeral Oration, they welcome the “vain myths” we introduce to make our wartime decisions seem painless and our moral dilemmas disappear. Only the mother Clytemnestra refuses to be lulled by the stories or disappear happily within the walls of her palace. The tragedian can give full voice to the complex role of those stories; the rhetoric of the political leader obscures the ambiguity and “vanity” of those myths. Given the wide familiarity with Pericles’s Funeral Oration, I devote most of my attention to Euripides’s Iphigenia at Aulis and conclude with a discussion of Pericles’s famous speech.
10.1177/00905917261452990.title: The Stories We Tell: Euripides’s Iphigenia at Aulis and Pericles’s Funeral Oration

10.1177/00905917261455411.title: Book Review: Postcolonial Global Justice , by Chan, Shuk Ying Postcolonial Global Justice, by ChanShuk YingPrinceton University Press, 2025, 280 pp.

10.1177/00905917261462875.abstract: The defense of gay rights and other liberal values by some right-wing populists is often perceived as an opportunistic strategy to justify anti-Muslim policies. But this explanation for co-optation of liberal values by parties that are considered to be in conflict with liberalism circumvents a proper analysis of the phenomenon. I will therefore investigate this element within populist politics as a problem of liberalism, rather than of populism. Doing so, this paper holds that co-optation of liberal values by right-wing populists follows from a distinctly liberal dialectic and, genealogically, represents a distinct strand of liberalism. Firstly, I will discuss the origins of populism in the Netherlands and present them as an exemplary case of what Adam Tebble calls “identity liberalism.” Secondly, I will analyze two foundational texts of the Dutch Party for Freedom to demonstrate its indebtedness to liberalism, and the correspondence of its argumentation to the philosophical problem known as the Böckenförde dilemma. Finally, I will show how identity liberalism is a conceivable, although not necessary, response to this dilemma. The politicization of liberal values by right-wing populists proves to be an attempt to solve the Böckenförde dilemma by turning these values into a marker of identity. This results in a type of liberalism that turns the initially inclusive liberalism into a politically exclusive doctrine.
10.1177/00905917261462875.title: Limits to Tolerance: The Politicization of Liberal Values

10.1177/00905917261463527.abstract: This essay argues that hunger functions as one of the primary passions driving political association in Thomas Hobbes’s materialist political philosophy. Despite the extensive scholarly focus on fear and the social contract, the pivotal role of bodily needs—particularly hunger—in shaping Hobbes’s entire political framework remains underexamined. By attending closely to hunger within Hobbes’s political thought, we can understand how his metaphysical materialism directly informed his political ideas, providing unique insights into the bodily basis of political legitimacy and prefiguring later materialist philosophies. The analysis critically engages with Samantha Frost’s materialist interpretation of Hobbes whilst also incorporating insights from Gregory Kavka and contemporary phenomenological approaches to embodied vulnerability. Through an examination of seventeenth-century English economic conditions, and drawing on Maurice Merleau-Ponty’s phenomenological work, the essay demonstrates that, according to Hobbes, political legitimacy fundamentally depends on the sovereign’s ability to ensure not just survival, but also the material conditions that enable a “delightful living.” This bodily political theory reveals hunger to be more than just a mechanical need; it is also an experiential disruption to the perceptual and social foundations necessary for political community.
10.1177/00905917261463527.title: The Bodily Foundations of Sovereignty: Hunger and Material Necessity in Hobbes’s Political Philosophy

10.1177/00905917261463789.title: Book Review: Deadly Refusals: Kurdish Decolonization in Times of Terrorism , by Serra Hakyemez Deadly Refusals: Kurdish Decolonization in Times of Terrorism, by HakyemezSerra. University of Minnesota Press, 2026, 312 pp.

10.1177/00905917261467336.abstract: This article offers a feminist reworking of Adriana Cavarero’s conceptualization of horrorism as a form of extreme violence that targets and dehumanizes its victims through dismemberment and an ontological assault on human uniqueness. While Cavarero’s intervention is motivated by a commitment to resisting patriarchal logics of war and reorienting political thought toward care, we argue that her framework depends on an overly fixed opposition between the monstrous perpetrator and the defenseless victim, exemplified in her reading of Medusa in contrast with the Christian Madonna. The binary risks reproducing the very logics of exclusion and moral absolutism it seeks to disrupt. Demonstrating the point, we engage in a critical rereading of Medusa across classical and later interpretive traditions that demonstrates how she cannot be reduced to an emblem of absolute monstrosity, but instead appears as a plural figure: victim, goddess, protector, and generative presence—as well as a destructive monster. This reading destabilizes Cavarero’s conceptualization of both horrorism and victimhood, revealing the political and narrative instability of these categories. In reaction, we develop a feminist framework for responding to contemporary violence that shifts analysis away from moralized typologies toward a relational and narratively mediated understanding of violence. This approach retains Cavarero’s commitments to relationality and uniqueness, but rejects the closure produced by the neologism “horrorism,” instead foregrounding the entanglement of care and violence and the contested processes through which both are recognized and named.
10.1177/00905917261467336.title: Care and Contemporary Violence: Deconstructing the Monstrous in/as Cavarero’s Horrorism

10.1177/00905917261474038.abstract: Political theorists have long focused their understanding of democratic education on the institution of the school, particularly the public school, to the exclusion of broader visions of education beyond schooling. But as criticisms of schooling from outside the academy mount, it becomes imperative to examine the origins of American educational thought to determine whether opposition to schooling has an older historical source. This essay locates the roots of school skepticism in an alternative American educational tradition beginning with Benjamin Franklin that drew on Locke’s pedagogical arguments to devalue institutional schooling in favor of self-education. Franklin’s educational vision harnessed the independence of the young in early America by incentivizing learning through friendship and self-interest, and resorted to schools only as a guardrail against the abuse of freedom, incorporating them but minimizing their role in education. In this, Franklin initiated the Americanization of Lockean pedagogy, or the school-skeptical tradition in American thought.
10.1177/00905917261474038.title: Benjamin Franklin and Democratic Education Beyond Schooling

10.1177/00905917261476646.title: Book Review: Free Gifts. Capitalism and the Politics of Nature , by Alyssa Battistoni Free Gifts. Capitalism and the Politics of Nature, by BattistoniAlyssa, Princeton and Oxford: Princeton University Press, 2025, 328 pp.

10.1177/00905917261483273.title: Book Review: Founding Fanatics: Extremism and the Formation of American Democracy , by Eber-Schmid Noah Founding Fanatics: Extremism and the Formation of American Democracy, by Eber-SchmidNoah, New York: Oxford, 2025, 228 pp.

10.1177/00905917261484161.title: Book Review: Property Disobedience as Protest: Rethinking Political Nonviolence , by Scheuerman, William E. Property Disobedience as Protest: Rethinking Political Nonviolence, by ScheuermanWilliam E., Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2026, 232pp.

10.1177/01914537261434915.abstract: For Gilles Deleuze and Jacques Rancière, representation is a crucial intersection between aesthetic and political concerns. Examining this nexus reveals the conditions necessary for minorities to gain visibility and voice in the collective public sphere. The ongoing crisis of democracy today raises fundamental questions about the relationship between democracy and representation: Is democracy a system in which all voices are accounted for? Does the election of autocratic leaders indicate an anti-democratic shift, or does it, in fact, express a radical dissensus that is intrinsic to democracy itself? Juxtaposing the perspectives of Deleuze and Rancière, I offer a critical examination of the limits of representation – not merely as a procedural mechanism of exclusion and inclusion, but as a philosophical framework with far-reaching political implications.
10.1177/01914537261434915.title: Gilles Deleuze and Jacques Rancière on the Limits of Representation

10.1177/01914537261434922.abstract: What is digital fascism? What is digital capitalism? How are they related? This article theorises digital fascism as a contemporary form of right-wing authoritarianism rooted in capitalism and reorganised through digital infrastructures. Building on the Frankfurt School’s analysis of authoritarianism, it reconceptualises fascism as a terroristic, anti-democratic mode of organisation – leadership cults, nationalism, friend/enemy polarisation, and militant patriarchy – whose resurgence is catalysed by capitalist crises. The paper advances a dual framework: fascist practices (cognition, communication, co-production) and digital structures (platforms, algorithms, datafication) recursively produce one another – the tripleC dynamic – enabling user-generated hate, post-truth propaganda, algorithmic targeting, cyber-attacks, and digitally mediated violence. Ten historical hypotheses map shifts from broadcast propaganda to influencer networks, from street militias to partially automated conflict, and from overt anti-democracy to “creeping” authoritarianism that claims democratic legitimacy. Integrating political economy evidence, the article demonstrates how key fractions of digital, financial, and fossil/transport capital fund and legitimise emergent authoritarian projects, crystallising an authoritarian digital capitalism whose boundary with digital fascism is porous. The conclusion argues for a digital democracy that counters the fusion of big business and big power in the digital age.
10.1177/01914537261434922.title: Digital Fascism and Digital Capitalism

10.1177/01914537261434929.abstract: How can constituent power be simultaneously constrained by law and genuinely democratic? This question has haunted constitutional theory since Sieyès distinguished constituent from constituted power. This article argues that political liberalism’s attempts to resolve this paradox generate two structural aporias. First, anti-foundationalist approaches to constituent power inevitably produce an invisible foundation: normative standards like “the most reasonable” operate as quasi-transcendental constraints even while disclaiming metaphysical commitments. Second, locating sovereignty in a transgenerational people creates an absent sovereign: ultimate democratic authority resides in an entity accessible only through juridical interpretation, never directly present to living citizens. Through critical engagement with Alessandro Ferrara’s Sovereignty across Generations (2023) and recent scholarship on intergenerational constitutionalism, I demonstrate that these aporias are not contingent flaws in particular theories but constitutive features of political liberalism’s broader project. Drawing on Lefort’s concept of democracy’s “empty place of power” and Arendt’s notion of natality, I argue that constitutional democracy depends on sustaining permanent tensions between popular sovereignty and normative constraint, between democratic self-governance and inherited commitments. Political liberalism’s future lies in embracing rather than eliminating its internal contradictions, accepting that sovereignty must remain contested if freedom is to endure without metaphysical foundations.
10.1177/01914537261434929.title: The Absent Sovereign and the Invisible Foundation: Political Liberalism’s Aporias in Theorizing Constituent Power

10.1177/01914537261434944.abstract: This article argues that certain irredeemable evildoers qualify—at least in some cases—as post-persons under certain normative accounts of personhood. Post-persons are conventionally understood as individuals who, due to injury, sickness, or cognitive decline, no longer meet the criteria for personhood where personhood is understood in terms of certain cognitive capacities. However, this article extends the concept to cases of moral failure in a way that has hitherto been neglected in the debate. Drawing on a Kantian-Arendtian conception of personhood, it argues that personhood includes not just rational or cognitive capacities, but moral reasoning and the capacity for remorse. Irredeemable evildoers—those whose actions are profoundly cruel and who persistently reject accountability—may forfeit their moral standing as persons. This shift from biological to moral criteria has serious implications for how we understand and treat such individuals.
10.1177/01914537261434944.title: Irredeemable Evildoers as Post-Persons

10.1177/01914537261438156.abstract: Political philosophers increasingly work within institutional environments shaped by metrified evaluation, hypercompetition, and publish-or-perish expectations. This article does not argue that political philosophy has empirically declined or become uniformly conservative. On the contrary, contemporary political theory shows significant pluralisation, including greater visibility for feminist, decolonial, ethnographic, and public-facing approaches. The central claim is instead that prevailing incentive structures generate predictable epistemic pathologies. By systematically rewarding work that is strategically legible, rapidly publishable, and easily refereed, they discourage slower, riskier, and more conceptually ambitious inquiry – especially among early-career scholars whose professional survival depends on repeated publication in a narrow set of high-status venues. Drawing on analyses of perverse incentives in the sciences, the article shows how analogous dynamics operate within political philosophy. It concludes by arguing that reforms to hiring, publishing, and evaluation practices could better align professional incentives with the epistemic goods political philosophy has reason to value.
10.1177/01914537261438156.title: What Incentive Structures Do to Political Philosophy: Epistemic Pathologies and Institutional Design

10.1177/01914537261438157.abstract: This article critically interrogates Max Horkheimer’s and Jürgen Habermas’s criticisms of Husserl’s idea of phenomenological philosophy as a rigorous science. It argues that both critical theorists basically misconstrue Husserl’s understanding of philosophical method and, consequently, miss an opportunity to engage not only with transcendental phenomenology’s critique of modern mathematical natural science but also with its significance for the renewal of a concept of substantive reason consistent with critical theory. Although Horkheimer posits, without ever properly clarifying, such a concept of reason and Habermas’s project centres on rethinking this concept, the lingering positivist and pragmatist presuppositions of both thinkers hinders serious engagement with Husserl’s thought.
10.1177/01914537261438157.title: Critical Theory, Transcendental Phenomenology, and the Status of Reason: Horkheimer and Habermas on Husserl’s Idea of Rigorous Philosophical Science

10.1177/01914537261438413.abstract: Who or what produces surplus value across the economy-ecology nexus? The question is central to Marxism and to eco-Marxism more specifically. This article argues that only labor-power produces value and develops what it calls the work theory of value . It argues, first, that abstract labor, the source of all value, comes onto the historical scene as labor-power. Second, it shows that labor-power has both a use-value, its capacity to do thermodynamic “work,” and an exchange-value, its wage, and that neither of these are unique to labor-power. Third and fourth, the article offers an immanent critique of labor-power and capital respectively. On this basis, the article concludes that labor-power “produces” value because it is an eccentric commodity, the unique part of the economy that has the power to refuse the transition from ecology to economy. In its struggle with capital, labor-power transforms ecological energy into economic “work” or value.
10.1177/01914537261438413.title: The Eccentric Commodity: Why Only Labor-Power Produces Value

10.1177/01914537261440195.abstract: This paper argues that the imagination plays an essential role in the (de)legitimization of power in two respects. First, the claim to power is legitimated by reciprocal belief in that claim, belief being a product of the imagination. I strengthen Paul Ricoeur’s argument that “ideology” creates reciprocal belief in the claim to power by substantiating his new theory of surplus-value and by situating ideological images within his general philosophy of imagination. Second, the formation and collapse of belief in legitimacy is explainable by reference to the dialectic between the reproductive (ideological) and productive (utopic) imagination. The productive imagination delegitimizes power by creating alternative realities in which the beliefs that legitimate power are undermined. In the course of defending these twin claims, I develop a theory of political legitimacy informed by the philosophy of imagination, one sub-branch of which is social imagination theory.
10.1177/01914537261440195.title: The Role of the Imagination in Legitimizing Power

10.1177/01914537261442114.abstract: In an article published in 1965, Carl Schmitt discusses political theology in the context of Protestant legal theories and calls for more political theological reflection on Calvinist thought. In this paper, I intend to answer Schmitt’s call and adopt his political theological method as a ‘sociology of juristic concepts’, and apply it to the concept of ‘sphere sovereignty’ that was developed by Dutch Neo-Calvinist thinkers in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. In contrast to the decisionist concept of sovereignty that Schmitt derived from Catholic authors, the Neo-Calvinist concept of sphere sovereignty is intended to limit the power of the sovereign and secure the independence of other institutions, primarily that of the church. A political theology of sphere sovereignty simultaneously contributes to Max Weber’s study of Calvinist economic influence on modernity. On this basis, some preliminary conclusions are provided about the relationship between Calvinism and secular modernity.
10.1177/01914537261442114.title: The Political Theology of Sphere Sovereignty

10.1177/01914537261443299.abstract: This article critiques a strain of critical philosophy of race that presumes an ability to remove the evaluative “distortions” of race-based judgements from perceptual accounts, exemplified by Charles Mills’ liberal recovery project. Utilizing Cinga Samson’s Okwe Nkunzana 6 as an example of a perceived human figure, it argues that one’s apprehension of the world requires an idealist approach where individual valuations guide their definition of worldly phenomena. Drawing from J. Reid Miller’s account of evaluative perception alongside George Yancy and P. F. Strawson, I explain how perceptual accounts of any subject necessarily include evaluative judgements based on embodied characteristics. I then reexamine the role of ideology in subject formation to explain the necessary disjunction between perceivers on said judgements. “Evaluative idealism” challenges the realist presumptions inherent in Mills and other antiracist prescriptives that imagine a value-neutral world beyond race-based ethical valuations. These valuations are then a necessary component of human perception.
10.1177/01914537261443299.title: Eyes and Darkness: Race and Idealism Through Cinga Samson’s Okwe Nkunzana 6

10.1177/01914537261443661.abstract: This article examines how digitalization challenges the foundations of constitutionalism and, in particular, the notion of constitutional revolutions. It contends that Cyber-Physical Social Systems (CPSS), whose advent is already under way in industry, infrastructure, city management, mobility, and housing, have set a new logic in motion that relies on the replication of the social world through the so-called ‘digital twinning’. Drawing on societal constitutionalism and social theory, the article argues that this has significant consequences for how power is constitutionalized, since the emerging ‘smart’ governance tends to permeate society and to dissolve the abstraction necessary for constitutional revolutions. While contemporary proposals from constitutional theory, such as digital constitutionalism and cybernetic socialism, address these transformations, they fall short of reviving the radical dimension of constitutional change. Finally, the article looks at how to re-specify the revolutionary legacy and how the notion of constituent power could play out vis-à-vis the digital sphere.
10.1177/01914537261443661.title: We, the Replicated: Constitutional Revolutions After Digital Twinning and Cyber-Physical Social Systems

10.1177/01914537261449754.abstract: This paper demonstrates the potential of democratic civility as a means of safeguarding democracy in times of populism and polarization. I construe democratic civility as a normative framework for interactions among citizens in civil society, anchored in a commitment to relating to one’s fellow citizens as respected adversaries. Conceptualizing democratic civility in this way advances the scholarly literature in three ways. First, by anchoring norms of civility in disagreement, democratic civility allows us to appreciate the transformative potential of populism and polarization while retaining sufficient normative resources to restrain their challenge to democracy. Second, democratic civility highlights shortcomings in recent critical and radical contributions to debates on civility and strikes a balance between skeptics and proponents of civility. Finally, democratic civility reveals how scholarship on democratic defense and depolarization has neglected the merits of civil society and provides a normative blueprint for evaluating new avenues for safeguarding democracy.
10.1177/01914537261449754.title: Democratic Civility in Times of Populism and Polarization

10.1177/01914537261449763.abstract: This article introduces the concept of postsecular antisemitism to name a condition in which prevailing frameworks struggle to register antisemitic harm that operates through the entanglement of religious and secular grammars. It argues that the assumption of normative separability between religious and secular domains, inherited from the secularization thesis and only partially challenged by the postsecular turn, continues to pre-structure what becomes legible within social theory. To develop this argument, the article stages a comparison between early and late Critical Theory. Whereas Horkheimer and Adorno refused to separate religious and secular elements into discrete explanatory domains, Habermas's influential postsecular approach assumes their normative separability even as the secularization prediction is abandoned. Drawing on recent cases of digital antisemitism, which make religious–secular entanglement visible, the article shows the limits of Habermas's procedural model and extends it through a constellational reconstruction of Adorno's approach. The analysis demonstrates how antisemitic harm can be displaced from critical scrutiny through its assignment across the religious–secular divide, clarifying how classificatory distinctions organize a gap between harm and the frameworks meant to register it. In doing so, it opens onto a broader reorientation of social theory beyond inherited assumptions of religious–secular separability.
10.1177/01914537261449763.title: Postsecular Antisemitism: Adorno, Habermas, and the Frames of Exclusion

10.1177/01914537261449766.abstract: This essay aims to reconstruct a liberal international political theory of New Confucianism by integrating Charles Taylor’s ontology-based and Andrew Linklater’s civility-based approaches to intercultural dialogue and transcultural values. It aligns the New Confucian vision of a “world of great harmony,” rooted in Wang Yangming’s idea of “all-under-Heaven as one family,” with modern cosmopolitan discourse to develop a philosophical sketch of Confucian cosmopolitanism. The study addresses four central issues in the construction of a universal moral community and its relationship with the political community: (1) the moral basis of human rights, (2) the institutional recognition of human rights, (3) the convergence of norms of civility, and (4) the moral grounding for promoting global civility. Through this framework, it advances a normative Confucian vision of weak cosmopolitanism that promotes a shared global moral consensus on human rights and civility while respecting state sovereignty and cultural diversity. It also aims to engage with cultural relativism in China.
10.1177/01914537261449766.title: A Philosophical Sketch of Confucian Cosmopolitanism: The Liberal International Political Theory of New Confucianism

10.1177/01914537261449770.abstract: The recent political turn in theorizing the corporation has drawn attention to the extensive power that corporations possess, but has not yet provided a systematic normative account of corporate political power. This article proposes a “political capability approach” to address this. It identifies four forms of corporate political power: law-making, governance, discursive, and democratic will-shaping. The approach differentiates politically significant corporations from ordinary ones along two dimensions: vertically, by how many of these capabilities a corporation possesses in combination; and horizontally, by the scale and reach of each. Conventional metrics such as firm size or wealth are imperfect proxies for political power. The political capability approach instead connects normative evaluation directly to the concrete powers corporations exercise. It offers a more nuanced and empirically grounded basis for assessing which corporations warrant democratic justification, and for matching regulatory remedies to the specific capabilities that threaten democratic values.
10.1177/01914537261449770.title: A Political Capability Approach to Corporate Power: A “Political” Political Theory of the Corporation

10.1177/01914537261449771.abstract: This paper examines the role of emotions in recognizing others’ vulnerability and motivating care practices, proposing a Kantian model centered on the emotion of respect. The argument develops through a critical engagement with Michael Slote’s empathy-based approach, which assigns empathy a central role in perceiving vulnerability and generating moral motivation. I argue that approaches grounded exclusively in empathy risk producing asymmetric and unbalanced moral relationships. As an alternative, I propose shifting the focus from empathy to respect. The paper first analyzes vulnerability in relation to autonomy, understood as the capacity to freely pursue one’s conception of happiness, and defines vulnerability as a limitation in the full exercise of autonomous agency. Respect, on a Kantian view, enables recognition of the equal value of autonomy in oneself and others, even in relationships involving vulnerability. Moreover, respect makes violations of this value salient and motivates re-empowerment practices aimed at restoring autonomy. The final section applies this respect-based framework to Italians’ moral and social responsibilities toward immigrants.
10.1177/01914537261449771.title: A Respect-Based Approach to Vulnerability

10.1177/01914537261449785.abstract: Frantz Fanon’s writings remain controversial for the force and openness with which they advocate violence in the context of decolonial political struggle. Prima facie, Fanon appears to suggest that decolonial political violence is somehow inherently good; this places him in tension with a certain common-sense thought about the ethics of political violence, which is that it is only OK to commit acts of violence when they cannot be avoided. In this paper however, I argue that this tension with the ‘common-sense view’ is only seeming. I show this by establishing that what Fanon is really interested in is the ability of the native to exercise what Jonathan Gingerich has recently dubbed ‘spontaneous freedom’. Via work by Hannah Arendt, which Gingerich also cites, I argue that this shouldn’t surprise us, since spontaneous freedom is necessary for the establishing and maintenance of political communities. In colonial societies, as Fanon argues, violence is the only means the native has for expressing their free, spontaneous agency. This is why it cannot be avoided.
10.1177/01914537261449785.title: Fanon, Violence, and Spontaneous Freedom

10.1177/01914537261450645.abstract: In both 1990’s Conditions Handsome and Unhandsome and 2004’s Cities of Words , Stanley Cavell presents his contribution to democratic thought as an addendum to John Rawls’s Theory of Justice . In this essay I consider the implications of this for Cavell’s understanding of democracy, focusing on his discussion of “the wager of democracy” in the later text. When one attends to the details of that discussion, as I do at some length, it becomes clear that this is not truly a wager of democracy , but rather one of liberal justice . I argue that our times require a genuine wager of democracy, one geared towards a collective future that emphasizes solidarity and collective agency over equality, consent, and individualism. Ironically, Cavell’s own work outside these chapters makes important contributions to our understanding of what this would entail. I conclude that Cavell’s corpus is less consistent and coherent than previously thought, and that, if we are to bring out his true importance to democratic culture, we need to read him to a certain extent against himself and much more critically of his liberal individualism than scholars have thus far done.
10.1177/01914537261450645.title: Cavell’s Wager, and Ours: Thinking With and Against Cavell in Dark Times

10.1177/01914537261454425.abstract: Big data and empirical social science share an often-subterraneous assumption, namely, positivism. Some of their jointly hidden premises are that experiences, preferences, and culture are all equally quantifiable, testable, and measurable. Further, their view is a reification of the status quo, a harmonistic view of society. On the other hand, the critical view espouses social antagonism , the view that society essentially consists of a struggle between groups. Critical theory argues against the critical rationalists that positivism (and thus, empirical social science) is guilty of a political agnosticism and, therefore, services the ends of bureaucracy and administration. This paper draws out some latent beliefs of big data as a new version of positivism and shows that big data inherits the problems of empirical social science. In particular, algorithms and data analytics for predictive policing, aggressively personalized advertisement, and prison recidivism stand out as substantial evidence of the new positivism that surges in administered society.
10.1177/01914537261454425.title: The New Positivism: A Hegelian Critique

10.1177/01914537261457140.abstract: Algorithmic governance is sometimes compared to Hobbes’s Leviathan. Here I argue that, while algorithmic governance shares some similarities with the Hobbesian schema, it goes further in its suppression of contestation. To show this, I read Hobbes against Rancière’s reduction of him to a theorist of consensus to make two basic points. First, it is important for Hobbes that laws be public and rationally comprehensible. By contrast, algorithmic governance is notoriously opaque. Second, Hobbes also retains a sense of equity as an appeal against universally applied legal decisions, allowing decisions to be tailored to individual cases. Algorithmic governance does not typically involve equity-based appeal, a point that is especially clear in the context of bureaucratic governance structures, where algorithmic systems generate results that cannot be either understood or appealed. The result in Rancière’s terms is that classificatory, algorithmic systems are even more powerful agents of depoliticization than Leviathan.
10.1177/01914537261457140.title: Erasing Agonism: How Algorithmic Governance Goes Further than Leviathan

10.1177/01914537261458698.abstract: Afro-pessimism poses one of the most profound challenges to contemporary political theory. By conceptualizing Blackness as social death, it argues that anti-Blackness is not a contingent injustice but the ontological ground of modernity. If Blackness names structural non-being, then universality—the category of the Human—appears intrinsically anti-Black. This article engages Afro-pessimism as a serious theoretical interlocutor in order to test the claim that antagonism grounds a negative universality. It argues, first, that Afro-pessimism correctly identifies anti-Blackness as the paradigmatic modern inscription of universality’s constitutive antagonism. However, it contends that Afro-pessimism risks converting structural centrality into ontological exception by positing Blackness as metaphysical singularity. Drawing on Lacanian psychoanalysis, Rancière’s account of the “part of no-part,” Žižek’s theory of antagonistic universality, McGowan’s account of shared limitation, and Kapoor and Zalloua’s theory of immanent antagonism, the article proposes that antagonism is universal but its social embodiment is racially stratified. Lack is structural; yet its symbolic management and libidinal displacement are historically organized through anti-Blackness and racial capitalism. Anti-Blackness thus reveals the traumatic kernel of universality without exhausting its logic. Such a negative conception of universality preserves the singularity of anti-Black violence while reopening the possibility of solidarity grounded not in analogy or identity but in shared structural division.
10.1177/01914537261458698.title: Anti-Blackness, Social Death, and Negative Universality

10.1177/01914537261458711.abstract: The recent wave of human rights-based climate litigation has raised the question of whether states can be held responsible for the impact of their greenhouse gas emissions on human rights outside their territory. Given the lack of legal consensus, this paper examines this question in light of philosophical theories of human rights. I argue that if the “humanist” conception of human rights holds, then states must bear extraterritorial obligations in the context of climate change. Most opponents of these obligations rely on alternative “practical” conceptions. However, I defend that even if we follow the practice of human rights, as these conceptions insist, its internal norms require the allocation of extraterritorial climate obligations. Thus, I aim not only to give normative support to climate advocates, but also, to contribute to the development of a practice-based approach to the philosophy of human rights which goes beyond the borders of the state.
10.1177/01914537261458711.title: Climate Change, Human Rights, and Extraterritorial Obligations

10.1177/01914537261460910.abstract: The European Commission has argued that the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) adopted in 2018 created a solid framework of digital trust. This paper critically examines the statement. Firstly, a Kantian approach to trust is outlined. In the second section, key aspects of the historical development of commercial trade in personal data and the regulatory efforts of the EU are analyzed. The third part of the paper considers the concept of consent both as a philosophical concept and as the main legal tool for protecting citizens’ data, arguing that the idea that citizens are able to make rational and informed choices about consent to sharing of data is currently fictitious. The final section draws on the Kantian conception of trust to evaluate the EU’s efforts to enable trustworthy data stewardship for its citizens in the digital information environment. The Kantian analysis concludes that even though the GDPR has the potential to supply citizens with trustworthy data protection, its enforcement procedures as well as the 2025 proposed amendments to the GDPR work against trustworthy data stewardship.
10.1177/01914537261460910.title: The EU Model of Digital Trust: A Kantian View on EU’s Recommendation of Citizens’ Trust in the GDPR

10.1177/01914537261463694.abstract: This article challenges the view that Adorno and Deleuze represent antithetical positions, arguing that both share the goal of harnessing the unconscious as a resource for critique. To reconstruct and relate their accounts, it looks beyond Freud to their readings of Kant. It shows that both thinkers appropriate psychoanalysis to actualize latent potentials within the “Copernican turn,” thereby rethinking critique. Adorno locates this potential in reason, transforming the thing-in-itself into a thinking of nonidentity. To this end, he politicizes Freud’s theory of symptom interpretation by reading suffering as an index of social pathologies. Deleuze, by contrast, focuses on sensibility, reworking Freud’s theory of the death drive to radicalize Kantian aesthetics into a productive thinking that unfolds desire. The article concludes by historicizing these accounts—Adorno in relation to fascism and the culture industry, Deleuze in relation to May ’68—and evaluates the contemporary significance of the unconscious for social criticism.
10.1177/01914537261463694.title: The Unconscious of Critique: Adorno and Deleuze as Readers of Kant and Freud

10.1177/01914537261467097.abstract: This paper introduces “nihilistic authoritarianism” as a useful concept for political analysis. This term has not been employed before in the scholarly literature, even though the basic idea is familiar from the history of political thought. It is not unusual to say that authoritarians desire power for its own sake. But the basic nihilism of such an idea has not been adequately analyzed. This idea is distinguished from “Platonic authoritarianism,” which consolidates power around a teleological commitment to a set of ethical values or social goals that transcends the political realm. Nihilistic authoritarianism is different. It is “autotelic” in the sense that it does not seek to actualize some further telos or to satisfy some principled justificatory schema. It also tends to consider political power as “autonomous” in the sense that “the political” is severed from other systems of value. Because of its strangeness, nihilistic authoritarianism is often misunderstood and misdiagnosed. The analysis presented here builds upon work found in critical theory and in more recent scholarly discussions of authoritarianism, while offering historical and literary references that help flesh out the phenomenon of nihilistic authoritarianism. In conclusion, a remedy is briefly suggested, which focuses on a broader integration of political power and other ethical and social ends.
10.1177/01914537261467097.title: Nihilistic Authoritarianism: Power as an End-in-Itself

10.1177/01914537261467101.abstract: Jürgen Habermas represents the transitional second generation of the Frankfurt School that must grapple with our contemporary, globalized times. Habermas’ move from communicative action to inquiring into the pre-political foundations of democracy takes Western philosophy to task but does not push the envelope far enough. Sections from The Philosophical Discourse of Modernity and an interview with Eduardo Mendieta (titled A Conversation About God and the World ) reveal an extant Eurocentric bias. I show that these very same texts contain strands that redeem critical theory for the contemporary, multicultural world(s) we inhabit today. I then take up Dr. B. R. Ambedkar—an Indian pragmatist contemporaneous with the Frankfurt School—as an example of how critical theory (by Max Horkheimer’s principles) might be done in a different cultural setting while remaining pragmatically sensitive to its particularities.
10.1177/01914537261467101.title: Going Beyond Occidental Theory: Critical Theory and Ambedkar’s Anti-Caste Praxis

10.1177/01914537261467108.abstract: Factionalism broadly describes the occurrence of conflicts between varying groups (or factions) within a social movement. Factionalism is often thought to be a negative feature of social movements. The goal of this paper is to (a) motivate the significance of the concept of factionalism for social and political philosophy and (b) give a definition of factionalism that captures the sense in which factionalism is a deep political problem. Specifically, the paper argues that factionalism is a form of anti-solidarity; factional groups are groups that, in virtue of their normal functionings, promote anti-solidaristic relations. Consequently, factionalism is particularly harmful because it has a transformative effect on movement actors: namely, it creates actors who are unwilling or unable to engage in collective political struggle. In a slogan: factionalism atomizes.
10.1177/01914537261467108.title: What Is Factionalism?

10.1177/01914537261468855.abstract: This article examines the semantic structure of the left-right political binary in contemporary Anglophone discourse. It argues that the fusion of “right” as directional orientation with “right” as moral correctness produces a form of semantic over-determination that complicates the articulation of democratic legitimacy in periods of political crisis. The claim is not that directional metaphors determine political outcomes, but that they furnish a discursive resource that can be mobilized in struggles over authority, order, and rectitude. To illuminate the contingency of this fusion, the article turns to the East Asian concept of zheng 正 (uprightness), whose semantic independence from handedness reveals that the association between direction and correctness is historically specific rather than conceptually necessary. Rather than proposing zheng as a replacement for the left-right political vocabulary, the article develops it as a diagnostic lens through which to distinguish questions of moral correctness, political legitimacy, and political orientation that English tends to conflate. By placing the Confucian doctrine of zhengming (Rectification of Names) into dialogue with contemporary democratic discourse, the article argues that the comparative value of zheng lies less in offering an alternative political language than in exposing the contingency of our own. It concludes that comparative political philosophy can contribute to democratic self-understanding not by replacing existing vocabularies but by making their underlying conceptual architecture newly visible.
10.1177/01914537261468855.title: Upright: Zheng 正 and the Semantics of Political Legitimacy

10.1177/01914537261471946.abstract: With its Afrological roots, debates about jazz improvisation almost invariably involve a discussion of freedom. This article argues that jazz improvisation is not concerned with individual liberty but focused on collective escape. This article proposes that improvisation is politically efficacious insofar that it is the motor of perennial revolution. That improvisation can transform apparatus of control from within is optimistic. Connecting Gilles Deleuze’s conception of exhaustion with Fred Moten's notion of escape, however, tempers this optimism and describes the ardour of the task. The variation of musical structures – and the habituated social relations to which they are tied – is exhausted by improvisation. This is not a destructive process but a creative one, producing novel connections and spaces in which political communities can be reimagined. Improvisation does not install some new hierarchy but opens itself to this same exhaustive process.
10.1177/01914537261471946.title: Exhaustion and Escape: The Political Efficacy of Jazz Improvisation

10.1177/01914537261475361.abstract: Drawing on Heller’s sustained dialogue with Kant and Marx, the paper argues for the continuing relevance of her social philosophy while also foregrounding unexpected affinities between these two classic figures in their respective conceptions of social and political community. I first examine Heller’s interpretation of the Marxian ethical-political legacy, paying particular attention to social experiments such as the Paris Commune and their significance for a radical Enlightenment project that rethinks the relationship between state and society. I then inspect Heller’s engagement with Kant and Marx on the historical continuity of republicanism, highlighting the rejection of instrumental domination and the demand for symmetric reciprocity among social agents. Finally, I analyze Heller’s theory of needs, particularly the concept of “radical needs,” and argue for its relevance to contemporary debates on democracy, social reproduction and non-paternalistic forms of political organization.
10.1177/01914537261475361.title: From Marx to Kant: Social Domination and Emancipatory Praxis in Ágnes Heller

10.1177/01914537261475362.abstract: Drawing from Kant’s philosophy of history, this article defends the view that, if peace is a duty, war cannot be a right. I argue that (1) (perpetual) peace can be accounted for as a historical duty : a goal that humankind ought to achieve throughout a historically situated process of moralization – according to the moral vocation of the human being itself – that essentially relies on juridical and political conditions. I then argue that (2) war represents a collective state of minority based on the inversion of the maxims of enlightened reason, of common human understanding, of wisdom. The upshot is that (3) war is always a practice contrary to morals and the seal of the breakdown of practical rationality and all bonds of community. Following Kant, the only viable option is international law in a cosmopolitical framework, whereby the rule of law ought to take war’s place as the means to the solution of all controversies.
10.1177/01914537261475362.title: The Duty of Peace and the Minority of War. Arguments From Kant

10.1177/01914537261475363.abstract: Maurizio Ferraris’ “new realism” rejects postmodern constructionism and insists on the unamendable independence of reality. Yet his dismissal of interpretation-friendly ontological accounts as inherently anti-realist overlooks richer possibilities within the hermeneutic tradition. I argue that Luigi Pareyson’s hermeneutic ontology provides the missing ground for Ferraris’ strong realist insights. Through a triadic analysis in which I pair Ferraris’ concepts of unamendability , positivity , and documentality with Pareyson’s treatment of inexhaustibility , congeniality , and testimoniality , respectively, I demonstrate that to interpret is to participate in the active constitution and disclosure of the real. Pareyson’s theory of “ontological personalism” effectively shows that the resistance of reality derives from its relational excess, not abstract independence. Synthesizing their views yields a realist hermeneutics capable of affirming truth’s binding character while recognizing the situated and plural nature of all knowledge claims. Against naïve objectivism and subjective relativism alike, Pareyson carves a fruitful path for contemporary debates about the nature of reality, scientific objectivity, and the politics of truth.
10.1177/01914537261475363.title: Realist Hermeneutics: Pareyson’s Challenge to New Realism

10.1177/01914537261475364.abstract: In the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals , Kant names beneficence, or promotion of another’s happiness, as the way we attain “positive” agreement with the humanity in another person (GMS 4:430). I argue, however, that beneficence is not the only way, or necessarily the preferred way, to secure this. By exploring the discussions of commerce and interaction found in Kant’s later practical philosophy, particularly the section on cosmopolitan right in the Metaphysics of Morals , I show that Kant makes available a substantively different way we can positively express recognition of others as ends in themselves. This alternative emphasizes not promoting another’s happiness but instead letting others influence both one’s own ends and other aspects of one’s identity.
10.1177/01914537261475364.title: Beyond Beneficence: Commerce and Interaction in Relation to Kant’s Formula of Humanity

10.1177/01914537261475366.abstract: This paper presents a pragmatist interpretation of John Stuart Mill’s arguments defending freedom of expression, drawing a comparison between Mill’s arguments in On Liberty and the work of Charles Peirce. I argue that Mill’s commitment to fallibilism in his argument for supporting free expression is more closely aligned with pragmatist concerns for collaborative inquiry than the liberal concern of mediating competing perspectives. This interpretation is supported by key contingencies in Mill’s argument, framed by his assumption that freedom of opinion facilitates a pursuit of truth. Exposure of such contingencies provides the basis for a more precise theoretical groundwork for outlining limits of free speech without necessary reference to Mill’s harm principle, with freedom of opinion being contingent upon said opinion’s pragmatic contribution to collaborative inquiry in the collective pursuit of truth. Freedom of opinion entails being receptive to genuine doubt and remaining open to revising our personal commitments and opinions.
10.1177/01914537261475366.title: Mill’s Pragmatism on Free Speech and Inquiry

10.1177/01914537261479780.abstract: This paper engages with recent debates about the value and future of work by proposing a shift in perspective: instead of asking whether work is normatively good or bad, the focus is placed on how work operates. Drawing on Michel Foucault’s concept of the dispositive, I conceptualise work as a historically specific and strategic arrangement of discourses, institutions, practices, and norms that binds individuals to the social world. Using Kathi Weeks’ theory of work’s antinomies, I show how contradiction is not incidental to work but central to its mode of operation. This framework makes it possible to reassess both contemporary attempts to recover the moral worth of work and post-work imaginaries that aim to abolish it. The paper argues that prominent normative accounts of work (e.g. Honneth, Gheaus and Herzog) overlook the mechanisms through which work is constituted as meaningful, while post-work theories, though politically generative, tend to underestimate the infrastructural and affective grip of the work dispositive. Reframing work as a dispositive thus offers a more critical and nuanced account of how it continues to shape subjectivity, social order, and ethical life—even in its imagined absence.
10.1177/01914537261479780.title: How Work Works on Work as a Dispositive

10.1177/01914537261481238.abstract: This paper treats anthropocentrism as a relational standing-order rather than only as a claim about intrinsic value. Anthropocentric arrangements give default priority to human convenience and self-image while shifting vulnerability and accountability costs elsewhere. The argument integrates moral deskilling, responsibility-gap analysis, relational standing, and vulnerability-first reasoning to explain a recurring pattern across nonhuman animals, environmental relations, and AI-mediated systems. Distorted relations damage intellectual capacities of understanding, judgment, and verification; emotional capacities of empathy, aversion, and attachment; and volitional capacities of commitment, responsibility-taking, and self-control. I analyze relational breakdown through instrumentalization, miscalibrated social response, responsibility diffusion, and attentional or empathic pollution. AI serves as an amplifier case because conversational, recommender, and automation systems can make these elements visible at scale. The paper proposes a minimal protocol: responsibility ownership, vulnerability-first attention, public anchors of traceability, contestability, and corrigibility, and capacity preservation.
10.1177/01914537261481238.title: A Minimal Protocol for Right Relations: Reframing the Critique of Anthropocentrism Through Responsibility, Vulnerability, and Public Anchors

10.1177/01914537261481239.abstract: Small nations occupy an ambiguous position within modern political life: they are formally recognized political subjects, yet their historical experience is persistently shaped by exposure to external domination, geopolitical dependency, and the recurring possibility of rupture. Their political existence is thus marked not by stable continuity alone, but by a heightened sensitivity to vulnerability, contingency, and the threat of non-existence. Despite this, contemporary political theory has struggled to conceptualize small nations beyond descriptive accounts of nationalism or episodic disruptions of an otherwise stable political order. Drawing on Jan Patočka’s political phenomenology, this article reconceptualizes vulnerability as a constitutive and collective condition of political life. Rather than treating vulnerability as an anomaly to be overcome, it analyzes how exposure to historical rupture shapes political agency, responsibility, and solidarity. By interpreting small nations as exposed communities , the article shows how political meaning and judgment emerge under conditions in which continuity cannot be assumed and guarantees remain fragile. In doing so, it challenges dominant assumptions about stability, sovereignty, and political mastery, and advances a critical phenomenological framework for rethinking political vulnerability beyond contexts of relative security.
10.1177/01914537261481239.title: Precarious Collectives: Rethinking Political Vulnerability Through Jan Patočka

10.1177/01914537261481242.abstract: According to Adorno, all attempts to change society “immediately come up against the overwhelming force of inertia in the prevailing situation, and seem condemned to impotence.” This article explores the way the phenomenon of social and institutional inertia has been addressed in recent Critical Theory. It poses two central questions: firstly, what is social inertia, and what causes it? And secondly, how do we judge when institutions or social norms are “inert” or “obsolete”? It first briefly discusses the historical background of the problem of inertia, obsolescence and second nature in Hegel, Marx and the first generation of the Frankfurt School, and then discusses the central questions primarily with reference to recent work by Jaeggi and Menke and, to a lesser extent, Rosa and Von Redecker.
10.1177/01914537261481242.title: Social Inertia in Critical Theory

10.1177/01914537261481243.abstract: Louis Althusser shows how interpellation functions as a mechanism for the constituting of subjects delineated through ideology. While Althusser focuses his analysis on verbal interpellation, critical theorists have shown that interpellation need not be limited to vocative hails. In this article, I show how one can interpellate with their bodily motility, comportment, and even physiological functions. In particular, I argue that racist ideologies can become naturalized onto bodies in such a way that individuals can interpellate racialized others as inhabiting inferior social positions. Racist embodied interpellations call racialized subjects to see themselves occupying stereotypical images which can fundamentally impact identity shaping processes. However, it is not the case that this subject formation is ontologically totalizing. Rather, embodied interpellations can cause the hailed racialized subject to confront the conflict between their own self-image and the dominant stereotypical perception of them. Quill Kukla offers a systematic overview of interpellation and describes two features of a successful interpellation. I utilize a concrete example that illustrates the importance of this topic from the literature in philosophy of race and show how the example entails the features of a successful interpellation as outlined by Kukla.
10.1177/01914537261481243.title: Embodied Interpellation: Racist Bodily Interactions and Racialized Subject Formation

10.1177/01914537261481244.abstract: This article traces a single, three-stage argument. It begins by documenting, with empirical precision, how digital platforms functioned as genuine instruments of horizontal mobilization during the North African uprisings of 2010–2012. It then analyses how those same platforms were rapidly incorporated into new and frequently more sophisticated architectures of social control, transforming what had been emancipatory tools into what Foucault would call dispositifs of docility. Finally, it asks what theoretical apparatus is adequate to comprehend this transition—and argues that the most productive framework is a deliberate synthesis of Foucault’s analytics of biopower and disciplinary normalization with Bauman’s diagnosis of liquid modernity. The contribution of Bauman is not merely decorative: his account of how solid disciplinary confinement mutates under liquid conditions into consensual, self-administered surveillance explains precisely why the digital panopticon is so much more difficult to resist than its institutional predecessors. The article also examines the epistemological dimensions of this subjection, attending to the structural marginalization of non-Western knowledge traditions through the normative alignment filters of Large Language Models. The argument is organized as a continuous analytical thread, not as a review of theoretical positions, and concludes with implications for decolonial critical theory.
10.1177/01914537261481244.title: The Architecture of Docility: Digital Platforms, Post-Revolutionary North Africa, and the Foucault–Bauman Dispositif

10.1177/01914537261481245.abstract: The present paper advances a reading of contemporary political apathy by rejecting its reduction to contingent sociological factors, and instead situating it within a transformation of the conditions of belief. Drawing on a Hegelian–Marxian lineage, it reinterprets the notion of Weltgeist as a secularized, ‘infra-material’ structure of shared intelligibility that conditions political participation. The argument contends that late capitalism has not merely commodified social relations but has attenuated the horizon within which belief acquires binding force, thereby producing a diffuse disaffection that manifests most acutely among younger cohorts in the ‘Western’ block. Against empiricist accounts of abstentionism, the paper proposes that disengagement is symptomatic of a deeper exhaustion of symbolic efficacy: political forms persist, but their capacity to command conviction has waned. Through a combination of philosophical analysis and cultural exempla – including Mark Fisher-style pop-cultural analysis – the study traces how ideological structures are both reproduced and hollowed out in everyday experience. The result is the loss of a shared grammar of belief. The emerging paradox is one whereby individuals continue to be addressed as political subjects, yet no longer experience that address as either ideologically compelling or existentially binding. Methodologically, this study adopts an interdisciplinary philosophical approach which combines phenomenological analysis, ideological critique, and selective sociological case studies, and that deliberately avoids exhaustive empirical explanations, in order to articulate, in a more ‘contemporaneous’ manner, the structural conditions of political intelligibility. By rearticulating political apathy as a structural and infra-material phenomenon, the paper seeks to reopen the epistemic question of political agency beyond the limits of both liberal institutionalism and orthodox materialism.
10.1177/01914537261481245.title: Whatever Happened to the Weltgeist?

10.1177/01914537261481246.abstract: This article critically explores council democracy as a utopian state order, on the basis of anarchist and Marxist works from western Europe and the United States, post-World War 2. As a system of national government, council democracy cannot possibly deliver on its utopian promises. Collective self-rule cannot put an end to domination/hierarchy/rule but will engender another variety of ‘democratic hierarchy’. Comprehensive citizen participation locks citizens in an overregulated ‘democratic bureaucracy’, and delivers no feasible, working formula of government. In a paradox, council democracy is likely greatly to reduce the share of the population participating in the country’s political process, thus carrying less rather than more democratic legitimacy than representative democracy.
10.1177/01914537261481246.title: Collective Self-Rule and Comprehensive Participation: A Critique of Council Democracy

10.1177/01914537261481247.abstract: Arthur Schopenhauer’s philosophy has been systematically excluded from the canon of radical political thought, dismissed as quietist resignation incompatible with emancipatory projects. This article challenges that exclusion by developing the concept of the pluriversal subject, a political subjectivity derived from Schopenhauer’s metaphysics of will, ethics of compassion (Mitleid), and aesthetic cognition. Where Laclau’s empty signifier demands that particular claims be made equivalent—sacrificing irreducible difference at the moment of articulation—and Žižek’s neo-Hegelian framework reinstates a privileged subject-position grounded in class antagonism, the pluriversal subject achieves solidarity through compassionate recognition of shared suffering without homogenizing the plurality of political claims. Drawing on Schopenhauer’s epistemological break from the Kantian-Hegelian tradition, his engagement with non-Western philosophical traditions, the activation of his ideas through the Nietzschean-Deleuzian lineage and Latin American decolonial thought (Mignolo, Quijano), the article demonstrates that his metaphysics furnishes a non-rationalist, non-identitarian ground for radical democratic politics under conditions of pluriversality.
10.1177/01914537261481247.title: Schopenhauer, Compassion, and the Radical Political Subject

10.1177/01914537261481248.abstract: Contemporary diagnoses of resurgent authoritarianism frequently attribute it to the political mobilization of fear, drawing on a long tradition that casts fear as the antithesis of freedom. This article argues that such a framework is conceptually inadequate in the face of climate breakdown. It critically engages scholarship that cautions against environmental fear and catastrophist discourse, identifying three key assumptions underpinning most of these critiques: that environmental fears are politically homologous to other historically theorized forms of fear; that fear directly fosters authoritarian tendencies at the individual level; and that fear consolidates reactionary power while weakening emancipatory movements at the collective level. Against this affective determinism and threat functionalism, the article draws on ecofeminist and anti-militarist thought to reconceptualize fear not as a regressive affect opposed to democratic agency, but as an ambivalent, critical orientation toward shared vulnerability. In this context, affective self-defense emerges as key: a mode of political praxis grounded in the open, collective acknowledgement and articulation of fear - rather than its suppression or instrumentalization - as a first step in the organization of resistance and care.
10.1177/01914537261481248.title: Reclaiming Fear in the Age of Climate Breakdown: From the Biopolitics of Catastrophe to Affective Self-Defense

10.1177/01914537261481252.abstract: This article offers a new reading of decadence in Nietzsche, not as a time of despair or sclerosis, but as one of individuality and freedom. It does so by focusing on decadence’s emancipatory potential for exceptional individuals. For Nietzsche, the best philosophers, artists, and heroes do not merely emerge despite, but thanks to, decadence. Decadent times come with the collapse of institutions, conventions, and values—a self-destructive milieu that proves catastrophic for the many, but offers the possibility of emancipation for the few. I then show that some of Nietzsche’s core concepts are tied to this account of decadence, and suggest that Nietzsche’s view can offer a counterpoint to competing accounts of decadence from reactionary critics of modernity.
10.1177/01914537261481252.title: Nietzsche on Decadence as Freedom

10.1177/01914537261481258.abstract: Recent philosophers of secularization have given religion a more central place in their thinking about secular modernity and liberal democracy. This article argues that such theories have overlooked an important dimension of the contemporary social and political landscape, namely how the framework of separating ‘religious’ and ‘secular’ spheres can paradoxically affirm the hegemonic position of Christianity and marginalize non-Christian minorities. Drawing on the work of Gil Anidjar, the article instead develops a critical narrative of secularization which points to continuations of Christian hegemony in the ‘secular’ realm, despite and through the religion-secular binary. Bringing this to the forefront is crucial for understanding how secularism can be compatible with the rise in Christian nationalist politics in Europe and North America, as well as the marginalization of racial and religious minorities. Moreover, the article argues, rethinking secularization raises important new questions for normative theory about religion and politics.
10.1177/01914537261481258.title: Rethinking Secularization: The Religion-Secular Binary, Christianity, and the Politics of Exclusion

10.1177/01914537261481740.abstract: Social experiences of unfairness resist standard distributional accounts. This article argues that comparative relations do not merely shape responses to unequal outcomes but participate in constituting the sense of entitlement through which those outcomes are experienced as unfair. Drawing on René Girard’s social theory of mimetic desire, Leon Festinger’s social comparison theory, Axel Honneth’s account of recognition, and empirical research on inequity aversion from behavioural economics and comparative psychology, it develops a single mechanism—comparative entitlement formation—linking proximate comparison, the felt claim it generates, grievance, and, under determinate conditions, displacement onto vulnerable third parties. The argument is positioned between two literatures that approach the phenomenon from opposite directions and leave the same gap: egalitarian political philosophy has moved from the distribution of bundles toward the quality of social relations without supplying an account of how a comparative sense of entitlement is formed, while the recent literature on political grievance documents comparative resentment in detail without theorising the mechanism that generates it. Two consequences follow. First, the characteristic irrationality of unfairness experience—its disproportionate intensity under conditions of social proximity and similarity—reflects the mechanics of comparative entitlement formation rather than a failure of rational judgement. Second, the harms produced when such entitlements are frustrated are second-order costs of institutional arrangements: they are generated by distributive structures, borne by parties outside the initial justification, and cannot be externalised from the basic structure. The article specifies the conditions under which the mechanism operates, the evidential criteria for identifying its products, and the limits beyond which it does not extend.
10.1177/01914537261481740.title: Comparative Desire and Social Violence: Mimetic Structure, Inequity, and the Scapegoat Dynamic

10.1177/01914537261484989.abstract: This paper addresses the problem of sexual misrecognition: some groups are excluded from being seen as sexually desirable or are hypersexualised. This shapes their sexual subjectivity – how they understand themselves as sexual agents. Despite widespread initiatives calling for recognition in the domain of sexuality, the need for sexual recognition has remained undertheorised in recognition theory. Building on debates on the ambivalence of recognition, I argue that sexuality has a uniquely complex relationship to recognition. While sexual recognition is necessary for subjectivity, it also reinforces subjection to power structures. Moreover, sexuality continually transgresses sociality and subjectivity itself. Using Jeanette Chedda’s erotic story in Damn Horny as a case study, I demonstrate how sexual recognition transgresses ideals of mutuality and equality, and theorise transformative possibilities for cultivating sexual subjectivity differently.
10.1177/01914537261484989.title: The Ambivalence of Recognition in Sexual Subjectivity

10.1177/02632764251398683.abstract: This interview with Philippe Descola, conducted on two occasions separated by the Covid pandemic, delves into his evolving theoretical framework concerning the anthropology of images. Descola reflects on his transition from written discourse in Beyond Nature and Culture to visual representation in Les Formes du visible . The discussion explores the intersection of structuralism, phenomenology, and iconology, highlighting Descola’s engagement with Aby Warburg’s theories and the works of Hans Belting and Horst Bredekamp. Reference is made to Descola’s four ontologies – animism, totemism, analogism, and naturalism – and their corresponding modes of identification and figuration. Through these lenses, Descola elucidates how different cultures conceptualize and depict their worlds, emphasizing the intentional autonomy of images and their role as efficacious agents.
