10.1177/07255136261464668.abstract: This comment on Villegas and Watt's reflective overview of Jeffrey Alexander's scholarly contributions, addresses canonization, the value of sociological tensions and neglected empirical components of his work.
10.1177/07255136261464668.title: Tensions and insights: More on ‘Reading Jeffrey C. Alexander’

10.1177/07255136261464671.abstract: What is the basis of canonization for social theorists? An accounting of the career of the prominent American sociologist Jeffrey Alexanders points to the basis of this reputational claim and its limitations. Alexander is one of the most widely respected theorists of the past half-century but viewing his broad interests in politics and civil society and his promotion of the Strong Program in cultural sociology provides a justification for his widely-acclaimed importance and the basis for the paired articles to which this squib is a response.
10.1177/07255136261464671.title: Saint Jeff

10.1177/07255136261464674.abstract: The article expands upon Villegas and Watts’ call for Jeffrey C. Alexander's work to be recognised as part of a renewed sociological canon by exploring the contemporary political complexity of establishing a neoclassical paradigm generally and the inclusion of Alexander specifically. Drawing on the sociology of intellectual movements, it is argued that elevating the status of Alexander would afford the discipline an important way to come to terms with recent shifts in democracy, nationalism and global power.
10.1177/07255136261464674.title: The politics and promise of Alexanderian neoclassical sociology

10.1177/07255136261464675.abstract: What makes a body of work ‘canonical’? In his writings over the years Jeffrey C. Alexander offers some phenomenologically convincing answers, each suggesting that the power of canonical texts is simultaneously context-immanent and context-transcending. However, a critical theory of ‘the canon’ cannot confine itself to phenomenological description. A critical theory is necessary due to the social constitution of the meanings of canonical texts. This gives rise to an endemic risk of ideological biases and the danger that canonization will reproduce and reinforce dominant perceptions of intellectual value, excluding or marginalizing authors and works who do not fit well with these perceptions. Accordingly, theories cognizant of this risk must explain the context-transcending component of the normativity of canonical works in a non-reductive way. This is a challenge for critical sociology.
10.1177/07255136261464675.title: Criticizing ‘the canon:’ A challenge for cultural sociology

10.1177/07255136261464682.abstract: No contemporary social-theoretical thinker has been more attuned to matters of verbal representation, literary genres, and the dramatic force of words and imagery than Jeffrey C. Alexander. Taking its lead from Villegas and Watts’ appreciation of him, this paper offers a jeu d’esprit of intellectual appreciation that traverses the ancient and modern worlds. It considers various literary genres and tropes involved in the creation of appreciative biographical writing. Riffing on terms such as Alexanderian, Alexandrian, Alexandrine and Alexanderesque, it relates Jeffrey C. Alexander, as biographical persona, to his antique namesake, Alexander the Great. The Greatness of the modern person(a) is brought into high relief through comparison with his ancient counterpart. The paper follows in the parallel footsteps of Alexander the ancient and Alexander the modern, seeking to exhibit some of their own respective forms of audacity in daring to make such a comparison.
10.1177/07255136261464682.title: From Alexander the Great to Alexander's Greatness, and back again: An ancient/modern jeu d’esprit of intellectual appreciation

10.1177/07255136261467761.abstract: Richard Wagner's Bayreuth Festival is presented as a ‘goldmine’ case study for sociology. Durkheimian approaches to the body overwhelmingly draw on the Elementary Forms to emphasize its productive role. Bodily ritual, rhythm and regulation help us experience the solidary force of the sacred. Durkheim's essay on The Duality of Human Nature adds complexity to this picture. Here Durkheim sees the body as blocking access to higher forms of social thought, as being egoistic rather than solidaristic, and as preventing focused attention on civilizational projects. This paper presents a new set of Durkheimian questions. It directs sociological inquiry to research the body not only as a resource but also as a barrier to transcendence. Furthermore, this paper takes up the challenge with reference to the experiences of opera fans at Bayreuth. A broader Durkheimian agenda would offer a more capacious sociology of the body and the sacred.
10.1177/07255136261467761.title: Durkheim, the body and the sacred: The neglected lesson of Homo duplex illustrated by the Wagner Bayreuth Festival

10.1177/07255136261467762.abstract: Angela Davis argues that Billie Holiday's music retains an “undiminished appeal” across generations because it can simultaneously “confirm and subvert racist and sexist representations of women” in romantic love. In this article, Davis's argument is extended through an examination of Holiday's narratives about and lived experience with a different kind of love: friendship. Friendship is detailed first as an ideal in the aesthetic partnership Holiday shared with tenor saxophonist Lester Young. Then, friendship's constraints are considered through Holiday's narratives about connections she made in childhood and with Benny Goodman, Artie Shaw, and Orson Welles. Where Holiday's love songs highlight the confines of sexism and racism, her reflections on friendship include classism and sexuality, and thereby provide insight into the ways intersectionality works to squeeze the potential for freedom and shared growth by coalescing around the identities that are either had by, or presumed of, those who share the friendship.
10.1177/07255136261467762.title: Billie Holiday on the constraints of friendship and a lived ideal

10.1177/07255136261467763.abstract: This article reimagines Postcolonial Security Studies (PSS) through the allegory of ancestors. It examines two generations of responses to coloniality in Security Studies – Third World Security Studies and Decolonial Security Studies – highlighting their fundamental contribution to the formation and evolution of PSS, while noting their partial disconnection from the ideas and traditions of the South. These often-ignored contributions could offer a deeper understanding of violence, state formation and liberation rooted in anti-colonial struggles. Rather than finding an epistemic rupture, the article argues for recovering liberation entities from formal and informal referents that carry memory and meaning. The examples of Brazil's Tambor de Sopapo and South Africa's Makhanda demonstrate how marginalised legacies might reorient the field. The article advances a people-centred PSS grounded in historical and community-based perspectives. This approach challenges Eurocentric frameworks and affirms the significance of knowledges and knowings of the South in theorising Security.
10.1177/07255136261467763.title: Never forget your ancestors: Reimagining postcolonial security studies

10.1177/07255136261467764.title: The eternal return: Bourdieu and reflexivity A review essay of: Bourdieu P (2025) Return to Reflexivity. Edited by Bourdieu J and Heilbron J, translated by Collier P. Cambridge: Polity Press.

10.1177/07255136261467765.abstract: This article examines dystopian literature as a critical counterpart to sociology, emphasizing its role in social self-description. The author introduces the concept of the sublimation of the negative, inspired by Niklas Luhmann, to explain how dystopias transform the negative side of self-descriptive social codes into tools for critical thought. The re-introduction of the distinction of good/evil allows dystopia to unmask the latent ‘social evil’ hidden within the utopias of efficiency promoted by other systems such as politics, science, or the economy, which are often blind to their own human costs. Unlike sociology, which often avoids speculative and future-oriented inquiries, dystopias embrace imaginative alternatives, addressing epistemic gaps such as de-futurization and the marginalization of subjective experience. Through analyses of works such as Gabriel de Tarde's The Underground Man , Edward Morgan Forster's The Machine Stops and Janusz A. Zajdel's Limes inferior , the article demonstrates dystopia's ability to transcend sociological explanatory schemes.
10.1177/07255136261467765.title: Dystopia and the limits of sociological thought: A critical exploration

10.1177/07255136261467766.abstract: This article examines how sustainability is rendered publicly legitimate in the current phase of green capitalism. Rather than treating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) as mere ideology or Solarpunk as external critique, it approaches both as modalities of public testing within a shared moral field. Drawing on Boltanski and Thévenot's sociology of justification, it argues that ecological legitimacy today is structured by a dominant normative test embedded in ESG discourse and a subordinate yet consequential sensible test, in which sustainability must also appear credible within shared perceptual horizons. To conceptualize this second dimension, the article introduces the notion of épreuve de sensibilité : a public test of rightness operating on the affective and aesthetic plane. Through a comparative analysis of European ESG regulatory texts (2019–2025) and a multilingual corpus of Solarpunk narratives (2012–2024), it shows how ecological morality is stabilized as procedural coherence in governance and staged as perceptual consonance in cultural imaginaries
10.1177/07255136261467766.title: Captured by the sun? Solarpunk, environmental, social, and governance criteria, and the pragmatics of green justification

10.1177/07255136261470444.abstract: This review essay critically engages Andrew Hartman's Karl Marx in America , a reception history of three different classes of readings of Marx's writings in the United States. The essay's main contention is that Hartman's text, however unintentionally, seems to deviate from and thus challenges the anti-foundational principles that orient the genre of reception history. For, echoing Shakespeare's, Hegel's, and Marx's uses of the metaphor of the “Old Mole,” Hartman's own commitment to a labor-oriented version of “Marx”—from the three he charts in his topography of the Marx–America dialectic—works its way through Karl Marx in America , appearing at the end of text to subvert the groundless doctrines that guide reception histories.
10.1177/07255136261470444.title: “Well grubbed, old mole!”: On Karl Marx in America by Andrew Hartman, University of Chicago Press, 2025

10.1177/07255136261473942.abstract: This interview with the philosopher Raymond Geuss, Professor Emeritus of Philosophy at the University of Cambridge, explores the questions animating his 2026 book Tracks in Chaos: Philosophical Orientation and Political Reflection (Polity). The book's title invokes Heidegger's image of the Holzweg – forest tracks cut through labour that often lead nowhere – which Geuss develops into a figure for philosophy as a historically situated, constrained, and dependent activity rather than an autonomous system. Drawing on his formation in Heidegger, Marx, and Adorno, he defends a suspicion of ordinary language and everyday concepts, proposing a ‘binary vision’ for operating within social practices while seeing through them. He distinguishes three senses of authority, none of which philosophy can claim, and separates ‘moralising’ from moral judgement proper. The interview closes with his diagnosis of a disintegrating West, marked by concentrated wealth and power, financialisation, technological deskilling, and a pervasive loss of orientation.
10.1177/07255136261473942.title: Paths to nowhere: An interview with Raymond Geuss about Tracks in Chaos

10.1177/07255136261473945.title: Book Review: A Hopeful Political Imagination: Courage and Fantastic Critique in the Age of Meltdown by Oscar Guardiola-Rivera Guardiola-RiveraOscar. A Hopeful Political Imagination: Courage and Fantastic Critique in the Age of Meltdown. New York: Bloomsbury Academic, 2025. 280 pp. ISBN (hardback) 9781666974454.

10.1177/07255136261480121.abstract: This article undertakes a historical-critical investigation of the intertwining of critical theory and functionalism in steps. It takes Adorno's critique of functionalism in architecture as a point of departure to distinguish the specific sense in which ‘functionalism’ is defined and subsequently rejected. The following section scrutinizes how critical theory deploys functionalist explanation, consciously or unconsciously, as the operative dynamic of its social diagnosis. On this basis, the third section utilises previously articulated methodological distinctions to outline critical theory's attempts at a normative reconstruction of the category of ‘function’. Then the inquiry pivots to the debates within analytical Marxism to examine critical theory's over-reliance on ‘objective teleology’ within its social diagnosis. Finally, the paper returns to the primary texts of sociological functionalism to refute critical theory's stereotype that equates function with end, thereby recovering more sophisticated understandings of functionalism for sociological analysis.
10.1177/07255136261480121.title: ‘Functionalist prejudice’: Critical theory and teleology

10.1177/07255136261480126.abstract: With the precipitous decline of functionalism as a theoretical paradigm, sociologists have become increasingly skeptical of descriptive claims about the functions of social phenomena. Despite this, ongoing debates about the function term in biology and philosophy have led many to reconsider the utility of functionalist language. Contributing to these debates, this article examines the value of talk about societal level functions. Specifically, I examine whether contemporary theories of the function term allow us to make objective distinctions between the functions of an item for society and the effects it has on society. Assessing several prominent accounts, I show that current approaches to the function/effect distinction continue to leave us with conceptual problems when applied at the societal level. The analysis suggests that the function term offers few explanatory benefits, and that we are right to remain wary of present efforts to revitalize functionalist thought.
10.1177/07255136261480126.title: Functional analysis at the societal level: Are there any pathways forward?

10.1177/07255136261480129.abstract: This contribution explores power and solidarity in Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology, bringing together his reflections on the social world in Phenomenology of Perception with his appraisal of sociology and Marxism in Signs and Adventures of the Dialectic . I argue that Merleau-Ponty reconfigures power as the crystallization of social interest that connects individuals and groups despite the differences in their social and political membership. This paves the way for a reconsideration of solidarity as the power to institute a different sense of reality from the shared experience of work and oppression. I conclude with an illustration of the contingency of solidarity in connection with the social struggle that led to the Italian law 199/2016 against the exploitation of undocumented workers.
10.1177/07255136261480129.title: Power and solidarity in Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology

10.1177/07255136261480130.abstract: This article argues that democratic double standards are not episodes of normative inconsistency but a mutable political technology for the differential distribution of legitimacy. The concept names a historically changing ensemble of institutional apparatuses, justificatory rationalities and material infrastructures through which the threshold of democratic legitimacy is unevenly allocated while its political function persists. It is distinguished from organised hypocrisy, ideology and discourse by four features: a function/mechanism distinction, institutional materiality, genealogical temporality and colonial asymmetry. The argument unfolds through a theory-generating genealogy organised around the Chile–Brazil axis – a historically dense dyad that condenses the technology in unusually legible form. Three moments of mutation are reconstructed: anti-communist destabilisation in Chile, the regionalisation of repression through Operation Condor and the reorganisation of political antagonism in Brazil. Integrating governmentality and the coloniality of power, it approaches Latin America as a theoretical archive for theorising the unevenness of democratic universalism.
10.1177/07255136261480130.title: Democratic double standards as a mutable political technology: A historical genealogy from Latin America

10.1177/07255136261485212.abstract: Contemporary critical theory elevates social norms to the status of positive knowledge and proclaims a politics of normative rightness to realise positive freedom and material equality in capitalist society. By accepting the positivity of norms, it fetishises them and prevents their denunciation, which alone exposes them. Based on the critical theories of Marx and Adorno, the article examines social norms as norms of a historically specific social content. In this process, the freedom of form is exposed in its content as the ‘freedom to starve’ (Adorno). Critique of exploitation does not call for normative arguments to understand its normative deficiencies with a view to achieving improvements. To understand the social norms, one must think in and through them to grasp their secret in the freedom of labour, which is the freedom of needy individuals to secure wage income. The circumstance that their prospects depend on the profitability of their labour connects the (promise of) freedom with exploitation.
10.1177/07255136261485212.title: Normative values and social critique: On Adorno and Marx

10.1177/07255136261485214.abstract: Neal Harris's Critical Theory and the Critique of Alternative Societies represents a significant contribution to the revival of first-generation Frankfurt School critical theory and its application to the contemporary alternative societies movement. This review essay evaluates Harris's central argument – that experimental pluralism among alternative societies is undermined by insufficient critique and an actionist displacement of strategic thinking – by placing it in dialogue with the existing scholarship on real utopias, workers’ cooperatives, mutual aid and universal basic income. The essay affirms the explanatory power of Harris's Frankfurt School framework, particularly his deployment of reification, instrumental rationality and repressive desublimation, while raising critical questions about the scope of the analysis, the tension between negativity and praxis and the risk of reproducing a specifically Western, male-centred theoretical horizon. The review ultimately endorses Harris's call for a renewed synthesis of critique and activism as an urgent priority for critical social theory.
10.1177/07255136261485214.title: Critique at the crossroads: On Neal Harris's Critical Theory and the Critique of Alternative Societies A review essay of Neal Harris (2026), Critical Theory and the Critique of Alternative Societies: Co-operatives, Mutual Aid and Universal Basic Income, Manchester: Manchester University Press, 254 pp. ISBN 978 1 5261 7222 8.

10.1177/07255136261487198.abstract: This introductory article critiques dominant, teleological social science narratives that position organised violence as a declining historical phenomenon. Instead, it asserts the structural centrality of warfare as a primary catalyst for institutional, political and societal transformation across human history. The author examines the dynamic relationship between organised violence and systemic social change, demonstrating how large-scale conflicts continue to reshape contemporary social orders. Finally, the text analyses the distinct features of war and peace in the modern era and provides a comprehensive overview of the nine academic contributions that compose this special issue.
10.1177/07255136261487198.title: War and peace in the early 21st century: An introduction

10.1177/07255136261487199.abstract: Culturally specific collective memories often give rise to potent and emotional historical analogues, used to mobilize people and to understand new situations. This article examines such emotional analogues through the still dominant but highly selective Finnish collective memory of the Winter War, which shaped the Finnish public discourse of the War in Ukraine after 2022. The Winter War constitutes a central building block for Finnish national identity. The similarities between the Winter War and the War in Ukraine helped make the latter more relatable among the Finnish society. The emotions raised by the analogue helped with the mobilization of sympathy for the Ukrainian cause. Simultaneously, the piecemeal use of the Winter War analogue transposed mythical expectations from Finnish collective memory on Ukrainians in a manner that biased attempts to understand the ongoing war. By linking socially constructed collective war memories to emotional historical analogues, the article emphasizes the importance of cultural sociology of war.
10.1177/07255136261487199.title: Collective memories, emotional analogues and war: How the Winter War shaped the Finnish public understanding of the War in Ukraine

10.1177/07255136261487201.abstract: This article examines the disappearance of the liberal peace paradigm. I examine how peace itself ceases to exist by drawing on the case of Kibbutz Be’eri, long associated with Israel's peace camp and known for its close ties with residents of Gaza, in which dozens of residents were killed or taken hostage, and its response to the October 7 massacre. The Be’eri residents were confronted with a triple shock: (a) the sudden and unexpected massacre; (b) the profound break of trust and feelings of abandonment from the state; and (c) the failure of their core belief in the liberal peace paradigm. I argue that three interconnected features – Trump's version of peace that excludes peace; the state-led projects of narratives of resilience, bravery, and heroism; and the Be’eri residents’ public disclosure of pain – made (liberal) peace obsolete and ousted it from the political horizon.
10.1177/07255136261487201.title: Is peace becoming obsolete? The Kibbutz Be’eri file

10.1177/07255136261487202.abstract: This essay asks whether warmaking can discipline the contemporary strongman regimes, as Tilly's account of European state formation might suggest it once did absolutism. To probe this question, it briefly revisits two non-European cases: New Kingdom Ancient Egypt and Warring States China. In neither does the European pattern hold. These historical cases help us identify the scope conditions for the mechanism identified by Tilly. Put briefly, warmaking generates the resistance that can constrain a personalised centre if the mechanisms of extraction are still being built rather than inherited, if the resisters to the centre hold their own autonomous resources, and if the pace of centralisation is slow enough to give the resisters time to organise. Most contemporary strongman regimes lack at least the first two of these, suggesting that warmaking in the twenty-first century will not provide the constraint on personalised, centralised sovereignty as it did in early modern Europe.
10.1177/07255136261487202.title: Strongmen and warmaking

10.1177/07255136261487203.abstract: This article examines how the embodied and material consequences of violent conflict shape long-term processes of post-war reconciliation and closure. Wars subject human bodies to death, disappearance, displacement, torture and other forms of extreme harm, producing effects that reverberate across generations. Yet, despite the central role of corporeality in conflict, limited attention has been paid to how bodily experiences, or the absence of bodies, inform efforts to repair and transform violence, including reconciliation initiatives. Focusing on the unresolved issue of missing persons, this article explores how the absence of bodies constrains or enables possibilities for reconciliation over extended periods. It does so through an analysis of the First World War's Western Front in Belgium and France, where around 700,000 soldiers remain without known graves. By tracing the century-long afterlives of these disappearances, the article highlights the enduring influence of corporeal loss on post-war social and political transformation.
10.1177/07255136261487203.title: Reconciliation without closure: The long-term legacies of disappearances after the First World War

10.1177/07255136261487204.abstract: The American military–industrial complex is currently undergoing a profound transformation, recasting the triangle of political, military and corporate power anatomised by C. Wright Mills. Anchored in federally directed scientific research and a shared elite commitment to the geopolitical primacy of the militarised national state, the Cold War historical formation of the military–industrial complex was bound by a ‘military metaphysics’ that posited war as the era's defining necessity. This order has progressively unravelled with the shifting locus of technological development to the commercial sector. Pivoting away from the procurement process dominated by the defence primes during the War on Terror, the Pentagon has for the last decade courted Silicon Valley's tech giants and venture-backed start-ups in the pursuit of decisive military advantage amidst intensifying geopolitical competition. While the triangle's institutional orders persist, their hierarchy is now being inverted. Through its growing infrastructural power, ideological assertiveness and colonisation of political and military elites, a tech-capital pole is increasingly setting the terms for the whole. A new technological metaphysics is ascendant, affirming technological supremacy as the fundamental horizon and refiguring the state as only one, possibly dispensable, vehicle for its realisation.
10.1177/07255136261487204.title: Inverting the triangle of power: The military–industrial complex after Silicon Valley

10.1177/07255136261487205.abstract: Geoeconomic competition has returned to the world polity. This paper compares the situation before the world wars to that of the contemporary world. The paper argues that war is not likely to result from geoeconomic competition—though war may well result from more traditional reasons.
10.1177/07255136261487205.title: The return of geoeconomics: How scared should we be?

10.1177/07255136261487456.abstract: Nick Land is a British philosopher who has been leading the Dark Enlightenment movement. This paper examines the philosophical foundations of Land's right-wing trajectory and asks how the digital is integrated into his political economy and anti-humanist worldview. It situates Land within a broader context in which contemporary crises of neoliberal capitalism coincide with authoritarian and neo-reactionary currents often grouped under the label ‘Dark Enlightenment’. The analysis reconstructs continuities between Land's early work and his post-2013 writings by identifying five characteristic motifs that constitute the TOXIC schema, a mnemonic for the five key features of Nick Land's thought: T, the termination of Kant's influence; O, opposition to universalism and humanism; X, xeno-capitalism; I, informatic transhumanism; C, capitalist accelerationism. The paper analyses these five features. Land's position on capitalism as an autonomous, cybernetic, self-organising machinic system, based on Deleuze and Guattari's works, makes his work attractive to Silicon Valley gurus. His xeno-capitalism is a model for authoritarian statecraft (CEO-monarchy and ‘exit’ politics), while informatic acceleration is a project of insulating techno-capital from democratic constraint. The result is a distinctive form of right-wing accelerationism that links digital capitalism to authoritarian political imaginaries.
10.1177/07255136261487456.title: The TOXIC schema: How Nick Land's Dark Enlightenment works

10.1177/07255136261487457.abstract: This article challenges the reduction of blockchain to an institutional technology for lowering transaction costs by interpreting it as an autopoietic system of operational closure. Drawing on Francisco Varela's theory of biological autonomy and Cornelius Castoriadis’ account of political autonomy, it distinguishes between functional autonomy, understood as systemic self-maintenance, and political autonomy, understood as collective self-institution. The article argues that blockchain governance is marked by a rigidity paradox: the deterministic mechanisms that secure trustless coordination also risk foreclosing the indeterminacy required for democratic deliberation. Through the cases of the Ethereum hard fork and KONG Land, the article shows how algorithmic consensus can produce a form of functional sovereignty while displacing the interpretive and instituting dimensions of law. It concludes by proposing the need to rethink decentralized governance as an open rather than closed autopoiesis.
10.1177/07255136261487457.title: Algorithmic autopoiesis and the operational closure of law: The performativity of consensus as the production of socio-political reality

10.1177/07255136261489603.abstract: Functional analysis has often been criticized for its associations with teleology, conservatism and adaptationist reasoning. We argue that these limitations stem less from functional reasoning itself than from the assumptions historically attached to it. Building on Robert K. Merton and drawing on Gould and Lewontin's post-adaptationist critique of evolutionary explanation, we develop Pluralistic Functional Analysis as an analytical framework compatible with diverse sociological theories. We propose five heuristics for analysing the consequences of social phenomena that systematically incorporate actors’ orientations, historical emergence, embeddedness and functional alternatives. The analytical value of this framework lies in reconstructing functional analysis as a pluralistic mode of sociological explanation that accounts for stability, transformation and contingency without presupposing systemic needs or harmony. Rather than reviving functionalism, we show that functional reasoning is already embedded across diverse sociological theories and that Pluralistic Functional Analysis provides a complementary analytical framework for making these forms of reasoning analytically explicit and systematically comparable.
10.1177/07255136261489603.title: Why function still matters: A heuristic for pluralism and ambivalence in sociological explanation

10.1177/14748851261429363.abstract: The concept of sovereignty is often confined to power-centric, state-bound aspects of politics, leaving its normative dimension under-theorised. This article argues that sovereignty cannot be treated as a normatively inert notion, nor reduced to the nation-state. It offers a revised, historically grounded account of sovereignty as containing an abstract normative ideal of political authority oriented toward the common good and irreducible to empirical claims, national borders, or fixed institutional forms. The article conceptualises sovereignty’s normative dimension through the notion of the “normative loop,” which captures the interconnection among sovereign power, the public realm, and the common good. It then elaborates four desiderata that an account of the common good must satisfy to function within this framework. Finally, the article explores the framework’s implications for political legitimacy and autonomy. The upshot is that the value of external autonomy hinges on internal legitimacy, which in turn is grounded in a fiduciary duty to the common good. This provides an alternative to both sovereigntist nostalgia and realist, power-centric, state-bound accounts of sovereignty.
10.1177/14748851261429363.title: The normative loop at the heart of sovereignty: Public authority, legitimacy and the common good

10.1177/14748851261438075.abstract: This article asks how contemporary labor domination is sustained through the organization of knowledge, evidence, and procedure. Building on work in epistemic injustice, it introduces the concept of “processual epistemic burdens,” meaning the cumulative mental exhaustion and iterative cognitive labor imposed on disadvantaged actors who must repeatedly interpret events, assemble evidence, translate their experience in ways that are legible to relevant institutions and authorities, and defend their claims over time. Much of the epistemic injustice literature is oriented to discrete and episodic harms, yet insufficiently accounts for the protracted process by which the oppressed must struggle for recognition. Centering the platform gig economy as an archetypal case, this article shows how algorithmic opacity, fragmented accountability, and adversarial litigation compel workers to become perpetual investigators, translators, and litigants. Reconceptualizing domination as epistemically mediated, the article shows that reducing epistemic injustice in the digital economy requires a more equitable distribution of epistemic labor.
10.1177/14748851261438075.title: Processual epistemic burdens and the struggles for recognition: Epistemic injustice in the platform economy

10.1177/14748851261450181.abstract: What resources does the history of political thought offer for confronting the democratic and ecological crises of the present? Through a reconstruction of the political thought of William Morris within the context of late nineteenth century socialism, I show how he built a vision of ecological flourishing on the foundation of the democratic freedom of workers, which I call “regrowth communism.” According to Morris, only in the struggle of workers for freedom through fellowship is earthly flourishing possible, since mastery degrades both human and nonhuman life. Reading Morris's vision of economic freedom and earthly wealth in the late nineteenth century not only gives us a fuller picture of this moment in the history of political thought, but also a vision of a democratic and sustainable form of life that might provide hope in this moment of dual crises.
10.1177/14748851261450181.title: The cause of labor is the hope of the earth: William Morris and regrowth communism

10.1177/14748851261450188.abstract: Nicholas Smyth's recent argument that political conservatism fails to constitute a comprehensive political theory rests on overly restrictive criteria for what qualifies as political theory. Smyth argues that conservatism fails to provide action-guiding principles when institutions conflict and cannot maintain its distinctiveness when forced to create new institutions. His criteria for political theory, however, are overly restrictive and demand abstract doctrines that exclude practical political engagement. I contend that political theories are better understood as normative visions that orient political action rather than abstract principles. Following Burke's critique of theoretical abstraction and Aristotle's emphasis on practical wisdom, I argue that conservatism constitutes a coherent political theory when understood as a vision oriented toward preserving institutions. By reconceptualizing political theories as visions rather than abstract doctrines, and by offering a more nuanced understanding of institutions as communities rather than mere patterns of norms, I demonstrate that conservatism qualifies as a normative, action-guiding political theory focused on preserving institutions.
10.1177/14748851261450188.title: Is there really no such thing as a political conservative? A response to Smyth

10.1177/14748851261451993.abstract: The average citizen scores poorly on tests that measure political knowledge. Does this suggest anything about whether such citizens are politically competent? In this paper, I argue that citizens are so competent, despite lacking what is typically construed as “political knowledge.” This is because citizens possess a kind of knowledge in common, one that has yet to be taken seriously by skeptics and supporters of democracy alike: citizens have knowledge of other persons, which grounds their politically-salient competence for mutual consideration.
10.1177/14748851261451993.title: Knowing (with) other citizens

10.1177/14748851261454461.abstract: Roads are highly dangerous and unequal places. This paper argues that their risks and benefits are not simply one category of the many benefits and burdens of social cooperation to be considered by a theory of justice. Rather, against the backdrop of a regime of land enclosure, certain sorts of inequalities in the roads are pro tanto morally objectionable simply as such. A system of publicly accessible roads is a precondition for justifiable enclosure of land. Further, the justifiability of enclosure depends on the system of roads fulfilling certain functions for all those subject to the regime of enclosure. This condition imposes constraints on the use of heavy vehicles within the road system. It is doubtful whether existing road systems in fact live up to this justificatory condition.
10.1177/14748851261454461.title: The moral significance of road space: Movement and transportation in a regime of enclosure

10.1177/14748851261461496.abstract: Is surrogacy a form of legitimate work? Or does the nature of pregnancy and parenthood render surrogacy illegitimate? In this essay, I argue that the best strategy in defence of commercial surrogacy – which I call the ‘surrogacy-as-legitimate-work’ strategy – relies on two implicit assumptions and that once we make them explicit, we are forced to see that commercial surrogacy inevitably leads to a conflict of core moral rights. As I hope to show, if commercial surrogacy is a type of work, it is work that cannot simultaneously protect the right of the surrogate to opt out and the right of the intending parent to exercise ultimate authority over the foetus.
10.1177/14748851261461496.title: Is commercial surrogacy legitimate work?

10.1177/14748851261463198.abstract: This paper contributes to contemporary debates in political theory about the power of business corporations by offering a genealogy of the corporation through the lens of a series of historical mutations of the corporate form. Originally, there were two corporate forms, both non-profit: member corporations (today's associations) and property corporations (today's charitable foundations). The contemporary business corporation arguably is a hybrid of both of these original forms, introducing unique commercial features (shares with profit distribution rights that are transferable). These commercial features are largely responsible for the corporation's extractive nature, that is, its tendency to prey on non-shareholder interests. The future of the corporation may well lie in a partial return to the two original non-profit forms. Two corporate forms developed in the nineteenth century can provide the format for such a return: cooperatives (which reinforce the idea of membership) and foundation-owned companies. The cooperative structure is a halfway house between a business corporation and a member corporation (association), and in a parallel fashion, a foundation-owned company is a halfway house between a business corporation and a property corporation (foundation). If we want to reduce corporations’ extractive nature, facilitating the spread of cooperatives and foundation-owned companies seems the way forward.
10.1177/14748851261463198.title: The corporation—a return to origins?

10.1177/14748851261463202.abstract: Public debate and scholarly discussions about a crisis of institutional trust focus on an external perspective: declining citizen trust, indicating that institutions lose legitimacy. While important, this perspective does not capture a conceptually distinct and politically salient form of institutional dysfunction occurring inside institutions that can undercut their trustworthiness. We develop an internal perspective on institutional trustworthiness. It focuses on the endogenous conditions under which officeholders are warranted in trusting that their interrelated actions can uphold institutional functioning. We argue that such warranted trust is grounded in the joint realization of two commitments: (1) to mutual accountability in exercising office power and (2) to the assumption of interrelated responsibility to uphold institutional action. We call the configuration in which these commitments are jointly realized “endogenous institutional trustworthiness.” We argue that endogenous institutional trustworthiness is irreducible to standard requirements of professional ethics. It is a distinct normative standard that specifies when officeholders are warranted in trusting one another under conditions of epistemic and normative uncertainty. This internal perspective matters for political theory because it reveals a specific form of institutional breakdown and identifies a corresponding target for institutional repair that cannot be seen from the external perspective alone.
10.1177/14748851261463202.title: Endogenous institutional trustworthiness

10.1177/14748851261465341.abstract: This article is about a critique of capitalism I call the politics of racial despair, which sought to resurrect a racially defined culture against the impersonal domination of capital. This argument helps us understand an underlying logic behind racist critiques of markets, and I show how the politics of racial despair appealed to white racial identity to reenchant capitalism's decontextualized social relations. I discuss an example of the politics of racial despair forged in the Depression-era American South: the political theory of Donald Davidson, a member of the Southern Agrarians. Drawing on archival material, I show how the Southern Agrarians were part of a transnational politics of racial despair that sought to counter impersonal domination with a return to allegedly concrete forms of life—subsistence production and mythologies of race. Today, we see the stirrings of this racialized critique of capitalism. Davidson's political thought serves as a reminder that not all critiques of capitalism stem from a concern with equality or freedom, but can also serve malign ends.
10.1177/14748851261465341.title: Racial anticapitalism during the Great Depression

10.1177/14748851261467333.abstract: In recent years, states have expanded their formal legal powers to strip their subjects of citizenship. But should states have the power to revoke citizenship? If so, how may this power be permissibly exercised, and how ought it to be constrained? This article argues that some standard critiques of denationalization face some important limitations. These limitations stem from the fact that these critiques fail to identify the distinctiveness of citizenship as a status, and, thus, fail to identify an objection that is directly connected with citizenship loss. To supplement these critiques, I offer a framework for understanding the value of citizenship, which draws attention to the egalitarian functions of citizenship. This yields a novel interpretation and defense of the charge that denationalization is problematically inegalitarian: viz., denationalization threatens to impair the egalitarian functions of citizenship.
10.1177/14748851261467333.title: What is wrong with denationalization: Citizenship revocation and social equality

10.1177/14748851261472308.abstract: This paper explores the idea that technical progress could free humanity from necessity and labour. Taking inspiration from a remark in Arendt's Human Condition , I consider a tension immanent to that idea: the possibility that its realisation requires social transformations that culminate in a world incommensurable with our own and to which our concepts of freedom no longer apply. Drawing on resources from social theory, the philosophy of technology and critical theory, I defend this incommensurability thesis in two steps. I argue, first, that technical progress entails a social dynamic which leads to continuous upward shifts in the level of automation required to free people from work, plausibly extending beyond the sphere of production; second, that this leads the idea of freedom from labour ad absurdum : the widespread automation of human life would render modern concepts of freedom unintelligible.
10.1177/14748851261472308.title: Can technical progress make us free? On the idea of freedom from labour

10.1177/14748851261477196.abstract: Normative political theorists typically view displacement as a phenomenon that entails forced movement. In this article, I challenge this orthodoxy by arguing that displacement is fundamentally a loss of one's place and/or home that may occur either with or without such movement. After developing a series of conditions to explain when place-based changes precipitate ‘displacement without movement’, I contend that there are at least two key theoretical, ethical and political advantages to introducing this notion into normative political theory. First, the notion allows us to identify a common condition that unites the experiences of those who lose their place and/or home through forced movement and those who lose it in their habitual locations. Second, recognising this common condition may serve as a pathway to much-needed forms of solidarity among not only these two groups, but also non-displaced populations. I then discuss how the idea of displacement without movement may dilute the normative status that is often ascribed to displacement, while arguing that this implication is not problematic for my account. I conclude that displacement without movement should be viewed as a pressing global harm which deserves far greater attention by normative political theorists.
10.1177/14748851261477196.title: When home isn’t home anymore: Towards a political theory of displacement without movement

10.1177/14748851261477198.abstract: Despite its prominence in the history of political thought, the analogy between states and organisms has fallen into disrepute. Evolutionary theory, however, gives reason to reconsider it. The Price equation, a model drawn from theoretical biology, identifies specific conditions that facilitate the transition from a collection of individuals to a collective organism. It thereby provides a powerful framework for resolving the longstanding debate in political theory between those who view states as cohesive organisms and critics who emphasize rational individual choice. Our analysis suggests that organic theory can withstand the main criticisms offered by methodological individualists, but only with certain qualifications. Although organic theory is unlikely to apply to large, modern states, it may prove useful when applied to subnational entities.
10.1177/14748851261477198.title: From collection to collective: Institutional conditions for the organic state

10.1177/14748851261479205.abstract: This response to critics addresses the questions raised throughout the symposium on the various issues raised throughout the Greatest of All Plagues . I address some of Cordelli's concerns about Hobbes's empirical assumptions by turning to Tocqueville. I answer Kirkland's questions regarding the nature of reforms intended to rectify inequality—whether practical or moral. Finally, I address Arlen's objections that the book has focused too much on the moral dimensions of inequality at the possible cost of underemphasizing the dangers of oligarchy. This particular concern provides an opportunity to discuss Walzer's Spheres of Justice and the difficulties of walling off inequality from other spheres of social life.
10.1177/14748851261479205.title: Response to critics

10.1177/14748851261479207.abstract: This article contributes to contemporary debates about racial capitalism by turning to Stuart Hall, a Jamaican cultural theorist active in the British New Left and the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies. Hall made two moves to better diagnose the mediating role that “race” and racism played in the crises of post-war British capitalism. First, he adopted an imperial frame that situated Britain's industrialization in relation to its colonial sites of production. Second, Hall developed a “Marxism without final guarantees” that could explain how racialized difference becomes embedded within relations of production as a regulative norm. I argue his approach should be preferred to both formal and world-historical theories of racial capitalism, as the latter can fall back into an oversimplified economism. Hall's conjunctural analysis, by contrast, makes space for a more sustained consideration of both (a) the state and (b) a materialist account of popular culture.
10.1177/14748851261479207.title: Toward a conjunctural critique of racial capitalism

10.1177/14748851261479208.abstract: This essay explores the distinctive humanist method through which The Greatest of All Plagues investigates the presence of economic inequality in the history of political thought. It then follows the various thinkers in the book—from Plato to Marx—and observes that a vocabulary of virtue and wisdom not only accompanies but often underwrites criticisms of inequality deep into the 19th century. In conclusion, Williams’ book implicitly allows his readers to perceive how virtue ethics and criticisms of inequality have only become separated in the late modern period. In the 21st century, their rapprochement will deepen and energize inquiries into virtue ethics and egalitarian approaches to political economy alike.
10.1177/14748851261479208.title: Virtue, wisdom, and inequality: A response to David Lay Williams’ The Greatest of All Plagues

10.1177/14748851261479212.abstract: What is Hobbes's attitude toward economic inequality, and should his sovereign pursue radical redistribution? In The Greatest of All Plagues, David Lay Williams argues that the Hobbesian sovereign must widely disperse wealth, since preserving peace under the laws of nature requires it, and concentrated wealth threatens that peace. This essay challenges that claim. First, drawing on Hobbes's distinction between just and good laws, I argue redistribution is not a duty of justice for the sovereign, only something a prudent sovereign would choose to do. Second, given the acquisitive character of Hobbesian felicity, and given that wealth is merely one form of social power among several, stability and peace may not always be best secured through radical redistribution. Finally, I reflect on the limits of using Hobbes to critique modern inequality, suggesting a paradox: the more extreme inequality becomes, the weaker the Hobbesian case for having a sovereign is in the first place.
10.1177/14748851261479212.title: Hobbes, inequality, and redistribution

10.1177/14748851261479214.abstract: Debates on catastrophic artificial intelligence (AI) risk often frame artificial superintelligence as a problem of value alignment: the central task is to ensure that advanced systems act in accordance with human intentions or moral principles. This article argues that such a framing is necessary but insufficient. The danger posed by artificial superintelligence is not merely that it may pursue the wrong values, but that it may introduce a new concentration of autonomous and potentially dominating power. Drawing on political realism in both political theory and international relations, we reinterpret AI catastrophic risk as a structural problem of power under anarchy. The core concerns of AI safety—instrumental convergence, race dynamics, and loss of control—already rely on implicitly realist assumptions about survival, self-help, and the pursuit of power. Yet proposed solutions often retreat into moralism, asking states, firms, or machines to behave ethically without sufficiently altering the incentives that drive competitive acceleration. Against both moralistic reassurance and fatalistic resignation, we argue that realism offers a constructive response. Fear can coordinate divided actors when a threat is perceived as immediate, symmetric, and visible. Artificial superintelligence plausibly satisfies the first two conditions: current evidence of strategic deception and agentic misalignment suggests a shortening temporal horizon, while loss-of-control dynamics would expose even first movers to subordination. What is missing is political visibility. The task of AI governance is therefore to create common knowledge of ASI as a prospective hegemonic threat through shared evaluations, mandatory incident reporting, and institutionalized transparency of peril. The aim is not to moralize machines, but to organize power before it becomes uncontrollable.
10.1177/14748851261479214.title: Fear, power, and superintelligence: A realist reframing of AI catastrophic risk

10.1177/14748851261479217.abstract: In recent years, amidst the rise of authoritarianism and other injustices, political theorists are reevaluating the normative boundaries of political disobedience. This review compares and evaluates two recent contributions to this effort from Avia Pasternak and William E. Scheuerman. It identifies shared features such as the importance of democratic equality and the instrumental value of disobedience before explaining how they disagree about the concept and permissibility of violence. The review concludes that ultimately the fundamental divide between the authors is not whether citizens may ever use violence in defense of their basic rights and interests, but where and when the conditions obtain for permissibly doing so.
10.1177/14748851261479217.title: When, where, and how may citizens be violent?

10.1177/14748851261481500.abstract: This essay is a response to David Lay Williams’ reading of Plato’s political thought, in his book The Greatest of All Plagues: How Economic Inequality Shaped Political Thought from Plato to Marx . The review essay asks three questions: Does Williams see among practitioners of contemporary political thinking any sign of a return to the deeper moral and philosophical aspects of political theory and any sign of a move toward expanding on the safer statistical approaches he himself diagnoses as insufficient? Of the two modes of responding to radical inequality, the imposition of practical impediments to acquiring massive wealth versus the re-education of the population toward an attitude that does not value the excessive accumulation of wealth, does Williams see across the canon of thinkers he treats here any general preference for one over the other? And lastly, in response to Plato’s apparent observation of a tendency in human life to lose sight of the whole of the political community one exists in and to focus on smaller horizons of concern, are there any strategies in Plato or in the other thinkers he treats, that Williams would suggest are valuable in combatting this tendency?
10.1177/14748851261481500.title: On Williams on Plato

10.1177/14748851261481502.abstract: Introduction to the Symposium on Williams's The Greatest of All Plagues.
10.1177/14748851261481502.title: Introduction

10.1215/01903659-12297922.abstract: This article examines how post-1945 historiographic writings from France and Korea figure the anti-national “collaborator.” The transnational figuration and circulation of the collaborator reinforce its unique, constitutive role within networked nationalist formations. This article sketches a dialectics of the collaborator as a phenomenon that accounts for both the othering and the incorporation of this anti-national figure into contemporary nation-foundation narratives. Key theorizations from Jean-Paul Sartre, Henry Rousso, Im Chong-guk, and others have transformed collaboration as a postwar problem into the collaborator, a figure-object onto which nationalist anxieties are inscribed across different political affiliations. Tracing eras of remembrance, forgetting, and obsession, this article demonstrates that rhetorical figurations shape collective, cultural perceptions of who collaborators are and what they do for the contemporary nation.
10.1215/01903659-12297922.title: Exhuming the Collaborator

10.1215/01903659-12297935.abstract: This interview with literary critic Anna Kornbluh was conducted on October 18, 2024, in conjunction with her delivery of the 2024–25 Babcock Lecture at Hartwick College. With her most recent book, Immediacy; or, The Style of Too Late Capitalism (2024), Kornbluh has established herself as one of the most insightful and important critics of contemporary culture. In this conversation, she reflects on how she came to literary studies, the strangeness of realism, dialectical reading, and the role of style in literary criticism. Kornbluh also discusses political formalism and the value of institutions, the term neoliberalism, social media, the relationship between organizing and literary study, recent projects on climate counteraesthetics and middlebrow aesthetics, and the political realities of late 2024.
10.1215/01903659-12297935.title: Art Is for Everybody: An Interview with Anna Kornbluh

10.1215/01903659-12297948.abstract: This article examines the colonial genealogies of anti-immigrant discourse in France through the case of Éric Zemmour, one of France's most influential nativist politicians. It tracks the permutations of nativist discourse in Zemmour's writings, from his little-known 2008 novel Petit frère (Little Brother) to his best-selling essay La France n'a pas dit son dernier mot (France Has Not Had Its Last Word), which propelled his 2022 presidential run. What emerges from this case study is a fascinating glimpse into the colonial production of French nativism, from colonial Algeria to postcolonial France. In conclusion, the article turns to a controversial text that argues for a common recognition of the bifurcated indigeneity of Muslims and Jews of the Maghreb as a first step in claiming political belonging in postcolonial France, against French nativism: Houria Bouteldja's Whites, Jews, and Us (2016).
10.1215/01903659-12297948.title: Éric Zemmour and the Ambiguities of Indigeneity

10.1353/hph.2026.a986602.abstract: : A widespread view has it that, for Aristotle, perception's psychological and physiological aspects are phenomenal consciousness and its underlying material basis. I argue on the contrary that they are judgment/discrimination and receptivity: in virtue of our sense organs, we are receptive to objects of perception; in virtue of our souls, we judge or discriminate these objects. In effect, Aristotle divides perception's active and passive aspects between soul and body. I defend this view with special attention to Aristotle's claim that our senses receive form without matter in perception.
10.1353/hph.2026.a986602.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a986602.title: Soul and Body in Aristotle's Theory of Perception

10.1353/hph.2026.a986603.abstract: : The philosophers' dictum in Maimonides's Guide of the Perplexed I.68 has been classically read as Maimonides's own opinion that God's intellect in act is identical to the intellecting subject in act and intellectum in act, no different from a human intellect in act. This reading of the chapter generates multiple puzzles and contradicts Maimonides's views elsewhere. I argue instead that the chapter is Maimonides's skeptical critique of the philosophers' (not his own) conception of God's intellect, that careful analysis shows that Maimonides presents four differences between the human and divine intellects, and that the divine intellect, unlike the human, is entirely unknowable.
10.1353/hph.2026.a986603.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a986603.title: Maimonides's Skeptical Critique of a Divine Intellect, or the Curious Case of Guide I.68

10.1353/hph.2026.a986604.abstract: : I defend a new interpretation of Berkeley's theory of vision designed to solve a pair of interrelated interpretive problems: the first has to do with visual perception of three-dimensionality and the second with the psychological flexibility of the visual process. Though the first problem has been discussed extensively, previous solutions are unsatisfying; the second problem has not been discussed before. My interpretation breaks new ground and locates the resources to solve both problems by contextualizing Berkeley's theory of vision among underexplored aspects of his metaphysics and his views of human psychology.
10.1353/hph.2026.a986604.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a986604.title: Berkeley's Theory of Vision: A New Look

10.1353/hph.2026.a986606.abstract: : Anatomizing the nature of belief, Walter Bagehot (1826–77) distinguishes between an emotional state of conviction and an intellectual act of assent . According to Bagehot, the various causes of our nonrational convictions can all be traced back to the vestiges of an undiscriminating childhood impulse to acquiesce before all states of consciousness. I argue that he also regards the intellectual activity of assent as emerging from that same original credulity once it has been chastened by the corrective shocks of experience. I further show that Bagehot's picture of conviction, assent, and our omnivorous original credulity shapes various of his social and political doctrines.
10.1353/hph.2026.a986606.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a986606.title: Bagehot on Belief

10.1353/hph.2026.a986607.abstract: : In this essay, I highlight some of the most auspicious and impressive developments in Spinoza research since 2000. This is at best a partial survey, in both senses of the term. First, it is fairly subjective, reflecting my own interests and preferences. Second, given how much has been published on Spinoza in the past quarter century, there are many items that warrant mention that have not been included. Moreover, I limit my discussion to the literature in languages with which I feel safe in assuming most readers of this journal are familiar. I also offer a new, more accurate translation of the herem (ban) issued against Spinoza, to replace the variety of translations that have circulated for years.
10.1353/hph.2026.a986607.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a986607.title: Spinoza: Scholarship Since 2000

10.1353/hph.2026.a986620.abstract: : In the Groundwork and all three Critiques , Kant expresses the hope of unifying theoretical and practical reason in one system governed by a common principle—but does not clarify how he aims to achieve this unity. Here, I show that Kant refers to the "autonomy of ideas of reason" in his final decade, enabling a new approach to the unity of reason. This concept of autonomy, however, is not the moral autonomy of the self-legislating will, nor the spontaneity of theoretical reason. Instead, it corresponds to the autonomy ascribed to reflective judgment in representing both theoretical and practical ideas of reason in accordance with the principle of purposiveness, which I propose as the unifying principle Kant had been seeking.
10.1353/hph.2026.a986620.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a986620.title: The Unity of Reason, Reconsidered: On the "Autonomy of Ideas" in the Later Kant

10.1353/hph.2026.a994284.abstract: : The discussion of friendship in Eudemian Ethics VII is often taken as evidence that Aristotle relies on dialectic in this treatise. I argue that, although he uses some dialectical resources, these are insufficient for fully developing his account of friendship. His approach has four features: the arguments are philosophical, aiming at the nature and truth of friendship; he appeals to phainomena , including both endoxic and non-endoxic claims; resolving aporiai requires substantive philosophical knowledge; and, guided by epistemic optimism, he seeks to preserve what is true in existing beliefs. This contrasts with dialectical argument, which reasons from endoxic premises without aiming at endoxic conclusions.
10.1353/hph.2026.a994284.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a994284.title: Aristotle’s Nondialectical Inquiry into Friendship in the Eudemian Ethics

10.1353/hph.2026.a994285.abstract: : Many scholars hold that Albert the Great favors a distinction theory of the soul and its powers. According to this theory, the soul is a substance, while its powers are qualities. In this paper, I challenge this interpretation. I argue that Albert takes the soul itself to be the power to vivify the body. I also show that, for Albert, such powers as sight, which are qualities distinct from the soul, depend on this basic vivifying power. To this end, I expound Albert ’s claim that the power to vivify is “determined and specified ” by such powers as sight.
10.1353/hph.2026.a994285.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a994285.title: Albert the Great on the Soul and Its Powers

10.1353/hph.2026.a994286.abstract: : This paper explores the metaphysical significance of Leibniz ’s conception of elasticity and its development during the 1680s. The first part is devoted to the discussion of elasticity as a system property in the Hypothesis physica nova of 1671. A second section shows the transition, in the second half of the 1670s, from such a conception to an understanding of elasticity as a condition for the spontaneity and individuality of bodies. Finally, through an examination of writings from the 1680s about the transmission of sound and the elastic properties of materials, I will reconstruct the underlying metaphysical framework characterizing Leibniz ’s conception of elastic matter, namely the idea of a “mechanical mirroring ” which is proper to individual bodies.
10.1353/hph.2026.a994286.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a994286.title: Leibniz’s Metaphysics of Elasticity: From the System to the Individual

10.1353/hph.2026.a994287.abstract: : We provide the first in-depth analysis of Anton Wilhelm Amo ’s 1734 Tractatus de Arte Sobrie et Accurate Philosophandi by examining the fundamental role that intention plays in this work. Specifically, we argue that the “Intentional Principle, ” which states that everything that exists (except for God) is the effect of an intentional action, is key to understanding his account of the operations of human and divine spirits and his account of what exists (and why). In doing so, we demonstrate that Amo was a systematic thinker who grounded his philosophy in intention. Furthermore, we show that intentions are key to understanding Amo ’s views on what the ends of philosophy are and how philosophical inquiry ought to be pursued.
10.1353/hph.2026.a994287.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a994287.title: The Role of Intention in Anton Wilhelm Amo’s Philosophical Project

10.1353/hph.2026.a994288.abstract: : This paper shows how interpreting religious scriptures contributes to applied Kantian ethics. It addresses concerns in recent literature with introducing principles of practical reason in the historical and institutional spheres. Just as the formal principles of the moral law apply under all conditions, the pure religion of reason is critically applicable to diverse historically formed religions. Interpreting traditions through pure moral religion responds to the problem of actualizing principles of practical reason in the world. For Kant, the final purpose in the interpretation of holy books is the moral improvement of human beings and the actualization of the highest good in the world.
10.1353/hph.2026.a994288.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a994288.title: Kant and the Interpretation of Religious Scriptures

10.1353/hph.2026.a994289.abstract: : This paper introduces readers to a master ’s thesis defended by June Downey to the Philosophy Department of the University of Chicago in 1898. I have two goals. The first and major goal is to show that an unknown and unpublished piece of work from the end of the nineteenth century is, in fact, well worth reading. Downey ’s paper makes useful contributions to the field by foregrounding the importance of activity in Berkeley ’s metaphysics and in making a novel use of his Philosophical Commentaries . Finally, taking on board the usefulness of Downey ’s unknown work adds insights about the project of adding women to accounts of the history of philosophy.
10.1353/hph.2026.a994289.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a994289.title: June Downey’s Thesis on Berkeley on the Will

10.1353/hph.2026.a994290.abstract: : In a recent issue of the Journal of the History of Philosophy , Steven Nadler draws attention to the neglected argument of François Lamy that Malebranche ’s doctrine of occasionalism conflicts with his own criticism of Descartes ’s appeal to a “force of rest ” in physics. Nadler claims that this argument is well worth considering insofar as its conclusion seems to be “absolutely correct. ” In this discussion note, I offer reasons to doubt that Lamy is in fact correct in charging that there is an internal tension on this point in Malebranche ’s system. I also briefly consider the significance of Malebranche ’s critique of Descartes for early modern Cartesian physics.
10.1353/hph.2026.a994290.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a994290.title: Lamy, Malebranche, and the Force of Rest: Reply to Nadler

10.1353/hph.2026.a994291.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
10.1353/hph.2026.a994291.title: Response to Tad Schmaltz, “Lamy, Malebranche, and the Force of Rest: Reply to Nadler ”
