10.1353/sor.2026.a1000062.title: Disrupting Death: Technology, Grief, and the Afterlife. Guest Editors’ Introduction

10.1353/sor.2026.a1000063.abstract: : Digital grief applications, powered by generative artificial intelligence (AI), are coming on the market. How they will be received and used is a question not just of the technologies themselves and their affordances but also of the distinctive environment into which they are introduced. At present, this milieu is characterized by a highly psychologized understanding of grief and approach to mourning. It has taken shape over three time periods, from roughly the 1920s to today. First, socially prescribed grief roles and rituals steadily disappeared. Next, a Freudian science of grief work arose, which was subsequently replaced by a “new work of mourning.” The new work, currently normative, is centered on unique experience, personal storytelling, and continuing bonds with the deceased. The change has created a fertile context for AI-powered grieftech, and the article concludes with reflections on the new grief work and tech interaction.
10.1353/sor.2026.a1000063.title: Mourning Becomes Electric: Grief Without Ritual in the Age of AI

10.1353/sor.2026.a1000064.abstract: : My essay examines the growing role of social media in shaping the experience of grief and the construction of memory. It analyzes the narrative forms through which mourning is expressed online, giving rise to what is commonly called “online mourning.” These practices transform the traditional symbolic relationship between the presence and absence of the deceased by creating a public space where digital traces of the dead—such as their social media profiles—remain visible. Social media can thus function both as a symbolic bridge between the living and the afterlife and as a place where communities of mourners form around shared grief. These “thanatechnological” practices intersect with emerging rituals, such as QR codes on graves or virtual cemeteries, giving mourning a new public dimension.
10.1353/sor.2026.a1000064.title: Social Media as Thanatechnology

10.1353/sor.2026.a1000065.abstract: : Tech companies offering generative AI chatbots suggest that bereavement care can be supplemented or even replaced by a machine. To explore this claim, we conducted 25 interviews with grief-care professionals, including psychotherapists, chaplains, and grief group leaders, asking what counts as proper or full care and what persons require in the aftermath of loss. Situated against a troubling cultural backdrop of declining rituals, social isolation, and death denial, the professionals emphasized that grief is not a problem to be solved or a program of steps but a deeply human experience to be lived in the company of others. Supportive “witnesses,” they argued, are irreplaceable in the face of loss. Automated systems may provide limited benefits under certain circumstances, but genuine human care—embodied, attentive, discerning—cannot be outsourced.
10.1353/sor.2026.a1000065.title: Grief and Grief Technologies: Can Care Be Automated?

10.1353/sor.2026.a1000066.abstract: : In the face of shifts to a high-aging/low-fertility population, a post-growth economy, and a trend toward solo sociality, the family system that once handled mortuary care in Japan is coming undone. In this “era of dead without family,” a new wave of businesses, services, and initiatives is emerging to offer ending plans not dependent on kin or the family grave. The essay explores two different trends in Japan’s new ending industry ( shūkatsu ). One is the anticipatory planning that individuals are enjoined to take up ahead of time to avoid winding up in a plot for the disconnected in death. The other is new-style urban columbaria, high-tech and high-rise, that are becoming increasingly popular for even the reinterment of ancestral remains. Considering how the socio-ontology for honoring the dead is getting redesigned, the essay argues for a social imagination emerging here with potentially radical implications for the living.
10.1353/sor.2026.a1000066.title: Redesigning Deathcare in an Era of Family-less Dead: Case Study—Japan

10.1353/sor.2026.a1000067.abstract: : The contemporary condition is experienced by many as despair. Whether as a response to climate change, the threat of nuclear war, or the possibility of AI Armageddon, many people—and especially young persons—no longer believe that they have any possible future. The response to these looming catastrophes is too often posed in technoscientific terms that not only threaten to hasten our collective demise but also provide no values around which hope could be enacted. This essay explores how secular immortalists offer an extreme example of just this approach and the pseudoconception of hope it expresses.
10.1353/sor.2026.a1000067.title: The Ends of Life: Catastrophism, Immortalism, Hope

10.1353/sor.2026.a1000068.abstract: : Transhumanism posits humanity’s evolution by technological means. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, nano-technology, and genetics have shifted it toward the center of academic discourse and mainstream culture. Embraced by Silicon Valley billionaires as well as scholars, transhumanism comprises a full-blown movement. It shares features with Christian soteriology and is sometimes called a “techno-religion” or “secular theology.” It rejects the supernatural, however, arguing that technology will deliver humanity from death. An aggressively futurist mode of thought, transhumanism nevertheless has origins in the medieval past. In seeking to disavow these roots, it has inadvertently defined itself against them.
10.1353/sor.2026.a1000068.title: What Remains? Transhumanism’s Excarnate Future and Medieval Past

10.1353/sor.2026.a1000069.abstract: : This article gives a philosophical analysis of the nature and value of ghostbots, artificial intelligence simulations of the dead. We identify a pervasive and revealing ambiguity in how ghostbots are described by tech companies. They are both radical new technologies that preserve the “essence” of the dead and enable continuing “relationships” with them, and mere entertainment or memory aids that are comparable to photographs or recordings. We argue that this ambiguity is not accidental. Illusion plays an essential role in how ghostbots operate, and by their very nature they invite psychological conflict in users. We explore serious concerns raised by this dynamic for mourning, remembrance, and the good of grieving persons.
10.1353/sor.2026.a1000069.title: “It Feels Like, Almost, He’s Here”: On Simulating the Dead with AI

10.1353/sor.2026.a1000070.abstract: : Using speculative fiction as a cultural probe, this essay critiques “deathbots” as extensions of late neoliberal capitalism. By examining Black Mirror , Upload , and The Final Cut , I make the case that these stories demonstrate a colonization of grief where the dead become extractable data for profit and the bereaved become dependent users. The essay draws on Homi Bhabha’s concept of mimicry and Sherry Turkle’s “ELIZA effect” to show how artificial intelligence simulacra trap mourners in loops of sycophantic affirmation that interfere with real grief. These technologies, I argue, foster a “crisis of narration,” the inability to achieve the temporal closure necessary to mark an end to grief and transform the raw data of loss into shared meaning. Ultimately, digital afterlives foster emotional stasis rather than healing, necessitating a critical recovery of memory and communal rituals in an era of algorithmic intimacy.
10.1353/sor.2026.a1000070.title: Digital Necromancy and the Fictional Imaginary: Speculative Probes into Deathbots and the Neoliberal Afterlife

10.1353/sor.2026.a1000071.abstract: : The longing to speak to the beloved beyond death is humanity’s oldest yearning. I describe a modern phenomenon, the ghostbot, an artificial intelligence reconstruction of a human person, “created” by using text and images left behind after a person has died. Often this data is generated by a willing participant, who, knowing they are dying, wishes to memorialize themself. Most common, however, are postmortem ghostbots, also called “grief-bots,” which are sold as commodities to mourners by companies that then cobble together a semblance of an existent being from left-behind texts, social media posts, and images, and which are capable of interactive “speech” with the living. This article turns to the rabbinic medieval and modern philosophic texts to consider a normative response to the phenomenon.
10.1353/sor.2026.a1000071.title: Seeking the Witch of Endor: Ghostbots and the Presence of Absence in Jewish Thought

10.1353/sor.2026.a1000072.abstract: : Griefbots promise mourners either help to deal with their grief or an ongoing connection to the deceased. By providing a technological mediation of the relationship to death, these technologies threaten to come into conflict with religious practices of mourning. This article examines a similar conflict in which early Christians sought to transform Greco-Roman mourning practices. Christians demanded an affective transformation of grief into feelings of longing and a shift in graveside feasts into an opportunity for prayer and alms. This older encounter between cultural and religious practices can inform an analysis of the concerns and opportunities contemporary Christians might discern in new technologies of mourning.
10.1353/sor.2026.a1000072.title: Blessed Are They Who Mourn: Christian Perspectives on Griefbots

10.1353/sor.2026.a992283.abstract: : Socrates never wrote anything; he thought the technology of writing was dangerous for the self and the social fabric. That curmudgeonly stance has lately made Socrates a character in public debates about artificial intelligence (AI). Here I return to the source, unpacking what bothered Socrates about writing and whether it really does tell us anything about our technological moment. Socrates's arguments are more complex than you might think—it is not all about the purported link between writing and forgetfulness. What we should take from Socrates is a template for anticipating the epistemic effects of technological disruption.
10.1353/sor.2026.a992283.title: What Socrates Didn't Write

10.1353/sor.2026.a992284.abstract: : This essay uses Michel de Certeau's framing of modernity as a scriptural economy—and that concept's parafictional deployment in Tom McCarthy's 2015 novel Satin Island and the novel's debt to Claude Lévi-Strauss's famous chapter "A Writing Lesson"—to situate large language models (LLMs) in a tradition of writing and textual production rooted in capitalism and transactional practices. It argues that generative artificial intelligence should be understood not as the disruption of writing or an aberration but as the completion of the structural logic of the scriptural economy and that LLMs are very likely the final word on a system of production wherein writing is tokenized and transacted for extraction of value in ways that render the technology's current limitations, such as a propensity for hallucinations, largely beside the point. Lest there be any misunderstanding, this is not intended as a salutary diagnosis.
10.1353/sor.2026.a992284.title: The Writing Lesson Revisited: AI [and | in | is] the Scriptural Economy

10.1353/sor.2026.a992285.abstract: : The archive and the tools with which we now write have definitively changed, particularly since the advent of large language models. Writing with computation now entails something beyond word processing or developing human-authored algorithms to produce otherwise intentional compositions. Since at least the beginning of the twenty-first century, writing has been changed more by the way authors relate to the archive than by direct computational intervention. We are closer to the database than to our libraries. The archive reaches us in a new form with large language models as its ultimate implementation. How writers relate to the archive is crucial. Transactions may be implementational or existential—the former, inevitable and potentially generative; the latter, profoundly misdirected.
10.1353/sor.2026.a992285.title: Writing Implements

10.1353/sor.2026.a992286.abstract: : Have we come to the end of the sentence? This essay assesses the role of sentences in the default styles of the chatbots and takes occasion to consider its historical affordances as a form of exteriorization—one that coordinates linguistic elements and bounds revision. Tracing writing from its non-sentential origins through early modern grammatical theory makes clear that sentences are not the fundamental unit of writing but a culturally emergent compromise between temporal sequence and conceptual simultaneity. Attention to handwriting, word processing, and interactions with large language models shows how vertical layout, modularity, and symbolic substitution interact with sentence-centered prose. Speaking back on behalf of the sentence are Renee Gladman's prose architectures, city-sentences that offer an image of sentence-thinking as a form of life.
10.1353/sor.2026.a992286.title: The End of the Sentence

10.1353/sor.2026.a992287.abstract: : Looking at historical moments reveals key concerns for the relationships between thinking, writing, and technology. In the 1990s, hypertext writing tools reshaped the links between writing and thinking and shifted understandings of agency. In the 2000s, technical developments created new affordances for composing with video, adding to consumer and producer cameras a new device category: the prosumer. The blurring of consumer and producer offers a valuable lens for understanding our current moment with artificial intelligence (AI). Early responses to AI focused on how writing might be used to produce knowledge through the act of prompting. Current developments are marked by the emergence of prosumer tools for AI. These technologies call for extending AI literacy to include knowledge of the customization and system creation possibilities of these low-threshold tools. This approach translates into a model of prosumer AI literacy.
10.1353/sor.2026.a992287.title: Prosumer Approaches to AI: Techno-Social Moments and a Model for Literacy

10.1353/sor.2026.a992288.abstract: : When Vauhini Vara's 2021 personal essay about her grief, "Ghosts," written in conjunction with GPT-3, was published, proponents of the technology identified it as proof of the technology's creative capacities. This article takes a close look at Vara's popular essay to dispute such claims. Further, I read Vara's work for what it exposes about the tensions between specificity and convention that emerge in human-authored autobiographical writing, particularly but not only when it comes to loss and grief. What Vara's turn to generative artificial intelligence ultimately discloses is how personal expressions of grief emerge in and through the real and imagined communities that produce and shape them.
10.1353/sor.2026.a992288.title: Writing, and Reading, with Judgment: Vauhini Vara's "Ghosts," GPT-3, and Autobiographical Expressions of Everyday Grief

10.1353/sor.2026.a992289.abstract: : In this essay I consider the effects of contemporary technological developments on writing. Have digital innovations infiltrated literary genres and critical styles? With these questions in mind, I focus on what autobiographical projects and millennial fiction may tell us about twenty-first-century aesthetics through a mini case study of Molly Jong-Fast's 2025 memoir How to Lose Your Mother and her mother Erica Jong's 1973 best-selling novel Fear of Flying (reissued, most recently, in 2023). Throughout the essay I query the role played by age in the production and reception of writing across genres in our relentlessly digital era.
10.1353/sor.2026.a992289.title: Old Writing

10.1353/sor.2026.a992290.abstract: : Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is having a profound impact on key aspects of academic writing and is threatening to disrupt the intellectual development of student writers. This is due to its ability to automate thought processes alongside some enduring epistemological shortcomings. AI circumvents all safeguards of epistemic authority established in academia and challenges the deepest level of epistemology: the definition and justification of truth. This article proposes a framework for considering AI epistemology in relation to human epistemic development. The concept of epistemic literacy is introduced to help us understand these changes and inform twenty-first-century writing pedagogy.
10.1353/sor.2026.a992290.title: Cultivating Epistemic Consciousness: The Future of Independent and Critical Thinking in Student Writing

10.1353/sor.2026.a992291.abstract: : Writing as an infrastructural social technology has coevolved and interacted with social organization for five millennia. However, climate change is disrupting our intertwined socio-communicative systems, starting with the textual means of identifying scientific authority and making it relevant to government policy. Other textually mediated social systems are being disrupted by the material consequences of climate change and the fracturing of knowledge systems, including systems seemingly distant from climate change. Some of the disruptive pressures may be integrated into current arrangements, but others may instigate more fundamental social changes and newer forms of communicative mediation. Observing and understanding textual changes can help us innovate socio-communicative systems for our changing world.
10.1353/sor.2026.a992291.title: Climate Change Challenges Extended Society and Its Literate Mediation

10.1353/tae.2026.a986556.title: Editors’ Introduction to the April 2026 Issue

10.1353/tae.2026.a986558.abstract: : What happens if you rework the Marxist idea of a mode of production, extending it to a variety of intersecting, nonhuman processes? Well, perhaps, even more vibrant, volatile, and regionally diverse images of ecology unfold. Key examples of nonhuman-initiated modes of production include species crossings, glacier flows, the planetary ocean conveyor, storm production, hurricanes, photosynthesis, and, perhaps, the origin of time itself. In each case, constituents and products of the mode in question are specified, often involving self-organized consolidation of non-human agencies and forces of diverse sorts. The essay closes by exploring what happens when such nonhuman modes coalesce, collude, or collide with human initiated, neoliberal modes. Results include reduction in the supply of oxygen, accelerating glacier melts, probable closure of the ocean conveyor, intense wildfires, intensifying storms, and the expansion of drought zones, all delivered by impersonal planetary modes (such as El Niños, trade winds, a shifting jet stream, the tilt and wobble of the earth) differentially to diverse parts of the world. Such nonhuman modes both amplify the effects of neoliberal climate triggers, and distribute them asymmetrically to polar and tropical regions. The proposal is to advance further beyond construing nonhuman processes to be primarily receptacles of human practices, or even merely highly sensitive to human climate triggers. Doing so to address dynamic relations across such disparate processes. Appreciation of the grandeur of a world, whose self-organizing powers and products extend beyond both cultural internalism and humanocentric economic theories, may grow with exploration of such conjunctions.
10.1353/tae.2026.a986558.title: An Ecology of Nonhuman Modes of Production

10.1353/tae.2026.a986559.title: Arendt’s Eichmann in Jerusalem, a Second Red Scare Text for our Third Red Scare Moment

10.1353/tae.2026.a986560.abstract: : This article offers some tentative reflections on the question of what mode of theorizing might be particularly productive for the critical humanities in the face of the multiple urgencies of the present. Building on the methodology of conjunctural analysis inherited from British cultural studies, and taking inspiration from Donna Haraway’s notion of “tentacular thinking,” the contribution outlines a syncretic and pragmatically oriented “Kraken theory,” which thinks the contemporary moment along radically relational and processual lines, in terms of a cultural logic of impurity, whose many tentacles reach in numerous different directions, and which hence bridges or mediates between oppositions such as high vs. low, strong vs. weak, or paranoid vs. reparative theorizing.
10.1353/tae.2026.a986560.title: The Uses of Tentacularity: Towards a Kraken Theory for Earthly Survival

10.1353/tae.2026.a986561.abstract: : This essay discusses somatic awareness practices created by Elsa Gindler and taught by her students Charlotte Selver, Carola Speads, Susan Gregory, and Stefan Laeng. Gindler’s somatics originated in Germany in the 1930s and 1940s, and her emigré students continued the work into the context of the postwar US Human Potential Movement and into our own time. Somatic awareness echoes between fascist biopolitics, phenomenology, and liberatory turns to the body in critical and political theory, yet the freedom of body-awareness is uncontainable by any specific politics or context. Embodied knowing is not located but empty, beyond our thinking, concepts, and positions.
10.1353/tae.2026.a986561.title: “What Is It You Want to Learn?”: Somatic Awareness in the Tradition of Elsa Gindler

10.1353/tae.2026.a986562.abstract: : This article explores an emerging strain of far-right politics that makes two major claims: (1) that cultural decline can be tracked to a feminized, egalitarian society; and (2) restoring culture (or the nation) hinges upon resurrecting “true” masculinity. What distinguishes this movement is not simply an abstract investment in masculinity, but an investment in the hardened, purified male body as the path to renewal. As the article details, the far-right investment in the masculine body goes beyond a preening bodily aestheticism. Instead, these anxieties over gender ultimately represent a desire to write illiberal commitments into the structure of nature.
10.1353/tae.2026.a986562.title: Sun, Steel, and Raw Eggs: The Far-right Politics of the Male Body

10.1353/tae.2026.a986563.abstract: : Drawing on the Øens Have workshop, a performative experiment in multispecies sense-making, this article argues that environmental political theory remains limited by a sociocentric conception of representation that excludes nonhumans as agents of political articulation. Rather than merely extending human representation to other species, the article proposes a transfiguration of representation itself, recognizing that representative claims already emerge across species lines. From this perspective, the Øens Have experiment shows how representation might become a multispecies practice of mutual attunement—an ecocentric reorientation that not only widens the field of representation but transforms its ground, inviting us to imagine politics otherwise.
10.1353/tae.2026.a986563.title: How to Do More-Than-Human Politics: Towards an Ecocentric Model of Democratic Representation

10.1353/tae.2026.a986564.abstract: : Zoometrics—the shifting hierarchies that calibrate value between the more-or-less human and the more-or-less animal—is a core technology of settler colonialism. Such hierarchies govern life and death, authorizing both violence and care. Drawing on the literature on posthumanism, more-than-human geographies, political ecology, Black and decolonial studies, and critical animal studies, this project identifies strategies of humanization, dehumanization, and feralization performed in Gaza through companion, free-roaming, and military dogs, especially since October 2023. Most acutely, I trace how conceptual violence through zoometrics precedes, and often precisely predicts, physical violence. I write about dogs not to center their suffering over that of Palestinians, but to reveal how species difference intersects with race to rationalize and justify extreme atrocities. At the same time, the dogs in Gaza are not mere metaphors; they are living beings with relations and capacities that matter and resist.
10.1353/tae.2026.a986564.title: Zoometrics and the Dogs of Gaza: Species, Race, and Settler-Colonial Violence

10.1353/tae.2026.a986565.title: Preface to the 2024 Neal A. Maxwell Lecture in Political Theory and Contemporary Politics

10.1353/tae.2026.a986566.abstract: : This essay argues that contemporary feminist political imagination is constrained by the dominance of the “New York circle” in narratives of late 1960s and early ’70s radical feminism. This focus has marginalized other feminist groups and reinforced a “progress narrative” that dismisses all early radical feminism as irredeemably white, anti-lesbian, and anti-trans. In response, the essay recovers the Chicago Women’s Liberation Union (CWLU) as a model of intersectional, grassroots feminist activism. Through archival analysis, it reconstructs CWLU’s political theory and practices to offer an alternative feminist inheritance—one better suited to organizing beyond the state and surviving today’s political backlash.
10.1353/tae.2026.a986566.title: Organizing Feminism: Towards Centering the CWLU in Feminist Political Imagination

10.1353/tae.2026.a993494.abstract: : This essay includes a political repertoire for thought and action rooted in Black feminism that I call a politics of futurity . It consists of four parts: purpose, strategy, tactics, and goal. The first builds on the politics of care that I developed in Reckoning . The second adapts and extends Saidiya Hartman's method of critical fabulation augmented by a notion of political fabrication. The third suggests tactics derived from the folkloric character of the Trickster. And the fourth forwards the goal of democratic redesign and reconstruction, which we can think of as worldbuilding.
10.1353/tae.2026.a993494.title: Meditations on a Politics of Futurity: A Black Feminist Repertoire for Worldbuilding

10.1353/tae.2026.a993495.abstract: : This essay explores the implications of far-Right violence for democratic theory and feminist ethics by analyzing deliberative forums and violent confrontations over Charlottesville's Confederate monuments. The forums exemplified deliberation's best participatory qualities, but failed to prevent white supremacist violence at Unite the Right. I develop the concept of Embodied Confrontation—or assembling in public space to contest attempted construction of a neo-fascist people—to theorize one radically democratic practice that remains available when far-Right violence interrupts democratic processes. Complicating feminist theories of nonviolence, I critique binary violence/nonviolence distinctions and create space for self/community defense.
10.1353/tae.2026.a993495.title: Democracy & Violence in Charlottesville: Deliberation, Feminist Ethics, and Embodied Confrontation Against White Supremacy

10.1353/tae.2026.a993496.abstract: : This article argues that the Islamic Republic of Iran's codified and institutionalized gender apartheid created a unique form of militarized women's domestic role from which grief and mourning became protected, even expected, forms of expression for maternal subjects. Bringing Iran's unique historical and political context to bear on an analysis of bereaved mothers' affective resistance during the "Woman, Life, Freedom" (WLF) uprising, it demonstrates how mothers' expressions of "shared grief" constitute a life-affirming form of affective resistance that not only challenges sovereign erasure but also subverts traditional motherhood to perform a feminist politics of lamentation that enacts equality—revealing a maternal politics that threatens the performative undoing of Iran's essentialist gender apartheid and exposes the fragility of its theocratic rule.
10.1353/tae.2026.a993496.title: Affective Resistance Against Sovereign Erasure: Historicizing the (Maternal and) Feminist Politics of Shared Grief in Iran's Woman, Life, Freedom Uprising

10.1353/tae.2026.a993497.abstract: : Under contemporary digital conditions, political myth operates through memes that collapse the temporal interval liberal deliberation requires. Reading the case of Luigi Mangione, I show how memetic speech acts convert resistance into spectacle, foreclosing the possibility of revolt. Drawing on theorists of myth, performativity, and revolt—from Sorel and Foucault to Barthes, Butler, and Fanon—I argue that authoritarian myths thrive on virality's affective compression, while oppositional myths are metabolized as engagement before they can mobilize rupture. The Mangione phenomenon confronts liberal complicity: when systemic violence is normalized as order, refusing counter-violence may become yet another alibi for sanctioned death.
10.1353/tae.2026.a993497.title: Mythic Violence, Memes, and the Recursive Rhetorics of Resistance

10.1353/tae.2026.a993498.abstract: : Self-defense cases evince a primal scene of political life because they reveal the vulnerability to violence citizens may feel and highlight the power of discretionary judgment by jurors about which killings are excusable and which carry the liability of punishment by the state. This paper includes an account of a self-defense trial in La Plata, Argentina, which the author attended in May of 2024 and an interpretation of the factors, including the framework of "justifiable homicide," public distrust in the police, and empathy for the defendant, that led to the surprise acquittal.
10.1353/tae.2026.a993498.title: Justice in Strife: Argentina's New Jury Trials and the Meaning of Self-Defense

10.1353/tae.2026.a993499.abstract: : What is the meaning of "time" when one is "doing time'? Through a phenomenological analysis of first-person accounts, this article considers the imprint incarceration enacts upon a person's primary experience of time. This is termed carceral time, and includes experiences such as the social death of incarceration, temporal stasis, natal alienation, carceral captivity, and the foreclosing of diachronic agency. Retributivists—including Kant and Hegel—assert that punishment is justified when it is proportional to the crime. Yet, the proportionality of a prison sentence hinges on the assumption that carceral time can be calculated in terms of its equivalency or economic exchangeability to free people's experience of time. In evaluating whether incarceration is just, one must consider the impact it has on the incarcerated person. The testimonies on carceral time evince that incarceration indelibly inscribes the whole of an individual's temporal horizon and is not quantifiably proportional to ordinary 'free" experiences of time. This undermines the concept of proportional time at the heart of retributivist arguments, but also, potentially, the justness of the justice system. This article concludes by drawing on prominent carceral theorists, abolitionists, and critical phenomenologists to consider possible tactics of temporal repair termed 'decarceral time."
10.1353/tae.2026.a993499.title: Carceral Time & Decarceral Time: An Account of Prison Temporality

10.1353/tae.2026.a993500.abstract: : Drawing on ethnography, interviews, and archives, this essay charts intertwined histories of Black migrant labor, Chinese indenture, resource extraction, and race-making in the ruins of South Africa's gold mines. Connecting past to present, it examines the zama zama , informal migrant miners who work in abandoned mines, and the unmarked graves of Chinese mineworkers to understand how histories of extractive capitalism and racialized disposability reemerge, illustrating the enduring force of not only these histories but also their entanglements. It utilizes a subterranean archive of disappearing figures and buried traces and theorizes the afterlife of death.
10.1353/tae.2026.a993500.title: Subterranean Traces: Unearthing Death and Disposability in the Ruins of the Mine

10.1353/tae.2026.a993501.abstract: : In On Populist Reason , Ernesto Laclau takes Freud as his point of departure to argue that populism is not a pathological form of democracy, but its intrinsic rationality and possibility, and already embedded in democratic practices, ideals, and struggles. I delineate three of Laclau's Freudian premises and identify limitations or flaws in his appropriation. In distinguishing between a primary populism and a secondary populism, I argue that both Laclau's conception of symbolic representation and his presentation of the leader's role in group psychology fall prey to a version of sovereign loyalty that undermines independent agency and judgment.
10.1353/tae.2026.a993501.title: Primary Populism and Secondary Populism: Laclau, Symbolic Representation, and Group Psychology

10.53765/20512988.47.2.181.abstract: In the Melian Dialogue, Thucydides’ Athenians famously assert that justice is only relevant among those subject to ‘equal necessity’ ( apo tēs isēs anankēs ). But what exactly does this mean? Interpreters have long assumed it to be a statement of power’s priority over ethics, thus identifying the Athenians as prototypical political realists. In this article, however, I challenge this reading, as well as the ‘degenerative’ interpretation of the Athenian mindset built upon it. I argue that both are out of tune with Thucydides’ ‘interpretivist’ understanding of necessity ( anankē ) and the Melian Dialogue’s intertextual engagement with Greek epic. Together, these aspects of Thucydides’ political thought point towards a more critical exploration of the tensions internal to the position of the Melian oligarchs, who are both ‘strong’ within the city of Melos and ‘weak’ in the face of the Athenian threat. The result is a richer account of how subjective forces interact with objective circumstances to result in intractable conflict and tragic violence.
10.53765/20512988.47.2.181.title: Compelling Justice: Translating Necessity in Thucydides’ Melian Dialogue

10.53765/20512988.47.2.212.abstract: Aristotle is widely identified as foundational to the understanding of tyranny as a form of political enslavement, wherein the ruled are treated ‘like a slave’ insofar as they are subjected to the arbitrary will of another. This article challenges the collapse of Aristotelian tyranny into arbitrary rule by reconstructing what it means, on Aristotle’s understanding, for tyrants to rule ‘like a master’. Aristotle suggests that tyrants and slave masters are akin insofar as they are often driven by a longing for supremacy , a structurally embedded desire to secure a legible position of preeminent standing. The recognition of such supremacy is important for despots because it promises to vouchsafe their security from those whom they oppress. But Aristotle suggests that such desired standing is often internally unstable; oppressed actors like slaves and tyrannized citizens harbour a sense of worth or merit ( axia ) that is incompatible with the despotism of slavery or tyranny, and the repressive means through which despotic actors attempt to diminish expressions of axia among the oppressed can prove self-defeating. This article demonstrates that Aristotle’s insights into the psychological and structural dynamics that attend this longing for supremacy inform his treatments of slave systems found in Sparta, Thessaly and Crete, his insights into political repression under tyrannies, as well as other relationships characterized by asymmetrical power and unwilling subjection discussed throughout the Politics .
10.53765/20512988.47.2.212.title: ‘Like a Master:’ Aristotle on Tyranny, Slavery and the Longing for Supremacy

10.53765/20512988.47.2.241.abstract: Drawing on a comprehensive study of the ‘by nature’ (φv´σει) formulation across the extant Aristotelean corpus in light of the linguistic construction of ‘ slave by nature ’ (φv´σει δOũλς) in Politics I , this article thematizes two separate senses of ‘nature’ (φv´σις) embedded in Aristotle’s general theory of nature-based enslavement: dispositional and categorical. Whereas a dispositional account highlights the sociostructural nature ofslavery, a categorical perspective emphasizes an enslaved person’s pre-habituated traits or natural essence as passed down congenitally and climatologically. These two perspectives end up being co-constitutive in Aristotle’s justification of enslavement. Far from being an internal critique seeking to mitigate the many harms of slavery, Aristotle’s theory thus has the effect of supporting the continuous political reproduction and legitimation of the institution of slavery.
10.53765/20512988.47.2.241.title: Slavery by Disposition and by Categoricity: Revisiting Politics and Nature in Aristotle’s Nature-Based Justifications of Enslavement

10.53765/20512988.47.2.270.abstract: Scholarship on the political thought of Marsilius of Padua has long oscillated between portraying him as a covert democrat or an advocate of aristocratic rule. These competing interpretations hinge on differing claims about his influences, whether derived from the Aristotelianism of Moerbeke’s translation of the Politics or from the civic practices of the Italian comuni . While these perspectivesremain central, scholars have overlooked another crucial context: the corporatism of the University of Paris. This paper enriches existing interpretations of Marsilius’ political theory by arguing for a complementary influence of the university’s institutional structures on his conception of political order.
10.53765/20512988.47.2.270.title: Marsilius’ Defensor Pacis and the University of Paris

10.53765/20512988.47.2.295.abstract: Building on the political philosophy of Aristotle and Cicero, civil philosophers in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries believed that the commonwealth could neither come into existence, nor subsist, without commerce. This article explores this belief, with a focus on French and English thought. In order to do this, it recovers the iridescent meanings of ‘commerce’ in later civil philosophy, including its related terms ‘company’, ‘communication’, ‘society’, ‘conversation’ and ‘trade’. In contrast to its more restricted modern meaning, commerce in early modern thought denoted the complex web of human relations and exchange that led to the formation of communities, from the family and friendship, to trading companies and the commonwealth itself.
10.53765/20512988.47.2.295.title: ‘Commerce’ and ‘Commonwealth’ in France and England, 1550-1615

10.53765/20512988.47.2.326.abstract: Examination of Montesquieu’s treatment of legislators in his Spirit of the Laws provides a new perspective on the scholarly debate as to whether Montesquieu approaches the global diversity he documents there with the attitude of a particularist or of a universalist. As he reveals that previous philosophic writers have served as legislators, so he himself becomes one; Montesquieu offers, in Book 12, a table of laws and corresponding punishments. This is his own legislative act, as it prescribes and does not describe. His legislation is, he declares, according to nature. It is applicable everywhere once peoples’ spirits are prepared for it.
10.53765/20512988.47.2.326.title: Montesquieu on Legislators and as a Legislator: a Reconsideration of his Particularism and Universalism

10.53765/20512988.47.2.349.abstract: This article argues that while the instability and violence of the French Revolution has been overwhelmingly attributed to the transfer of unitary sovereignty from king to people, popular sovereignty was neither conceptually novel nor inherently destabilizing in 1789. We begin by drawing on early modern political theory, most importantly Bodin, d’Argenson and Rousseau, to argue that democracy was understood to be as much a form of government as a type of sovereignty. By tracing successive experiments from mixed government in 1789 to ‘revolutionary government’ in 1794 to imperial government under Napoleon, the article shows how suspicion towards government shaped revolutionary politics and drove institutional change. The Terror and the First Empire emerge not as inevitable outcomes of democracy, characterized by unitary popular sovereignty, but as contingent responses to perceived failures of previous governmental arrangements. By recovering a neglected history of democracy, this article renews the ambition of providing a political matrix for situating revolutionary politics within the longer historical arc of modern democratic politics.
10.53765/20512988.47.2.349.title: Sovereignty and Government in the French Revolution
